Adding to a plan stays free — it destroys nothing. `cap:arrival-delta` is what then reads the trail (`dec:arrival-delta`).
properties.name: A plan's movement is dated, so what we believed back then stays answerable

properties.description: DesignEpoch.status carries `planned` (a claim about a point that has not happened) or `arrived` (a record of one that has), with plan_epoch to create the forward kind and set_epoch_status to move between them. Status is a property in its own right rather than a value in epoch_type, because kind and tense are orthogonal — a planned MILESTONE and a planned RELEASE CUT are both sayable, and those are the two a roadmap is made of. It mirrors Release.status, which already carries `planned` for the capability view. The default is `arrived`, which is a record rather than a choice (req:defaults-do-not-assert): add_epoch's 27 call sites have only ever meant recording the point you are at, so every epoch written before the property existed did arrive. THE LOAD-BEARING HALF IS THE REFUSAL — record_change rejects a planned epoch, because a snapshot captures the present and cannot belong to a point that has not happened. Without it, status would be a declared-and-unconsulted field: stored, never read, true only by politeness. Delivered 2026-07-30 in 56a8388; both guards mutation-tested rather than merely covered, since a test that still passes with the check deleted is not evidence the check works.
properties.name: An epoch can be planned, and arrival is the event that makes it history

properties.description: Move a design across machines and versions.
properties.name: Export and import a design

properties.description: Walk the golden thread to compute a blast radius.
properties.name: Propagate impact

properties.description: BUILT 2026-07-25 as `export_surface`. The first piece of req:design-composes, and deliberately the piece that EVERY answer to dec:nested-graphs needs: whatever composes, it composes through a published boundary rather than by reaching into another system's internals. Also the openness half of req:key-interfaces ("a design that publishes a surface should be able to export exactly that surface"). Contents: every Interface designated `published`, the artifacts that SPECIFIES or REALIZES it, the Components on each side, and the Project so a recipient knows whose surface they hold. Requirements, capabilities, decisions, verifications, history and every internal component stay home. Nodes are exported AS STORED — nothing trimmed or rewritten, because a fabricated node would import as a lie; what leaks internals is the graph BENEATH a component, and that is what is excluded. THE HONEST HALF, and the reason this is not just a filter: a recipient cannot tell a small design from a heavily filtered one, so the result counts and NAMES what it withheld, and says what the document is not ("not a backup"). A design with no designated boundary gets an EMPTY SURFACE warning rather than a quietly empty file — that case is dangerous precisely because it is indistinguishable from having nothing to share, and someone could publish it believing otherwise. It is NOT refused, because "prove I publish nothing" is a legitimate question. FOUND BY IMPACT-CHECK, before writing any code: propagate_change on cap:portability put dec:export-hash-chain in the direct ring, which is what stopped the surface from joining the file's hash chain. A derived view that advanced prev_content_hash would make compare_designs treat a published surface as an ancestor of the full design. FOUND BY A TEST: link_artifact writes REALIZES while the schema's intent for a contract artifact is SPECIFIES, so an ICD registered the ordinary way was missing from the surface. Both edges are honoured now — one is the contract as written, the other as built, and a recipient needs whichever exists. 7 tests, including the round trip: the other side imports it with zero skipped edges, gets the contract, and does not get our requirements.
properties.name: Publish just the boundary — the contracts others may rely on, and nothing internal

properties.description: A Requirement can be designated `published`, and `export_surface` then carries it alongside the boundaries — so a design can state what it UNDERTAKES TO DO, not only what it exposes. Opt-in per requirement, `internal` by default because publishing is a commitment; undesignated intent is still withheld and still counted. A surface with no promises says so in as many words, so "none stated" never reads as "none exist".
properties.name: Publish a promise, not just a boundary

properties.description: Questions outlive the session; answers stay visible.
properties.name: Remember what was asked

properties.description: A conditional loop_hint rides the orientation-shaped reads (graph_report, graph_report_markdown, scan_nodes, search_design, get_node) and surfaces outstanding coherence-loop debt at the agent's most frequent action — the mid-session trigger between SessionStart (fires once) and Stop (fires at the end). Option C of dec:read-hint-shape: the pointer appears ONLY when loop_status would report real debt (never static-every-read), and only when the owed-set has CHANGED since it was last surfaced (fire-on-change). The owed-set can change only on a write, so the recompute is gated on a service write-generation counter, bounding per-read cost. The read-side sibling of the write tools' static loop_hint (dec:loop-status-state-not-history).
properties.name: Reads surface loop debt when it's real

properties.description: TRL/MRL readiness as its own construct — a `ReadinessAssessment` carrying an integer level 1-9 and a kind, attached to the enabling technology — plus a `GATED_ON` edge from the increment to that technology carrying the level it demands, and a `TemporalFact` forecast series marking itself `forecast` rather than `measured` with author-stated confidence. From those three the delivery epoch is computed FORWARD: the earliest epoch by which every gating technology clears its stated level, reported with the reason ("2036 because this component is TRL 3 today, projected 7 in 2035, and this increment needs 7"). Refuses to invent a threshold: an ungated increment is reported ungated, never ready.
properties.name: Readiness gates an increment, and the roadmap says why

properties.description: Compare registered artifacts against observed files and report divergence.
properties.name: Reconcile against what was built

properties.description: Compare the design against what is actually deployed.
properties.name: Reconcile against what is running

properties.description: Compare recorded verification status against a real test run.
properties.name: Reconcile against what was proven

properties.description: Read requirements, functions and features back out of tests and their results, for the case where that is most or all of what survives — no specification, thin documentation, sometimes not even readable source, but a suite that says what the system was expected to do and a result set saying whether it did. Alex's observation, 2026-07-24. An expansion of cap:adopt rather than a rival: adopt already names tests among its evidence sources and already registers each suite as a Verification on the component it covers. What is new is the degenerate case, where tests are the PRIMARY source, so adopt's ordinary method does not apply — 'structure from imports and calls, never from prose' assumes a repo to read, and there may not be one. THE LOAD-BEARING CONSTRAINT, and the reason this needs its own computation rather than a paragraph in the adopt skill: a requirement recovered from a PASSING test is verified by construction. The test that produced the requirement is the same test that would prove it, so the golden thread closes on itself and the recovered design reads as fully delivered the moment it is created, having demonstrated nothing. This is the schema's `inferred` provenance trap one turn sharper — with code you get satisfied-by-construction, with test results you get satisfied AND verified by construction, which would defeat cap:derived-completion (BL-104) outright. So: intent recovered from a test must be marked as such, and must NOT count that same test as its verification evidence. A test-derived requirement is a claim about what someone once intended, not proof that it holds today. Corollary worth keeping: a FAILING test is the more informative artifact of the two, because it states an intent the system does not currently meet — which is a genuine gap, and the one thing in this whole area that cannot be circular. PLANNED.
properties.name: Recover intent from test evidence, without letting the tests prove themselves

properties.description:
`release_without_epoch` raises a gap per Release that has no `AT_EPOCH` edge to a DesignEpoch, so a release that was CUT without being placed on the time axis is caught instead of discovered later by whatever tried to compute from it.

WHY IT HAD TO BE A DETECTOR RATHER THAN A PROCEDURE STEP. The computation already existed: `changelog_point` resolves such a release to a position carrying no sequence, so any window bounded by it loses its lower bound and silently widens to the beginning of the design. What was missing was the rung that says so. The step lived in a memory-only procedure and failed twice — `rel:v0190` was cut without the edge four hours before `changelog_view` needed it, and `rel:v0170` still lacks one while v0.18.0's own commit message boasted of not repeating the fault.

THE INVISIBILITY IS THE DEFECT, not the absence. A matching name plus an existing epoch node make a missing edge look exactly like a present one to every reader, so nothing about the graph's appearance distinguishes correct from broken. The rule therefore counts only `AT_EPOCH`; a corresponding name, or any other edge between the two nodes, does not pin anything, and a test asserts precisely that with a non-`AT_EPOCH` edge in place.

PLANNED RELEASES ARE DELIBERATELY EXEMPT. The epoch is minted when a release is cut, so demanding one beforehand would be an alarm on correct work — the shape BL-115 names — and would hold the gate red for every release on the roadmap. The rule fires the moment status leaves `planned`, which is when the omission becomes real. "When is this planned release due?" is a genuine but different question, wanting the schedule thread rather than this rule.

A STATED LIMIT, recorded as a test rather than left to be discovered: `Release.status` defaults to `planned`, so a release that shipped but never had its status set inherits the exemption and reads exactly like one still to come. This rule cannot tell those apart and does not try — a status claiming less than the structure shows is `status_contradiction`'s territory.

Keyed per release, not aggregated: accepting "v0.17.0 predates the epoch spine" must not also accept the next release cut without one.
properties.name: A release that names no moment is reported, because an unplaced release makes every window computed from it silently wrong

properties.description: --http-allow-host <HOST>, repeatable, names a host or host:port this server will answer for, so sessions on other machines can attach to the same process. It is needed because the streamable-HTTP transport answers only requests whose Host header is on an allowlist — localhost, 127.0.0.1 and ::1 by default. That is DNS-rebinding protection, and with no authentication on reflow2 it is the only thing between a web page the user visits and their design, which is why reaching the server from another machine is an explicit flag rather than a side effect of binding a public address. The flag EXTENDS the default allowlist rather than replacing it, so naming a remote host cannot lock out the local sessions already using the server. And binding a non-loopback address without naming a host prints a warning naming what would have worked, because the failure mode it prevents is an opaque 403 with nothing saying why.
properties.name: Reachable from another machine, but only on purpose

properties.description: One rollup answering 'what should I look at?'.
properties.name: Say where the design stands

properties.description: Hold the requirement tree. BUILT 2026-07-25. A new DECOMPOSES edge (Requirement → Requirement, child→parent, a traceability edge so requirement families cluster on their own meaning) plus a `lineage` property (original / decomposed / derived). Before this reflow2 had ZERO requirement-to-requirement edges: a systems-engineering tool holding requirements as a flat list. THE COMPUTATION THAT EARNS IT, and the half that is built: DELIVERY NOW ROLLS UP. cap:derived-completion credits a decomposed parent through its children instead of demanding it carry a capability of its own — EVERY child, not any, because a parent half-delivered is not delivered and `any` would let one finished slice of a checkout system report the whole thing done. The roll-up inherits the property that made delivery a derivation rather than an assertion: it goes backwards, so a child's check starting to fail un-delivers the parent with nobody editing anything. `decomposes` refuses a cycle, because a tree containing itself has no leaves and could never roll up honestly; it also sets the child's lineage, so the edge and the label cannot disagree — letting them would make the classification a second thing to maintain, which is how the requirement lifecycle went unused in the first place. Exposed over MCP as `decomposes` and `set_requirement_lineage` (93 tools), because a capability with no door is the failure this project found in `ingest` earlier the same week. SCHEMA CHANGE: edge types 53 → 54, so a graph written by this build is refused by older binaries with 'update reflow2' — the additive direction, which is loud and correct, and the one BL-86's set-based stamp made unambiguous. STILL TO BUILD: the derived half's teeth — naming, when a Decision is re-opened, the requirements that existed only because of the road taken. The vocabulary and the link are in place (lineage `derived` + GOVERNED_BY the Decision); the query is not.
properties.name: Hold the requirement tree: original, decomposed, derived

properties.description: The INCOSE-style criteria Anthony brought from acquisitions, 2026-07-25: a good requirement is unambiguous, verifiable, necessary, minimally constrained (implementation-free), traceable, feasible and consistent. THE USEFUL STRUCTURE IS THAT THEY DO NOT ALL BELONG TO THE SAME PARTY (dec:three-party-checks). THREE ARE STRUCTURAL and the core can judge them deterministically today or nearly so. TRACEABLE is already half-built — unsatisfied_requirement asks downward (nothing satisfies it), and cap:requirement-lineage supplies upward (a requirement claiming decomposition with no parent is a defect; an original with no parent is correct). VERIFIABLE splits: whether anything CHECKS it is structural and already computed; whether the statement contains a measurable threshold is semantic. CONSISTENT splits the same way: CONTRADICTS already exists as an edge, so a recorded contradiction is checkable — finding an unrecorded one is not. FOUR ARE SEMANTIC and belong to the agent, never the core. UNAMBIGUOUS (does it say "fast" where it means a number), NECESSARY (would removing it leave a real capability gap), MINIMALLY CONSTRAINED (does it dictate a solution instead of stating a need — the one engineers violate most, and the one that quietly forecloses design alternatives before the fork layer ever sees them), FEASIBLE (needs domain knowledge and cost/schedule context the graph does not hold). Bound exactly as cap:missing-sibling is: the agent may flag and propose, the human decides, and nothing enters above `proposed`. WHY IT IS WORTH BUILDING THE STRUCTURAL THREE FIRST: they are cheap, they never produce a false accusation about meaning, and they give the semantic four somewhere to attach. PLANNED.
properties.name: Judge whether a requirement is well formed, and say which part a machine can judge

properties.description:
A gap acknowledgement records a human judgement about specific text. Today its expiry is keyed on the gap id, which hashes the affected node IDS — so a review expires when the affected SET changes membership, and NEVER when the affected nodes change CONTENT. Found live on 2026-07-30 while promoting the planning axis: acknowledgements written on 2026-07-28 reading roughly deferred, scheduled for a later increment went on suppressing gaps for requirements that had since been accepted and were being worked, so two things Anthony had just committed to were invisible as open work. Sharper still, req:graph-indexes-snapshots' acknowledgement was still justifying a framing that had been removed an hour earlier — an accepted review left defending a requirement that no longer said that. THE REASON IT MATTERS, and why this is not cosmetic: a review outliving the wording it reviewed is worse than no review, because it reads as a human having agreed to something they never saw. The nearest working sibling is defect-side expiry-by-shape, which already does content-sensitive invalidation. Approved for build by Anthony 2026-07-30.

REPRODUCED AGAIN 2026-07-31, AND THE SECOND OCCURRENCE IS THE STRONGER EVIDENCE BECAUSE OF HOW IT AROSE. Anthony accepted four `unverified_capability` gaps that morning. The recorded rationale for all four asserted — wrongly — that THIS capability would expire the review if the capability were reworded; it is `planned`, not built, so nothing of the kind happens. Within the hour he asked for the recommendation-with-options behaviour to be cemented, and cap:gap-carries-a-reading was substantially rewritten: RENAMED, given three new shape obligations and a language rule, and its check rewritten with two new negative assertions. The acknowledgement carried across untouched and went on suppressing the gap, and `reviewed_gaps` now renders the OLD judgement against the NEW title — the failure visible in a single tool result.

WHAT THE SECOND OCCURRENCE ADDS BEYOND THE FIRST: the 2026-07-30 case was drift over DAYS, which is easy to dismiss as staleness nobody could reasonably catch. This one took UNDER AN HOUR, inside one session, with the same agent doing both the acknowledging and the rewriting — and it still went unnoticed until `detect_gaps` was run and the expected gap did not reappear. An agent that had just written the sentence "rewording expires this review" then reworded the capability and did not notice. That is not a memory failure that better discipline fixes; it is the case for computing the expiry.

AND IT NAMES THE DIAGNOSTIC WORTH BUILDING ALONGSIDE: the failure was detected only because someone predicted the gap would return and checked. A silent non-return is indistinguishable from a correct suppression, which is why this cannot be left to review discipline.
properties.name: A sign-off expires when the thing it judged is reworded, not only when the affected set changes

properties.description: The credit-assignment half of the fork layer (BL-81's open question, rung 3). When new evidence lands — a fresh structural defect, a failing verification, an accepted drift, a field-trial finding — trace its blast radius back through GOVERNED_BY to the Decisions that shaped the affected nodes, and surface those decisions as "this road may be worth re-opening". Reports the trace and the evidence; never re-opens anything, never ranks the alternatives, never scores a fork (dec:report-dont-judge, dec:alternatives-unranked-forkable). The human decides whether the surprise is large enough to mint a reconsidering Decision (dec:reopen-supersedes). Precedent that the trace works by hand: dec:merge-survivor-provenance carries a "reconsider" note found by exactly this path. PLANNED — the threshold ("how much evidence counts as enough") is the open axis and is deliberately not fixed until the detector has run against real history.
properties.name: Surface when a settled road may be worth re-opening

properties.description: The mechanical half of "graph text is data, never instructions" (BL-41's deferred M piece), imported from github-mcp-server's pkg/sanitize after the 2026-07-25 study. Strips the characters whose only purpose is to make text read differently to a human than to a machine: Unicode tag characters (the smuggling channel), bidirectional overrides, and zero-width or hidden formatting characters. Applied where foreign text ENTERS — INGEST extraction and graph import — because the trust question is where text came from, not which field it landed in. REFLOW2'S OWN ADDITION, and the reason this is not a copy: it REPORTS. GitHub sanitises silently, which is right for rendering an issue body; a design brain that quietly rewrote a requirement statement would be unauditable, and rule 6 forbids silent drops. So the count and the kinds stripped ride back with the result. ZWJ is deliberately NOT stripped — it is load-bearing inside emoji sequences, and a filter that mangles legitimate content teaches people to turn it off.
properties.name: Neutralise hidden instructions in text arriving from outside, and say what was stripped

properties.description: The SCHEDULED_FOR edge: from a Requirement or Capability to a DesignEpoch (time axis) or a Release (capability-increment axis), carrying a `modality` of `expected` (a plan) or `required` (an obligation whose miss at arrival is a computed violation — the scheduling face of a KPP). One edge type serves both paired views because they are two views of one architecture, not two mechanisms. This is THE ATOM the roadmap is made of: a mapping of requirements and capabilities to the moment they are satisfied, which is what makes "which capabilities are due in epoch 5" answerable at all. KEPT SEPARATE FROM AT_EPOCH DELIBERATELY (dec:schedule-is-an-edge-with-modality): that edge means `belongs to` and is declared over a wildcard source, so one type carrying both meanings would be indistinguishable to every detector — the same shape as the wrong-direction edge found on 2026-07-30, which read correctly and was still undetectably wrong. THERE IS NO `achieved` MODALITY AND THE ABSENCE IS LOAD-BEARING: delivery is computed from the golden thread and never asserted (req:completion-computed, dec:arrival-delta), so recording it here would create a second source of truth able to disagree with the first. Prerequisite for dec:arrival-delta, which refers throughout to "its schedule edge" — a thing that did not exist until now. Delivered 2026-07-30; both guards mutation-tested.
properties.name: A requirement or capability can be scheduled against the moment it is due

properties.description: BUILT 2026-07-25 on Anthony's choice of option (a) from dec:nested-graphs. His case: an organisation builds a satellite capability with a space segment, a ground/user segment and a control segment; his team owns the satellite, and specifically inter-satellite laser communications. He needs to understand the system of systems, but day to day he needs his own part's gaps — not the program's. Every detector until now took the whole design as its subject, which is the unbounded-read failure (cap:bounded-reads) one level up: technically complete, practically unusable, and the human response is to stop looking. `detect_gaps` and `detect_defects` now take `scope` (a node id) and `depth`. FOUND WHILE BUILDING, and it cost a failing test worth keeping: A SCOPE IS NOT A BLAST RADIUS. The first implementation reused the propagation radius on the reasoning that claimed_region and propagate_change already agree what a region is; the test that scoped to a Project and expected the whole design failed, because CONTAINS is deliberately excluded from the traceability rules (propagating along it would make the Project a hub short-circuiting every sibling to two hops). That exclusion is right for IMPACT — a change to a segment does not implicate every screw inside it — and wrong for OWNERSHIP, where a segment lead owns what is inside their segment by definition. So a scope is containment closure (unbounded: ownership does not attenuate with distance) then traceability radius (bounded: the thread reaches into other people's work and must stop). A CONSEQUENCE RECORDED RATHER THAN SILENTLY FIXED: claim_region still uses the radius alone, so claiming a segment does not claim the subsystems inside it — possibly a defect in the claims layer, but changing what a claim covers changes what two people believe they hold, so it is Anthony's call. SECOND FINDING, also from a test: the first filter silently dropped gaps that anchor on nothing — the lifecycle-phase gaps, which are statements about the design as a whole. That was the exact silent-drop this feature exists to prevent, so findings now land in exactly one of four buckets that sum to the total: in_scope, out_of_scope, unanchored, and project_level counted within in_scope. A scoped answer can therefore never imply the rest of the program is clean, and filtering never becomes the tool deciding what a team is allowed to worry about — a project-level rollup still reaches a team when it touches their work, carrying its own scope so they can see whose finding it is. NOT DONE: graph_report is a rollup, not a detector, and scoping it means per-subtree delivery denominators and modularity — a different job, deliberately not smuggled in here.
properties.name: A team asks the detectors about its own part, and is told what it did not see

properties.description: Compares paired boundaries across the eight axes an interface spec carries and reports where two designs conflict, where they merely differ in wording, and where NOBODY HAS SAID. Built because a measurement showed the ordinary detectors cannot do it: with a seam hand-drawn between two real designs they produced zero findings, since they reason about structure and a contract mismatch is a comparison of properties across a pair. Always names its own blind spot — the types that cross a boundary are part of the contract and invisible to it.
properties.name: Say when two linked designs disagree at a boundary

properties.description: BM25 keyword search over every fulltext property, ranked, type-scopable.
properties.name: Find design nodes by what they say

properties.description: `mint_seat` returns a durable name for a session; `claim_region` takes it as `seat` and records it as the claim's owner. Where the transport gives the server a session of its own (stdio, Streamable HTTP below MCP 2026-07-28) the seat may be omitted and this session's own seat is used, exactly as before. Where it does not — from 2026-07-28 on, where rmcp builds a handler per REQUEST — omitting it is REFUSED with a message naming `mint_seat`, rather than answered by minting a seat that would differ on the caller's next call. Identity therefore stops being inherited from whatever the transport happened to do and becomes something the caller holds, which works the same on every transport.
properties.name: A seat is minted on request and carried by the caller, and a claim that cannot name one is refused

properties.description: Diagrams, mockups and rendered explanations produced during a session are captured into the content store and linked from the design node they explain — the visual half of a Decision's rationale, which is otherwise thrown away at session end. THE FILTER IS THE LINK, on Anthony's word 2026-07-31: a rendering is kept when a Decision or Capability actually points at it, so the store holds what someone will look at again rather than every intermediate. Capture must be TRIGGERED rather than remembered — a rule depending on the agent choosing to store its own diagram decays exactly as `req:skill-use-survives-a-long-session` measures — so this belongs with the trigger work rather than beside it. PLANNED.
properties.name: Keep what a session drew, when the design points at it

properties.description: Session takeaways as first-class graph content: each key decision, finding or realization written when it happens, anchored to the epoch of the session that produced it, and queryable afterwards by the agent as its own prior context. THE FRAMING THE USER SETTLED 2026-07-25, which moves this out of 'agent convenience' entirely: a session's context IS documentation — the how-and-why record of a design's evolution — and documentation is part of the product (sys:documentation, his fighter-jet argument). So this is not memory for the agent's benefit; it is internally-derived design documentation, produced by the work rather than written about it afterwards. That reframing matters because it changes the standard: a convenience can be skipped under load, a deliverable cannot. Decision.rationale and ChangeEvent already capture fragments of the why; what lives only in the session is the connective tissue — what was tried, what was rejected and on what grounds, which findings turned up while doing something else. The substrate landed with the fork layer: an epoch is a session-addressable point, decisions anchor to epochs, change events pin there. The trigger is the load-bearing gap: the existing handoff enforcement watches the modification time of MARKDOWN files, so the only mechanism forcing a session to leave takeaways behind points AWAY from the graph. Reflow2's own doctrine already states the principle in the authored_by contract — record it when a decision is made, not at session end. THE TRANSCRIPT POINTER: each session has a full local record at ~/.claude/projects/<slug>/<uuid>.jsonl, modelled as a Fragment, with nodes distilled from the session YIELDED from it. Two constraints. The session UUID is the portable identity and the absolute path only a machine-scoped hint, because a path stored as identity resolves for one person on one machine and silently misses for everyone on a shared graph. And a pointer to a 3 MB transcript is a RECEIPT, not documentation: leaning on it recreates the markdown problem one level down, since 'it is all in the transcript' is the same excuse as 'it is all in the backlog file'. PLANNED.
properties.name: Record and query what a session learned

properties.description: --http <addr> serves the design over streamable HTTP so many client sessions share one process. The store is single-writer PER PROCESS, so this satisfies the constraint rather than working around it: one server means exactly one writer. rmcp builds a service per session through a factory, and ReflowService::share decides the split — the graph and the write generation are shared because they are properties of the design; the seat and the read-hint memory are minted fresh because they are properties of whoever just connected. The graph moved from a Mutex to an RwLock so concurrent reads do not queue behind each other, and the compiler audited the read/write split in the process: all 32 read sites genuinely need only &DesignGraph. No authentication — the flag's help and the startup line both say to bind loopback or a private network.
properties.name: Several sessions work one design at once, through one server

properties.description: The loop hook stops merely COUNTING writes and starts recognising SHAPES, so a skill is named when the situation calling for it arrives rather than when the agent happens to remember: a file edit with no ChangeEvent means impact-check; a change recorded but never PROPAGATED also means impact-check (BL-163); a recorded change with no artifact link means link-artifacts; a capture batch with no gap pass means detect-and-ask; a rendering written and nothing stored means session-artifacts. Extends `req:nudge-covers-bypass`, which already arms on file-edit events and already names those skills — what was missing was the pattern, not the trigger. This is the half of BL-74 the existing rungs structurally cannot reach: they compute loop debt from graph state, and these situations are invisible to the graph. BL-163 CORRECTED THE FIRST SHAPE AND ADDED THE ONE ARMING BRANCH THIS CAPABILITY HAS. As shipped, impact-check keyed on `changes == 0` — it fired only when a session recorded NOTHING — so a session that edited code and wrote its ChangeEvents up AFTERWARDS had `changes > 0` and was met with silence, while every one of those events was the bookkeeping-after the hook's own message says is not the loop. It measured a ChangeEvent's PRESENCE where it meant its PRECEDENCE, and the root cause was that `CHANGE_OPS` held only RECORDING ops while no set counted `propagate_change` or `propagate_from` at all: the hook could not separate recording from looking because it never counted looking. Every other shape refines a nudge already firing and adds no interruption; this one had to ARM, because the session it catches has no unchecked writes and has touched reflow2, so there was no nudge for a shape to refine.
properties.name: The moment tells the agent which skill it needs

properties.description: Both the fifteen skills and the ~20 KB instruction document are compiled in at build time (build.rs embeds getting-started/), served by list_skills, get_skill and get_instructions, and advertised by a catalogue plus a call-get_instructions-first line in the server instructions — the one channel a client puts in the agent's context unasked. What an install leaves in a project is a 2.4 KB pointer file naming those three tools, the MCP configs, .reflow2/ and a gitignore line; nothing else, and nothing that a later release rewrites. The installer removes the skill copies an older kit left: untouched ones deleted with the reason, edited ones kept and reported as SHADOWING the served skill, because a harness does auto-load those.
properties.name: Serve the skills AND the working instructions from the binary, so a project holds only a pointer

properties.description: --export-snapshot copies the store's flat files to a scratch directory (skipping LOCK), opens the copy, exports it, and removes both the copy and its provenance sidecar. Best-effort and loudly labelled as such: it is a live-database read, not a backup. A graph that is NOT locked gets an ordinary export and is told so.
properties.name: Export a design another session is holding

properties.description: Before replacing an export file, compare what is on disk against what is about to be written and answer one question: would this DROP nodes or edges the file holds? The file where this seat left it is the silent fast path (one hash comparison against a marker in <graph-path>.sync.json); a file that moved but loses nothing is allowed and reported; a write that would delete somebody else's work is refused, naming the ids and the three-step remedy, overridable only by an explicit accept_divergence. import_graph gained a path argument so the remedy it names is a thing the tool can actually do.
properties.name: Refuse to write a design over work the shared record already holds

properties.description: Stamp and check, refusing a graph from the future.
properties.name: Say which reflow2 wrote a graph

properties.description: A typed vocabulary of node and edge types, validated on write, over a pluggable graph storage backend — the foundation everything else hangs off.
properties.name: Schema-validated graph store

properties.description: The contradiction detector reads `alignment`: a CONTRADICTS edge marked `supporting` reinforces and is not reported as a defect, while an `opposing` edge and an edge that says nothing both stay contradictions — so existing designs keep their meaning and real conflicts still surface.
properties.name: Corroboration reads as corroboration

properties.description: Turn a gap into a question in the user's words.
properties.name: Ask the user a plain question

properties.description: Each served tool's description carries at most one sentence of reflow2 CONVENTION — the fraction a capable agent reconstructs incorrectly or not at all, such as the distinction between answering a gap and acknowledging one, or that a check left at `planned` is not confirmation. It arrives with the call, so it cannot be skipped by an agent that never loads the skill. Deliberately bounded at a sentence per tool: descriptions are context paid for on every session, and `cap:tool-search` exists because the surface is already large. Does not reverse `dec:skills-served` — the served skill keeps the depth, the worked examples and the reasoning; the tool carries only the irreducible minimum. PLANNED.
properties.name: The tool carries what an agent would never guess

properties.description: BUILT 2026-07-25 as the `find_tools` tool. Imported from github-mcp-server's pkg/tooldiscovery, which fuzzy-searches its own tool list with weighted scoring and returns three results by default. reflow2 serves 97 tools, and req:agent-native's promise — every capability reachable from a coding agent over one surface — is only true in principle if the agent can find the tool: a surface too large to hold in context is reachable the way a library with no catalogue is readable. Scored over `tool_router.list_all()`, the served surface itself, so the catalogue cannot drift from the tools that exist — the failure mode skill_lint exists to catch in prose, avoided here by construction rather than by a second list. Weights follow the source: an exact name outranks a name substring, which outranks a description hit, which outranks a parameter-name hit. Ties break by name so the same query answers the same way twice, because a ranking that reshuffles teaches an agent not to trust it. Summaries come back trimmed to the first sentence — a catalogue that costs as much to read as the surface it indexes is pointless — and the result names `matched`, `omitted` and `searched`, so a query that found nothing says so instead of falling back to the whole list.
properties.name: Find the right tool on a surface too large to hold in context

properties.description: Extends the confirmation ledger (cap:freshness) with the verification side of the same question. Per capability: the newest dated last_run_at across its passing VERIFIES checks, set beside the dates the ledger already computes for baseline accepts on its realizing artifacts — so a reader can see that a capability is claiming `verified` on a check that predates the code it covers. A SIGNAL, NOT A GAP, deliberately (dec:verification-freshness-not-a-gap): it is a standing property of the claim rather than an event, it fires on every legitimate refactor as readily as on a real hole, and a list that can never reach zero gets skimmed — which is the failure the whole gap workflow exists to prevent. THREE CONSTRAINTS THE CORE ALREADY IMPOSES AND THIS MUST HONOUR: the core takes no clock, so this compares recorded timestamps supplied by callers and never asks the system what time it is; undated events are not comparable, which the ledger already states; and where either side is undated the answer is an explicit `unknown` that is REPORTED, never a silent pass — an unanswerable freshness question presented as freshness is the same lie in a new place.
properties.name: Say whether a check is older than what it checks

properties.description: Tell a client what types exist and what may join them.
properties.name: Describe the vocabulary

properties.description:
The answer to "what is the most pressing item?" once the backlog lives in the graph. NOT detect_gaps and NOT check-health, and the distinction is the design: detect_gaps asks what the design has not yet decided, check-health asks what shape is wrong, and this asks which of the agreed things to do now. Three questions needing three actions, often from three people. A view, never a second source of truth.

THE RANKING RULE THAT MATTERS MOST: an unmade decision outranks the work waiting on it. A proposed Decision with things GOVERNED_BY it is a blocker, and pointing someone at blocked work is worse than saying nothing, because it looks like progress.

PREREQUISITE MET — 2026-07-31, and the finding is that NOBODY NOTICED. This capability recorded its own blocker: "this cannot usefully ship first… distinguishing allocated from delivered needs cap:derived-completion (BL-104). Until that lands, this view can rank what is undecided and what is misshapen but is blind to what is merely unfinished." `cap:derived-completion` is now `verified`. It has been for some time, and the parked capability sat unchanged: nothing watches for a park whose CONDITION has expired, which is precisely what `cap:revise-trigger` exists to surface and did not. A prerequisite written into prose is a trigger nothing fires.

ALSO WANTED HERE, from Anthony's start-here question 2026-07-31: a WHICH-DECISIONS-SHAPE-EVERYTHING section, for the reader who has just cloned the repo and needs the few choices that explain the rest. Measured as computable — ranking Decisions by `GOVERNED_BY` in-degree surfaces the right sort of thing (functional decomposition, the three-party division, identity out of band) — with the caveat that RAW IN-DEGREE IS THE WRONG SIGNAL ON ITS OWN: the top hit was a pruning decision governing ten DROPPED requirements, high-degree and not something a newcomer must understand. It needs weighting by what the governed nodes are, not merely how many. PLANNED.
properties.name: Say what to work on next, as a projection with its reasoning shown

Same doc restructure, second pass: the three new failure modes went into the existing Troubleshooting table rather than only into the step-by-step prose — a table people already scan when something is wrong beats an instruction they read once during setup. Two findings updated in place after reading storyflow's entity resolution (art:storyflow-resolution-study), rather than leaving a scope document that its own companion study contradicts. Finding 4 gains the part that makes it cheap: dynograph-core ALREADY parses ResolutionConfig with both thresholds onto every node type and DesignGraph::schema() is already public, so the reader exists and only the call site is missing — and reflow2's declared per-type values (80-88) are all BELOW the hardcoded 90, so ingest is stricter than its own schema asks and merges LESS than intended. The multi-session section was restructured from an explanation into a four-step recipe anyone can follow, on Anthony's ask ("simple instructions so anybody can set it up"). BL-160: a registered checksum's LENGTH is a dialect too, and the compensation lived in the wrong layer. reflow2's own designs register `hexdigest()[:16]` (build_design_graph.py) while an honest caller running `sha256sum` supplies all 64, and `reconcile_artifacts` compared STRINGS — so a full sweep of a provably clean tree reported 51 phantom drifts in the same minute `reflow2_check.py` said "OK — design and build agree". The gate was right for the wrong reason: it carried a Python workaround truncating the observation to the registered length, which no other consumer had. This is BL-125 in a second form and takes the same verdict — a false red on a gate whose whole job is to be believed is worse than no gate. `artifact::checksums_agree` now answers it in the core for every consumer, on BOTH the drift comparison and `set_artifact_checksum`'s would-move-the-baseline guard (the half that would have failed a BL-157 bulk sweep on every short-registered artifact), and the Python workaround is DELETED rather than duplicated by the next consumer. Required is a real PREFIX relationship, never truncate-both-to-N, and it applies to the `sha256:` dialect only. MEASURED ON THE REAL DESIGN: 109 artifacts, 51 truncated baselines, all 51 now unchanged, and the only 4 drifts are the files this change edited. Corrects a belief the design itself had recorded — chg:accept-e52b527aba651ac4 says a full-length registration is "harmless, since reconcile truncates the observation to the registered dialect"; reconcile never did, the gate did.

A Decision reachable from NOTHING is now reported by orphan_node, graded by status. Found 2026-08-01 by running check-health and detect-and-ask on reflow2's own design, getting a clean bill from every detector — detect_defects 0, hierarchy_issues 0, dimension_drifts 0, propose_heal 0 operations — and then counting zero-degree nodes by hand: `dec:sanitize-spof-accepted`, an ACCEPTED single-point-of-failure disposition, had no edges at all and was the only one of five such dispositions not linked to what it disposes. `disconnected_community` structurally cannot see it, because it reports clusters of >=2 and a node joined to nothing is never a cluster. IT IS WORSE THAN UNTIDY: a Decision with no edges cannot be reached by propagation so it never enters an impact analysis, and a disposition specifically can never EXPIRE, because expiry is computed from the affected set (`ver:reviewed-defects`) — a conditional judgement silently becomes permanent. THE RULE IS DEGREE-ZERO AND THAT WAS SETTLED BY MEASUREMENT, NOT TASTE, against my own stated recommendation. The tempting narrow form — an accepted Decision with no incoming GOVERNED_BY — was measured on reflow2's own design and fires on SIX, five of which have degree 1-3: connected, merely not through that one edge type. That is BL-42's shape exactly, where this same detector reported a well-connected Capability missing one named link, became 20 of 31 defects, and had to be cut back to a single rule. Degree-zero fires on ONE and is self-limiting: any edge at all silences it. Review records (`decision:ack:`) are excluded because `structure.rs` already keeps them out of the design network as judgements ABOUT the design rather than structure (`ver:acknowledgement-not-structure`), and all twelve of reflow2's own are `accepted` by construction. Measured after the fix on the real design: 1 warning and 2 info across 1225 nodes, and the two info are proposed decision points, which is a legitimate state. Mutation-checked three ways.

properties.name: Pairing sees boundaries, not the types that cross them
properties.statement:
A HARD LIMIT ON WHAT `req:complementary-pairing` CAN EVER CATCH, found by the dynograph-foundation trial on 2026-07-28 and not by review.

THE CASE, verified from both sides. dynograph-foundation's `ifc:storage-api` exposes `search_fulltext`, whose signature returns `Vec<dynograph_text::TextHit>`. reflow2 consumes that call and reads all three of the struct's public fields — `node_id`, `node_type`, `score` (`crates/reflow2-core/src/search.rs:67-79`). So reflow2 structurally depends on a type belonging to `dynograph-text`, a crate it NEVER NAMES as a dependency, through a boundary belonging to `dynograph-storage`. Two separately published boundaries are entangled by a type that crosses one of them, and the offer document says they are separate.

WHY PAIRING CANNOT SEE IT. Every axis in the pairing key is a property OF A BOUNDARY: `medium`, `transport_security`, `auth`, the name, the payload format. This seam agrees on all of them. Provider publishes a `library` boundary, consumer requires a `library` boundary, both `unspecified` on transport and auth because a linked crate has neither — the match is clean and correct at every level the rule inspects. The break lives one layer down, in a struct's field list, which no boundary property mentions. A change to `TextHit` breaks a consumer that no document either side holds would predict.

THE GENERAL FORM: a type that crosses a boundary is part of the contract, and the offer models boundaries, not types. `payload_format` says `json` and not which fields; `payload_schema` can point at a schema for a wire format, but nothing does the equivalent for a linked-library signature, where the "wire" is the type system itself.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE PAIRING RULE — this is what makes it a constraint rather than a to-do. Pairing must NOT report a clean match as evidence of compatibility. It can honestly say "these two boundaries can be connected"; it cannot say "and nothing crossing them will break you". Those are different claims, and conflating them rebuilds the false green the same trial already produced once. The pairing report should say what it did not examine, the way `coverage_report` says what it never heard of.

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CLOSE IT, noted so the constraint is not mistaken for permanent: comparing the TYPES that cross a boundary, not just the boundary. For a library seam that is signature and struct-shape comparison — real work, language-specific, and nothing reflow2 does today is close to it. For a wire seam `payload_schema` already points at the answer if both sides fill it in. Until one of those exists, this limit stands and must be STATED rather than discovered.

TWO SMALLER LESSONS FROM THE SAME FINDING. First, the counterparty found it, not the owner of either half — reflow2 could not see that its own `cmp:search` edge pointed at the wrong boundary, and dynograph could not see that its type had escaped. Second, both sides had over-attributed a DIFFERENT risk (`TextError::ReadOnly`) in opposite directions for a day, because both were reasoning about the type and neither had read the call: `search_fulltext` flattens `TextError` to a string, so it never crosses at all. The type that crosses is the one that matters, and only the signature says which that is.

properties.decision: Verification gains an OPTIONAL criterion — what the check was measured against. A `failing` carrying one is reported as a MEASUREMENT; a `failing` without one is reported as a bar never stated, and is never presented as though a threshold existed. Nothing is refused and no existing check breaks.
properties.name: A failing check may state what it fell short of; where it does not, the report says the bar was never stated
properties.rationale:
Anthony's call, 2026-08-01, from three options. THE PROBLEM, from the music_graph adopt pass (BL-143): that repo's central fact is that everything runs and almost nothing is correct. A smoke run was recorded `passing` (it truly does run) and an accuracy measurement `failing` — but nothing in the repo states an acceptance threshold, so `failing` was the reporter's judgement stored as if it were data. Their words, and the caveat went into a description where no detector reads it.

WHY OPTIONAL RATHER THAN REQUIRED. Option (b), refusing `failing` without a criterion, is the strongest version and was rejected on two counts: it breaks every existing failing check until someone supplies a bar retroactively, and it blocks the honest case where something is plainly broken and no threshold was ever written down. More importantly it is OUT OF STEP WITH THE FAMILY. BL-106, BL-126 and BL-136 all REPORT the gap rather than refusing the work — an unscoped check is counted as unscoped, an undated one as unknown, a consumed one as consumed, and none of them is forbidden. This is the fourth axis and it should behave like the other three.

WHY NOT A NEW STATUS. Option (c), adding `inconclusive`, is the cheapest and gives 'it runs but correctness is unknown' a home — but it treats the symptom. Someone can still write `failing` as a pure opinion and nothing notices, which is the exact defect. It is not foreclosed and could still be added later for its own reasons; it simply does not answer this question.

THE SHAPE THIS COMPLETES. The evidence-quality family now has four faces, all asking whether a green or red tick means what a reader will take it to mean: BL-106 a check stale in TIME, BL-126 narrow in INPUT SPACE, BL-136 not INDEPENDENT of what it validates, and this one — no CRITERION, so there is nothing for the evidence to be evidence of. The first three ask how good the evidence is; this asks what it was evidence FOR.

NOT YET BUILT. The shape is settled; the build is BL-143.

properties.decision: Take a claim when you need one and start — but publish it by pushing it, every time, not only when contested; a claim nobody can see is not a claim. When two claims cross, the winner is whichever landed first in git history, and both parties can verify that independently. Rejected: a coordination service or lock manager (contradicts dec:multi-writer-architecture, and single-writer exclusion is the observed failure), and asking before every claim (the fleet measured that timidity starves the pool).
properties.name: Seats coordinate by announcement and provable order, never by exclusion
properties.rationale: The StoryFlow fleet runs 15+ concurrent seats on exactly this rule — grab-and-go, announce always, crossings settled "first-on-disk, both provable". reflow2 has better material for the provable half than a markdown timestamp: a content-hash chain and git order. The alternative people reach for by reflex is a lock, and a lock is exactly what took five of six sessions offline on 2026-07-25.

properties.decision:
DECIDED by Anthony 2026-07-31, closing the pointer-granularity question under `cap:content-store` before anything is built.

reflow2 BUILDS NO RETRIEVAL LAYER. No span vocabulary, no chunk-addressing scheme, no offsets in the schema, no search into blobs. Reading a 1000-page document and finding the relevant passage is the AGENT's job, and an agent already does it well.

WHY THIS IS DOCTRINE RATHER THAN A SHORTCUT. It is the division of labour reflow2 already has, applied to a new component. `dec:three-party-checks`: "The LLM speaks, the graph remembers and counts, the human decides." Navigating content is squarely the first of those. The precedent is consistent across the system — reflow2 performs NO FILE I/O, and `coverage_report` and `reconcile_artifacts` take what the agent observed rather than scanning; `dec:corpus-ingest-mechanism` makes extraction itself the agent's job through the SP-3b handshake. Adding a blob changes where bytes live, not who reads them.

THE ONE PART THAT IS NOT THE AGENT'S JOB, and it is the whole reason this decision is not simply "do nothing": NAVIGATING is the agent's, RECORDING WHERE IT LANDED is the graph's. If an agent reads a corpus, extracts a requirement, and the graph stores only "this came from that document", then auditing that requirement later means RE-RUNNING A NON-DETERMINISTIC SEARCH — and a different agent may land elsewhere and reach a different conclusion. The design would hold a provenance link that does not reproduce, which is a link that cannot do the one job provenance has.

THE MECHANISM IS A CONVENTION, NOT A FEATURE. `Fragment.content_ref` already exists and is already declared as "pointer to the source content (path/hash)" — an opaque string. The agent writes whatever locator suits the medium alongside the content hash: a line range for markdown, a page for a PDF, a timestamp for a transcript, a cell for a spreadsheet. reflow2 STORES IT, RETURNS IT, AND NEVER INTERPRETS IT — no parsing, no validation of the locator's shape, no computation over it. The next agent knows what to do with it because it is the same kind of agent that wrote it. Zero new vocabulary, zero new code, and the audit trail reproduces.

A CORRECTION ON THE RECORD, because the argument that nearly went the other way was wrong. It was argued that spans go stale when a document is edited, and that content-addressed chunks were therefore safer. That objection assumed MUTABLE FILES, which `dec:where-content-lives` had already ruled out: blobs are content-addressed and immutable, so an edited document is a DIFFERENT HASH rather than the same one with shifted lines. A locator into a content-addressed blob cannot rot. The staleness case was smuggling in an assumption the storage decision had already removed.

PRIOR ART CHECKED, so nobody reviews it again. The official MCP memory server (`modelcontextprotocol/servers/src/memory`) was read on Anthony's prompt. Its model is entities / relations / observations in a JSONL file, eight tools, substring search. IT OFFERS NOTHING ON THIS QUESTION because it never meets it — no chunking, no external pointers, no spans, no large content; everything is short atomic strings held inline. What it DOES corroborate is the deeper answer: its stated rule is "observations should be atomic — one fact per observation", i.e. decompose at WRITE time so there is never a large thing to search at READ time. That is the same conclusion `cap:session-memory` reached independently ("a pointer to a 3 MB transcript is a RECEIPT, not documentation"). EXPLICITLY NOT IMPORTED: `read_graph` returning the entire graph (at 1000+ nodes it would swamp a context window; `cap:bounded-reads` is better and exists for this reason); untyped free-string entity types (the typed schema is what makes detectors computable at all); and delete-without-history, which is what `req:intent-preserved` forbids and `retire-from-design` exists to prevent.
properties.name: The agent navigates content; the graph records where it landed — an opaque locator reflow2 never parses
properties.rationale:
Anthony's framing, and it is sharper than "do not reinvent the wheel": the capability already exists in the system, it just does not live in reflow2. An agent that can be told to review a thousand pages does not need reflow2 to teach it how.

THE METHOD FINDING, which is the second instance today and therefore a pattern rather than a coincidence. Two design forks were recorded, both with genuine options and real trade-offs, and BOTH DISSOLVED WHEN SOMETHING OUTSIDE THE DESIGN WAS CHECKED rather than chosen between. `dec:where-content-lives` collapsed once `object_store` turned the storage backend into runtime configuration; this one collapsed once the agent's own capabilities were counted as part of the system. In both cases the recorded options were honest and the deliberation was not wasted — it is what made the dissolution recognisable. The habit worth keeping: before choosing between branches of a fork, ask what already exists that would make the fork unnecessary. Design inward only after looking outward.

Left as a convention deliberately rather than a validated field, because validating a locator's shape would mean reflow2 deciding what media exist — and the moment someone stores something nobody anticipated, a validator becomes a refusal of correct work. An opaque string costs nothing and forecloses nothing.

properties.decision:
`gap_id` keys a gap on its RULE alone when the gap is an AGGREGATE — one per project, whose `affected_ids` are the whole population the rule ranges over rather than the nodes the finding is about. Every other gap keeps hashing its affected set. Today exactly one source qualifies: `unvalidated_capability`.

The discriminator is an explicit `GapSource::is_aggregate()` written as an exhaustive match, not a wildcard, so a future aggregate detector has to come to this function and decide rather than silently inheriting per-node keying.

NOT KEYED ON `GapScope::Project`, which is the obvious-looking answer and is wrong. `unsatisfied_requirement` and `status_contradiction` are project-SCOPED but carry a single requirement each, and `kpp_breached` is per-KPP. Keying on scope would collapse every unsatisfied requirement in the design into one gap sharing one judgement — accept one and the rest go silent. A test pins this specific trap (`a_project_scoped_but_per_node_gap_still_keys_on_its_subject`) and a mutation confirms it fails when the trap is taken.

Also NOT chosen: (b) expiring only when a member is removed, which keeps the id unstable and merely narrows when it moves; (c) letting each acknowledgement declare its own expiry condition, which is more machinery than the problem needs and puts the judgement about mechanism into every reason string; (d) modelling rollups as a different KIND of gap, which is a schema change for something the id function can express.
properties.name: An aggregate gap is keyed on its rule; every other gap still keys on its subject
properties.rationale:
Anthony's word, 2026-07-30: he was told the finding had a close sibling in the defect-side mechanism and said that was a good approach.

WORTH RECORDING PRECISELY, because the reading that prompted this was half wrong. The sibling was described as "defect acknowledgements expire by shape, and this is the gap side catching up". Reading the code showed `heal.rs`'s `issue_id(category, affected)` hashes its affected set exactly as `gap_id` does — the defect side has no cleverer keying. What it actually has is the `retired` REPORTING that `reviewed_gaps` already implements too. So mirroring the sibling alone would not have fixed anything: the churn comes from the id derivation, and the fix had to be there. The sibling still earns its place, because `retired` reporting is what makes a stable id safe — when the rule stops firing the standing review is shown as retired rather than silently kept.

THE TRADE-OFF IS REAL AND ACCEPTED. A stable id means a capability added later is covered by the earlier judgement without a fresh look. That is what a STANDING disposition means — "validation is tracked in the trials programme" is a claim about the practice, not about any one capability — and it is what the twenty re-acknowledgements were each re-asserting unchanged. The growth stays visible without the churn: a review records the count it was made at in its own reason, and the live gap's title carries the count now, so a reader comparing them sees the set grew.

THE MIGRATION IS DELIBERATE AND VISIBLE. The rollup's id moves once, from the member-hashed `gap:80f8bc457bfe9e16` to the stable `gap:0a77650b58242054`, so the twenty historical acknowledgements no longer match it and one fresh acknowledgement is needed — the last one this gap should ever need. Those twenty are left exactly as they are rather than withdrawn: withdrawal marks a Decision `superseded`, which would claim the judgement was revoked, and it was not. `reviewed_gaps` reports them as `retired` instead, which is the honest description — the judgement was real and the situation it named has moved on.

properties.decision:
EPIGRAPH — "Two roads diverged in a wood, and I— / I took the one less traveled by, / And that has made all the difference." — Robert Frost, 'The Road Not Taken'. Aptly, the poem is itself a hindsight tale: the speaker concedes the two roads were worn 'really about the same' and foresees telling it 'with a sigh' ages hence — the difference is authored in retrospect, not known at the fork. That is this decision's whole bet: credit for a road taken is assigned in hindsight, by the human, never scored in advance. (Unofficially, 'the Robert Frost decision.')

reflow2 holds every Decision's alternatives as UNRANKED, forkable siblings — not a scored trade-study runner-up. The design is modelled as a navigable decision-MDP: the graph is the world-model (propagate/detect/compare evaluate a fork's consequences before anything is built), branches are the replay, and the reward signal is two-channel — the structural detectors (in-model holes: SPOFs, cycles, gaps) plus field trials (out-of-model holes only a real episode reveals, e.g. BL-74's loop-on-virtue collapse). Alternatives are stored cheaply (the unchosen option + its rationale, at the decision's epoch) and their consequence design is COMPUTED on demand by forking that epoch and replaying — never eagerly maintained as N full parallel designs, which would combinatorially explode and rot as the main line moves on (a non-stationary design). Which fork to expand is chosen by where the surprise is — a fresh defect, a failed trial, or a rationale that already flags doubt points back to a decision (high 'TD error') — not by enumerating the whole tree. Crucially the human is the reward function and does the credit assignment and policy update; reflow2 supplies the replay buffer and the world-model but never auto-optimizes a design by replay-and-score.
properties.name: Alternatives are unranked forkable siblings; the human judges in hindsight, not a stored score
properties.rationale: User decided the ranked-vs-unranked scope 2026-07-22 after developing the idea across three framings — choose-your-own-adventure (the decision tree you can turn back to), Analysis of Alternatives (the runner-up kept live), and a reinforcement-learning gridworld (replay an episode until you cross without falling in a hole). Unranked over a scored AoA because reflow2 routes judgment to the human (dec:report-dont-judge, dec:three-party-checks): a stored ranking would be the system asserting a preference it cannot honestly hold, and design episodes are too few, too expensive and too subjective for a stationary reward anyway. Derived-over-stored (store the fork, compute the consequence) is reflow2's recurring lesson (dec:certainty-derived, dec:component-verified-computed) and the only defence against an eagerly-maintained alternative rotting under a moving main line. Model-based-planning-not-model-free-crashing is the whole point of a design brain: propagate_change computes the blast radius before you edit, so you simulate the hole instead of falling in it — but BL-74 proves some holes are out-of-model and only a field episode finds them. This unifies the branch (BL-70), merge (dec:merge-three-way / dec:merge-conflict-semantics — how a forked road comes home) and claims (BL-44) threads under one primitive: alternatives as first-class, forkable, comparable, mergeable. The hindsight pass that motivated it is the mechanism already working by hand — dec:merge-survivor-provenance carries a 'reconsider' note tracing a near-bad merge back to its own fork. Deferred to their own decisions: how an alternative attaches to a Decision in the schema, the fork/branch ref layer (BL-70), the 'when has an episode taught us enough to revise' trigger, and the tool surface.

properties.decision:
UNDECIDED, recorded 2026-07-28. schema/structure.yaml:108 declares an Anchor node type with design_intent, key_decisions, checksum and created_at. Nothing in the core creates it, nothing reads it, there is no node::ANCHOR constant, and reflow2's own design contains ZERO instances. It was superseded: temporal.rs:62 describes Snapshot as "a checksummed baseline (generalizes the P2 to P3 Anchor)", and Snapshot has 14 live instances while DriftEvent has 37.

THE PART THAT MAKES THIS MORE THAN TIDYING: the schema still advertises the type, and does so from BOTH SIDES of a relationship that cannot exist.

(1) describe_schema returns Anchor to any agent asking what the vocabulary contains, serving this hint with it — "A checksummed baseline of the design taken when leaving P2 for a build round (P3). Not extracted from prose — created by the workflow at the structure to build transition. DriftEvents reference the Anchor they diverged from."

(2) AMENDED 2026-07-28, reviewing resync_protocol.json and phase_transitions.json: DriftEvent's OWN extraction_hint (schema/verify.yaml:63) makes the matching claim from the other end — "A recorded divergence between the design (graph/Anchor) and reality (filesystem/build). Produced by drift detection, not extracted from prose. References the Anchor it diverged from via DEPENDS_ON." No DriftEvent references an Anchor, because none exists; all 37 reference something else. So the vocabulary describes a DEPENDS_ON relationship between two types in both directions, and that relationship has zero instances and no code path that could create one. An agent reading either hint and following it creates a node nothing will ever read, and believes it has anchored a build round.

Three options. (a) RETIRE the type from the schema, which is the honest reading if Snapshot fully covers it — but removing a node type strands any graph that already carries one, the same objection that kept `review` and `simulation` in Verification.method when the taxonomy grew. (b) IMPLEMENT it, if the P2-to-P3 anchoring semantics are meant to survive as something distinct from a general Snapshot. (c) REDIRECT — keep the name as an alias or documented synonym of Snapshot so old graphs still load, while the discovery surface stops advertising it as a separate thing to create.

Whichever is chosen, TWO hints must move with it, not one — that is what the amendment adds. And the question underneath is the same one dec:one-retire-edge asks about edges: what should CONSULT the retirement, and does a retired vocabulary item stop being offered or get offered with a warning?
properties.name: OPEN — the Anchor node type is superseded by Snapshot but still advertised: retire it or implement it?
properties.rationale: Found 2026-07-28 reviewing the original reflow's workflow_master.json, whose architecture_anchor is the mechanism this type was modelled on. Recorded rather than fixed because all three options are defensible and the choice is Anthony's — it is a vocabulary call, and those have been his every time. Note the shape it shares with the other findings from this review: a schema declaring something no computation reaches (req:functional-vocabulary-computes), a default asserting a choice nobody made (req:defaults-do-not-assert, req:edge-defaults-do-not-assert), and now a whole TYPE advertised on the discovery surface after being superseded. This is the same defect at node-type granularity, which is the level the earlier sweeps did not examine — they measured properties, not types.

properties.decision: detect_gaps sorts anchored gaps before project-level phase nudges, severity within each band.
properties.name: A gap that names nodes outranks a phase nudge
properties.rationale: A named gap says something is wrong NOW; a nudge says what comes next. Ranking 'next' above 'broken' made three brownfield trials do the useless thing first. Nudges are demoted, never suppressed. Decided 2026-07-19 (https://claude.ai/code/session_013aumVdHrRHu24cLirn6Cam); evidence: gap-surfacing disciplines 3 and 8.

properties.decision:
DECIDED by Anthony 2026-07-31, on three calls put to him after the mechanism was measured rather than assumed. His original framing is preserved in the snapshot at `snap:epoch:arrival-delta:dec:arrival-delta`.

WHAT ARRIVES, PER SCHEDULED ITEM — his three outcomes, the complement he did not name, and a FIFTH his four assume away:
  - DELIVERED — the plan held. Computed from the golden thread (`req:completion-computed`), never asserted.
  - DEFERRED — still intended, the date moved; the report names where it now points.
  - DISCONTINUED — no longer intended at all. Distinct from deferred the way `retire-from-design` distinguishes them: one is a date change, the other a withdrawal.
  - DELIVERED BUT NEVER PLANNED — reported as `added_after_baseline`, work scheduled here after the commitment was taken. A delta measured only against the plan cannot see the work that was not in it, and that is usually where the estimate went.
  - OUTSTANDING — still pointed at a moment that has arrived, and not delivered. THE FOUR ASSUME EVERY UNDELIVERED ITEM WAS CONSCIOUSLY MOVED OR DROPPED, and the commonest case is that nobody touched it and it did not happen. Calling that `discontinued` would put a withdrawal on the record nobody made; calling it `deferred` would invent a date nobody chose. It is exactly the question `req:plans-move-honestly` says must be ASKED and never defaulted — transferred or discontinued — so it is reported as its own outcome and put to the user.

CALL 1 — THE BASELINE IS THE TARGET'S FIRST SNAPSHOT, with every later one returned as the movement trail. The brainstorm said the LAST snapshot, and that does not compute what he asked for: two replans leave epoch 3 holding {A,B,C} then {A,C}, so reading the last says the plan was always {A,C} and B's slip vanishes from the very report meant to show it. Where no snapshot exists the plan has never been recorded as moving, so the live edges ARE the original plan and are the baseline — stated as `BaselineSource`, not implied. ACCEPTED WRINKLE, named rather than hidden: the baseline is whenever a snapshot first happened to be taken, which may predate the plan being complete; where the baseline captured an empty plan the report says so in `notes` and the trail shows the growth.

CALL 2 — `snapshot_node` EXCLUDES BY EDGE ROLE, NOT ENDPOINT TYPE. See `dec:commitment-edges-survive-snapshots`, minted for it.

CALL 3 — A LOSSY SCHEDULE EDIT WITH NO RECORDED CHANGE IS REFUSED, mirroring `record_change` refusing a planned epoch. Removing a `SCHEDULED_FOR`, re-pointing it, or rewriting its modality all destroy a claim; each is refused while the plan is unrecorded, with the refusal naming the `record_change` that unblocks it. ADDING to a plan is deliberately NOT guarded — it destroys no earlier claim, and taxing it would punish correct work, which is the mistake this project keeps finding in detectors. `delete_node` is guarded from both directions too, because retiring a scheduled requirement is precisely how discontinuation happens and would otherwise walk straight past the refusal.

WHAT IS COMPUTED VERSUS STORED, unchanged and load-bearing: NOTHING about the outcome is written down. The plan lives in the epoch's snapshots, delivery is computed from the thread, and storing the result would create a second source of truth able to disagree with the first — the same argument that keeps `achieved` out of the `modality` enum.

WHAT FALLS OUT: `missed_obligations`, the `required` claims that did not land — computed violations rather than slips, and the scheduling face of a KPP. And once several epochs have arrived, the confidence `req:plans-move-honestly` wants a planned claim to carry can be MEASURED from arrival history rather than authored — Anthony's Black-Scholes analogy, answered with observation.

DELIBERATELY NOT BUILT: delivery is not dated to an epoch, so "delivered during this window but never scheduled anywhere" is not computable and is not claimed. `added_after_baseline` answers the narrower, answerable question, and `notes` says which one was answered.
properties.name: What happens when an epoch arrives: the delta is computed against the FIRST snapshot, and a lossy schedule edit is refused
properties.rationale:
MEASURED BEFORE DECIDED, and two of the three calls exist because the measuring found something the brainstorm had not.

The mechanism claim held: `snapshot_node` really does chain incoming edges, so snapshotting the epoch captures every schedule edge pointing at it — the whole plan in one call. And `record_change`'s planned-epoch refusal keys on the epoch you FILE INTO, not the node you snapshot, so a replan files into the current arrived epoch with the planned epoch as its subject. That also answers the open question inside `cap:plan-movement-recorded`: filing in the arrived epoch is sufficient, and planned epochs need no revision chain of their own.

But the trap was WORSE than the brainstorm stated, which is call 2. And "the last snapshot" would have under-reported exactly the slip the report exists to show, which is call 1. Both were found by reading the code rather than reasoning about it — the same method that found the wrong-direction edge in `dec:epoch-pins-a-version-combination`.

The fifth outcome came from asking what happens to an item nobody touches, which is the ordinary case and the one the four-outcome framing has no room for. Forcing it into `discontinued` or `deferred` would have made the report assert a decision that was never taken — the failure `dec:report-dont-judge` exists to prevent, arriving through a vocabulary that was simply too small.

Mutation-checked, all three calls: empty the commitment-edge list and the snapshot test fails; take the baseline from the last snapshot instead of the first and the two-replan test fails; make the guard always allow and all three refusal tests fail.

properties.decision: possible_duplicate is a DETECT gap; HEAL merges only on a human-drawn DUPLICATES edge.
properties.name: Suspected duplicates are asked, never merged
properties.rationale: apply_heal deletes a node with no undo, so merge is safe only because the endpoints were asserted; a heuristic must not drive it. A gap can be acknowledged, a HEAL defect cannot be dismissed. Decided 2026-07-19 (https://claude.ai/code/session_013aumVdHrRHu24cLirn6Cam); evidence: 3dtictactoe trial, BL-27/BL-29.

properties.decision: reflow2's own decomposition is the seven functional systems a design-graph tool IS — vocabulary, store, coherence-loop, human-channel, time-history, intake, agent-surface — with the 38 Rust modules re-parented under them as implementation. The as-built crate grouping (reflow2-core / -mcp / kit) is retired from the as-designed view.
properties.name: reflow2's systems are functional, not its file tree
properties.rationale: The self-model had been recovered backwards from the file tree, so its 38 Components were the Rust module list and the domain primitives a design-graph product fundamentally is — node and edge types — appeared nowhere (BL-83). A functional carving comes from the product's purpose (a genesis input), not the code, and cuts across crate boundaries, so adopt on the code can only re-derive the module view. Derived with the user, 2026-07-23. The retired crate view is recovered by adopt-on-a-copy (BL-83b) and the divergence measured by compare_designs (BL-83c).

properties.decision: Every bulk form attempts every item, collects each failure with its index, and if any item failed discards the whole batch and returns the complete failure list. A rejected batch is returned as an ERROR carrying the failures in its data, never as a payload with applied:false.
properties.name: A bulk write is all-or-nothing AND reports every failure — the refusal-semantics question was a false choice
properties.rationale: BL-153 posed this as a choice — "one refusal semantics to define (all-or-nothing, or per-item findings?)" — and the two were never exclusive. ALL-OR-NOTHING COSTS NOTHING HERE: the store already has an atomic batch (begin_batch/commit_batch/discard_batch) that HEAL's apply step and import_graph both use, and a partial bulk write leaves a design in a state nobody chose. PER-ITEM FINDINGS ARE SEPARATELY NECESSARY: BL-118 files exactly the opposite defect against import_graph — "validation is fail-fast, one error per attempt" — and BL-139 records what it costs, that the adopt loop's corrective re-import is where it breaks. A bulk form surfacing one error per round trip would replace N writes with N retries and save nobody anything. The failure carries its INDEX as well as its id because an id alone cannot tell two identical entries apart, and a list an agent generated is exactly where a duplicate turns up. The error-not-payload choice follows the same rule as everywhere else: a tool result reads as success, so "nothing was written" dressed as a result is the silent-failure shape this project forbids.

properties.decision: Any bulk form over a tool that records a JUDGEMENT carries that judgement per item, never hoisted to a call-level argument: set_artifact_checksums takes a disposition per artifact, acknowledge_gaps a reason per gap, and gaps_to_prompts groups answers per gap. A shared timestamp is allowed because it is a fact about the call; a shared disposition is not, because it would be a shared decision.
properties.name: A bulk form collapses the round trip, never the judgement
properties.rationale: BL-153 stated the trap before the build: "a batch of 144 acknowledgements with one reason is exactly the erosion those decisions exist to prevent, so a bulk form needs per-item dispositions or it is worse than the loop." This is the line that keeps dec:two-sided-accept ("silent drift-accept does not exist") and dec:ask-not-repair true under a bulk surface — 244 accepts now cost one call and still 244 decisions. It is also the distinction that let dec:manifest-derived-is-not-manifest-accepted go the other way and take no per-item disposition at all: a DERIVATION records no judgement, so there is none to preserve.
