(3) THE GATE EXPLAINS ITSELF IN REVIEW — today the coherence gate fails a build; with github-mcp the same finding becomes a review comment naming the thread ("this moves art:X, which realizes cap:Y, which satisfies req:Z — and req:Z has no verification"), landing where humans actually decide. (4) TRACEABILITY IN THE PR BODY — the golden thread from requirement to artifact, written where a reviewer sees WHY and not only what. (5) CLAIMS AGAINST REAL DATA — claim_report overlaps computed against open PRs' changed files rather than announcements, and dec:advisory-concurrency's "first-on-disk, both provable" has an exact GitHub expression in which PR opened first. (6) RELEASE NOTES DERIVED from the graph — delivered requirements and the decisions in that epoch, cut and attached by github-mcp. THE OBJECTIONS, recorded beside the ideas. Context cost is real: reflow2 serves 106 tools and github-mcp is comparably large, so an agent holding both pays in tool-selection noise — both have an answer (find_tools, and GitHub's toolsets/dynamic discovery, noted in docs/github-mcp-nuggets.md) and neither answer is free. And the load-bearing one: reflow2's proposition is that it works with no service and no account. Any pairing must be ADDITIVE AND NEVER REQUIRED, or reflow2 excludes GitLab, self-hosted, air-gapped and classified environments — which is the population this tool was built for.
properties.name: OPEN — does reflow2 run in tandem with GitHub's MCP server, and where would the pairing pay?
properties.rationale: Raised as brainstorming while looking at how two people collaborate over plain git, so nothing here is scheduled and nothing is promoted. Kept as ONE decision rather than six because the pairings are a menu under a single question — whether reflow2 reaches for a second MCP surface at all — and answering that decides the shape of every item. Worth recording rather than leaving in conversation because two of the six touch decisions already on the record: (1) bears directly on dec:central-host, where the publishing case is named as the strongest argument for hosting a server, and GitHub-as-distribution would weaken that argument without any hosting at all; (2) bears on req:nudge-path-proven, which is accepted work about a notification path reflow2 cannot currently prove reaches anybody. The architectural observation is the part most likely to be forgotten and re-derived: MCP integration happens in the agent's context, not in either server's code, so the whole idea is skill-shaped and reversible — which is also why it can be tried cheaply on one pairing before deciding anything.

properties.decision: cmp:graph is the single store handle everything else hangs off, and it stays that way. The single_point_of_failure warning on it is accepted as intentional, not resolved by adding redundancy.
properties.name: The graph handle is an accepted single point of failure
properties.rationale: The architecture is explicit (AGENTS.md): DesignGraph is 'the single handle everything else hangs off' — one schema-validated CRUD surface so every coherence-loop module speaks to one store one way. Removing it strands schema, search and vocabulary (each with its file) plus the export chain, which is the BL-69 detector telling the truth about the spine. Redundancy is incoherent here twice over: these are modules compiled into one binary (they cannot fail independently of cmp:graph at run time — the same reasoning as the F6 library filter, which cannot see cmp:graph only because it provides no Interface node), and a second graph handle would mean two write paths to one store, exactly the incoherence the single handle exists to prevent. Accepted 2026-07-21 while dispositioning BL-69's corrected findings; sibling of dec:service-spof-accepted.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL — from the 2026-08-01 dynograph-foundation review. Nothing here is settled.

THE OBSERVATION: capabilities form a DEPENDS_ON DAG that detect_defects insists stays acyclic, and NOTHING ever asks what order it implies. reflow2 can say what is scheduled for an increment (SCHEDULED_FOR) and what is delivered (the golden thread), but not what can be started.

THE IDEA: dynograph_graph::topological_sort — Kahn's, deterministic (lexicographically smallest order), returns None on a cycle. Two distinct uses:
(a) A SIMPLIFICATION available today: budget.rs:312 hand-rolls Kahn's algorithm in about forty lines with a comment that says so. The foundation exports it.
(b) A NEW capability: given the capabilities scheduled for an increment, a valid build order — and the frontier of what has no unbuilt dependency, which is "what can I pick up now".

WHERE IT LANDS: BL-68 (TRL/MRL readiness gating) is about whether something is ready; this is about whether its DEPENDENCIES are ready, which is the other half of the same question. Also epoch planning.

CHEAP for (a). Moderate for (b), which needs a scope (a whole design? one increment? one component's subtree?) and a rendering.

THE HONEST COUNTER-ARGUMENTS: (a) is not free — the local version works on string-id arcs while the foundation one needs a Graph built through GraphBuilder, so it trades forty lines of Kahn's for an impedance adapter, and the local one is already tested. (b) risks asserting a schedule reflow2 has no business asserting: a topological order is ONE valid order of many, and presenting it as THE order would be the same overreach dec:report-dont-judge exists to prevent. The honest output is probably the READY FRONTIER (what is unblocked) rather than a full ordering.

Filed as a backlog row on Anthony's word (2026-08-01) — the work is tracked; the shape, especially frontier-vs-order, is open.
properties.name: OPEN — should reflow2 answer "what order can this increment be built in, and what is buildable now?"
properties.rationale: Found by grepping reflow2 for any existing ordering concept and hitting a hand-rolled Kahn's in budget.rs — evidence both that the need is real and that the foundation function was not known to be there.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL — from the 2026-08-01 dynograph-foundation review. Nothing here is settled.

THE IDEA: dynograph_graph::shortest_path (unused) returns the actual Path between two nodes. Two readings on a design graph:
(a) surprising_connections reports that two things bridge separate communities. It does not say through what. The path is the explanation a human needs before acting.
(b) "Why is this node in my blast radius?" propagate reports hop distance and impact direction; a named path is the artifact a person can read and check.

CHEAP: exact, already a dependency, and both call sites already hold the network.

WHERE IT LANDS: this is the BL-114 family again from a third direction — a finding that states a conclusion without stating the evidence it walked. BL-141(a) has just done exactly this for circular_dependency (name the contracts the cycle ran through), and that change was small and immediately useful on real data. The same argument applies here.

THE HONEST COUNTER-ARGUMENT: a shortest path is not necessarily the RESPONSIBLE path — several may exist, and showing one implies a causal story that may not be the operative one. BL-141(a) sidestepped this by naming the SET of contracts involved rather than a single route; the equivalent here might be "the edge types this coupling runs through" rather than one path. Worth deciding which before building.
properties.name: OPEN — should a finding say HOW two nodes are coupled, not only that they are?
properties.rationale: Grouped with the explain-what-you-walked family (BL-114, BL-141a) rather than presented as a new idea, because that is what it is — the third instance of the same shape.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL — from the 2026-08-01 dynograph-foundation review. Nothing here is settled.

THE OBSERVATION: reflow2 uses exactly TWO functions from dynograph-vector — mean and linear_regression_slope, both in dimensions.rs. The depth axis records DimensionObservations and computes drift as a slope WITHIN one dimension over time.

THE IDEA: pearson_correlation and spearman_rank_correlation (unused) would answer a question the axis cannot currently ask — do two dimensions move TOGETHER across components? "Does complexity track defect count?" "Does coupling track change frequency?" Spearman is the rank version, so it survives non-linear but monotone relationships and is the safer default on small samples.

CHEAP: pure functions, already a dependency, and the observations are already stored.

THE HONEST COUNTER-ARGUMENTS, and there are two. First, this is the most SPECULATIVE idea in the batch — no backlog item asks for it and no trial has reported wanting it, so it is a capability looking for a user. Second and more serious: correlation invites causal reading, and a design brain reporting "complexity correlates with defects" will be read as "complexity causes defects". The schema already takes this seriously — the CAUSES edge carries a `basis` enum (observed / correlational / causal / spurious) with the instruction "do not assert causal without a mechanism" — so the vocabulary for the caveat exists, but the report would have to carry it loudly.
properties.name: OPEN — should the depth axis compute CORRELATION between dimensions, not just drift within one?
properties.rationale: The only genuinely unexplored idea in dynograph-vector; the rest of that crate is either already used (mean, slope), already a parked question (embeddings), or thin (softmax, percentile).

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL — from the 2026-08-01 dynograph-foundation review. Nothing here is settled; recorded as a minor idea with a real objection.

THE IDEA: percentile and median (unused, in dynograph-vector::stats) would let surprising_connections report "the top 5% most surprising couplings in THIS design" rather than everything over a fixed score. A distributional cut self-calibrates to the graph it is run on; an absolute one does not, and a design with 100 nodes and one with 10,000 do not have the same natural scale.

THE HONEST COUNTER-ARGUMENT, and it is the projects own lesson: BL-23 established that when a detector punishes correct work, the answer is A DIFFERENT QUESTION, not a tuned threshold. A percentile is still a threshold — it just moves rather than sits still. Worse, a top-N-percent rule ALWAYS returns something, so a design with no surprising couplings at all would still be handed a list, which is exactly the false-signal failure the noise-floor work (BL-42) was about.

WHERE IT MIGHT STILL HELP: not as a cut, but as CONTEXT on a finding already made — "surprise 2.56, which is the highest in this design" is more useful to a reader than a bare number, and asserts nothing extra.
properties.name: OPEN — should surprise and severity be reported as distributional positions rather than absolute scores?
properties.rationale: Kept deliberately small and recorded with the objection first, because the naive form of this idea contradicts an established lesson and a later session should meet the objection at the same moment as the idea.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL — surfaced by the 2026-08-01 dynograph-foundation review, but NOT a new idea: this question already exists as PROSE in docs/requirements-coverage.md ("Note: are embeddings (an embeddings-rs sidecar) actually needed?"). Recording it here moves it from a document into the graph, which is the direction dec:what-lives-where argues for; it does not settle it.

WHAT IS AVAILABLE AND UNUSED: dynograph-vector ships an HNSW approximate-nearest-neighbour index (HnswConfig / HnswIndex / SearchResult, with filtered, batch and snapshot-persisted search) plus SIMD cosine similarity and the whole distance family. reflow2 uses none of it. search_design is BM25 lexical, and the schema carries embedding_field declarations on several node types that nothing populates.

THE CASE FOR: semantic search would find a requirement whose words differ from the query's. It would also strengthen resolution — the duplicate-detection path already has a fuzzy_then_vector strategy declared in the schema with the vector half unimplemented.

THE CASE AGAINST, and it is why this has stayed parked: embeddings need a MODEL, and reflow2-core is deliberately LLM-free and deterministic. An embedding provider at the core would break that, and putting it at the seam means a sidecar to install, version and keep in sync — which cuts against req:thin-install and the whole served-not-installed posture. Determinism is also load-bearing here: two runs of a detector must agree, and an ANN index is approximate by construction.

NOT AN IDEA I AM ADVOCATING — recorded so the question is findable in the graph rather than only in a documentation footnote.
properties.name: OPEN — should reflow2 adopt embeddings and the HNSW index, or stay on lexical search?
properties.rationale: Captured because the review found the HNSW index entirely unused and the question live only in prose. The honest status is "already parked, now visible" rather than "newly proposed".

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL — from the 2026-08-01 dynograph-foundation review. The most interesting idea in the batch and the least evidenced. Nothing here is settled.

THE CRATE: dynograph-game is not even a dependency of reflow2 today. It is closed-form normal-form analysis — per-player dominant strategies, pure Nash equilibria, Pareto-optimal outcomes, the interior 2x2 mixed equilibrium, and a headline classification `nash_is_pareto_suboptimal` with the Pareto outcome that dominates each suboptimal equilibrium.

THE FIT, and it is to a context Anthony has stated rather than one invented here: his real operating environment is several organisations with competing, partially-built, differently-motivated designs — A wants X, B wants Y, C built its own because it could not wait — and the job is making them interoperate when they were never designed to. That is a normal-form game. Players are organisations. Strategies are {adopt the shared interface, build our own}. And `nash_is_pareto_suboptimal` is exactly the interoperability tragedy: every organisation behaves rationally, every one builds its own, and the system of systems is collectively worse. The crate names both the equilibrium and the outcome that dominates it.

ADJACENT: dec:mosa-conformance is open, and MOSA is fundamentally an argument about the incentives to use open interfaces rather than about the interfaces themselves.

THE CONFLICT TO BE CLEAR ABOUT: the OBVIOUS application is analysis of alternatives — score the options, compute the equilibrium. That would CONTRADICT dec:alternatives-unranked-forkable, which is accepted and says "alternatives are unranked forkable siblings; the human judges in hindsight, not a stored score". Computing an equilibrium over design alternatives IS a stored recommendation. This must not be done without reopening that decision explicitly (dec:reopen-supersedes gives the mechanism). The interoperability reading does NOT conflict, because reflow2 would be reporting a structural property of an incentive situation a human described, not preferring a design — the same posture as dec:report-dont-judge.

THE HARD COST: payoffs are not in the graph and cannot be invented. This needs new vocabulary (players, strategies, payoff matrix) and a capture path, so it is M-to-L, not a spike. It is a product question about what reflow2 is for, and wants a conversation and a Decision before any code.
properties.name: OPEN — should reflow2 model multi-organisation interoperability as a normal-form game?
properties.rationale: Recorded because the fit to the stated multi-organisation context is unusually good, and recorded WITH the conflict against dec:alternatives-unranked-forkable stated in the same node, so nobody can pick this up later without meeting the objection.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL — Anthony's idea, 2026-08-01, and the first run has already paid (BL-153/154/155). What is open is not whether the measurement is useful, but how far it should go and what it must never become.

WHAT WAS DONE, and it is now `tools/surface_usage.py`: read the retained Claude Code transcripts, count tool calls, build the tool-to-tool transition graph, and run PageRank over it with self-loops removed. 46 sessions, 6,095 calls, 10 projects.

WHY THE GRAPH OPERATION EARNS ITS KEEP: it disagrees with raw counts. Volume puts `release_includes` first (1,008 calls, bookkeeping in 7 sessions); PageRank puts `detect_gaps`, `loop_status`, `export_graph`, `detect_defects` first — the coherence loop's read side, which is what workflows route THROUGH. High-volume-low-PageRank is a batching defect; high-PageRank is load-bearing. One measurement, two questions, and the tool that tops one does not top the other.

THE OPEN QUESTIONS, none answered:
(a) HOW FAR DOES IT GO? Today it is a manual, offline, read-only probe over transcripts a developer happens to have. The tempting next step is telemetry FROM the server — and that is a different product with different consent, privacy and trust properties. A design brain that watches its users is not obviously the same thing as one that keeps their design coherent.
(b) MAY ANY OF IT REACH THE GRAPH? `dec:loop-status-state-not-history` says loop debt is computed from graph state and never from run history, and 'looking is not writing' is a standing rule. That decision is about DEBT specifically, not about whether usage telemetry may exist at all — but nobody has ever said so out loud, and this is the moment to decide rather than to assume. The instrument as written writes nothing, which keeps the question open rather than answering it by accident.
(c) WHAT IS THE HONEST UNIT? Self-loop share proxies for a missing bulk form, and it worked. But a design brain optimised for fewer tool calls is not obviously optimised for better designs, and BL-23's lesson is that a number which punishes correct work needs a different question rather than a tuned threshold. There is no target self-loop share and there should not be one.
(d) OTHER PROJECTS' TRANSCRIPTS ARE OTHER PEOPLE'S WORK. Reading Anthony's own machine is one thing. If this ever runs over a consumer's sessions it needs their word first, and probably needs to never leave their machine.

THE HONEST LIMIT ALREADY FOUND: absence is weak evidence. `set_project_mode` appears as text in ten transcripts with zero recorded calls, so a tool used before the retention window is indistinguishable from one never used. Any 'unused' verdict from this instrument is a question, not a finding.
properties.name: OPEN — should real usage telemetry be a standing instrument for shaping the surface, and how far may it go?
properties.rationale: Recorded as an idea rather than a capability because the measurement is already built and useful while the QUESTIONS it raises — server-side telemetry, whether any of it may become graph state, consent over other people's transcripts — are genuinely undecided and would each be a different product. Anthony's idea; the first run produced three backlog rows.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL — from the 2026-08-01 dynograph-foundation review. Nothing here is settled.

THE IDEA: dynograph_graph::link_prediction_all / link_prediction_from (unused) score non-adjacent node pairs by how much their neighbourhoods overlap — common neighbours, Jaccard, or Adamic-Adar (which down-weights hubs). Read on a design graph: "these two look like they should be connected and are not — is there a missing SATISFIES, or DEPENDS_ON?"

WHERE IT LANDS: BL-114's unsolved half. That item records that disconnected_community SUGGESTS adding a bridge while its suggestion does not know the detector's own selectivity, so the advised bridge's only correct forms are edge types the measurement excludes. Link prediction would propose WHICH bridge, on evidence rather than on a template.

IT MUST BE AN ASK, NEVER A REPAIR. dec:ask-not-repair (suspected duplicates are asked, never merged) and dec:report-dont-judge both apply directly, and apply_heal already proposes-and-stops in rigid mode. A predicted edge written into the graph would be reflow2 inventing design.

THE HONEST COUNTER-ARGUMENT, and it may be fatal: a golden thread is largely a TREE. Trees have very few common neighbours, so neighbourhood-overlap scores may be near-zero almost everywhere and the signal may simply not exist on this shape of graph. That is measurable BEFORE any build — run it over reflow2's own 1179-node export and see whether anything scores. docs/sharpening.md is exactly the discipline for that, and this should not be built until the instrument says there is a signal.
properties.name: OPEN — should reflow2 propose MISSING edges from neighbourhood overlap, as a question rather than a repair?
properties.rationale: Included because it is the only unused foundation function that addresses BL-114's open half; recorded with its likely-fatal objection attached rather than argued down, so a later session inherits both.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL — from the 2026-08-01 dynograph-foundation review. Recorded for completeness; this is the WEAKEST of the ideas in this batch and is written down mainly so a later session knows it was considered and not chosen.

THE UNUSED FUNCTIONS: degree_centrality (with DegreeMode), closeness_centrality, eigenvector_centrality, and clustering (local clustering coefficient). All exact, all already available.

WHAT EACH WOULD MEAN HERE: closeness = how near a node is to everything else, so "how quickly does a change here reach the whole design". Eigenvector = importance by association with important nodes. Clustering coefficient = how tightly a node's neighbourhood is interconnected, a possible signal for over-coupled subsystems.

THE HONEST COUNTER-ARGUMENT, which is why this ranks last: betweenness is the RIGHT measure for the question reflow2 asks — how much of the golden thread routes THROUGH this node — and the others answer questions nobody has asked yet. Degree is already computed locally in structure.rs and needs no crate. Adding measures because they exist is how a report becomes a dashboard nobody reads, and reflow2 has an explicit instinct against that (dec:report-dont-judge, and BL-42's noise-floor lesson).

IF ANY: clustering coefficient is the only one with a question attached that reflow2 does not already answer — "is this subsystem more tangled inside than the design says it should be?" — and even that overlaps leiden communities.
properties.name: OPEN — is betweenness the right centrality, or should closeness / eigenvector / clustering also be read?
properties.rationale: Recorded deliberately as a considered-and-not-chosen idea. The brainstorm skill's rule is that roads not taken are part of the design's memory; without this node a later reviewer would rediscover four unused centrality functions and re-litigate them.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL — from a review of what dynograph-foundation offers that reflow2 does not yet use (2026-08-01, at Anthony's request). Nothing here is settled.

THE OBSERVATION: propagate.rs:389 ranks impacted nodes by GLOBAL betweenness centrality — `design_network()?.betweenness()`. That answers "is this node generally important in the design?", which is not the same question as "is this node relevant to the change I just made?". IP-9's stated intent is the second one.

THE IDEA: dynograph_graph::personalized_pagerank (already a dependency, unused) is random-walk-with-restart — the teleport mass returns to a SEED SET instead of spreading uniformly, so scores measure relevance to those seeds. Seeding it on the change's own seed nodes gives exactly the missing question.

CHEAP: the crate is already pinned, the function is exact on graphs this size, and propagate already builds the network. Small.

THE HONEST COUNTER-ARGUMENT, and it is a real one: betweenness is not wrong, it is answering a different and also-useful question. The existing doc comment defends it — "a change landing on a high-betweenness node has a wider SECONDARY blast radius" — which is about onward propagation, not relevance. So this may be an ADDITION rather than a replacement, and two ranking columns may be worse for a reader than one. Whether a reader wants both, or one, or a blend, is undecided and is the actual open question.

Filed as a backlog row on Anthony's word (2026-08-01) — the work is tracked; this Decision records that the SHAPE is still open.
properties.name: OPEN — should a blast radius rank by relevance TO THE CHANGE rather than by global importance?
properties.rationale: Surfaced by comparing reflow2's actual imports against dynograph-graph's exports: 8 of 17 are used. This was the strongest of the unused ones because it lands on the most-read output in the system and the mismatch between the question asked and the question answered is documented in reflow2's own doc comment.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL — from the 2026-08-01 dynograph-foundation review. Nothing here is settled.

THE OBSERVATION: cut_structure (used today) reports articulation POINTS — single nodes whose removal splits the network. That answers "what is a single point of failure". It does not answer "how separable are these two subsystems", which is a different and equally architectural question.

THE IDEA: dynograph_graph::max_flow_min_cut (Edmonds-Karp, exact, unused) returns the minimum-capacity set of EDGES whose removal disconnects a source from a target. Read on a design graph: "which contracts would you have to sever to split A from B, and how many?" Edge weights are already coupling weights, so the capacity has a meaning here rather than being invented.

WHERE IT LANDS: dec:mosa-conformance is OPEN and its own text says reflow2 "already computes most of the criteria" for modular open systems conformance. Severability is one of the ones it does not. req:modularity-computed is the standing requirement that severability be computed rather than asserted.

THE HONEST COUNTER-ARGUMENTS: min-cut needs a SOURCE and a TARGET, and nothing in the design says which two subsystems a user wants separated — so either the user picks the pair (a new question to ask) or reflow2 runs it over community pairs from leiden (defensible, but O(pairs) and the communities are themselves computed rather than declared). Also, low cut capacity is not automatically good: two subsystems SHOULD be coupled where the design says they should be, and a detector that rewards separation everywhere would push toward a design nobody wants — the same over-selectivity trap is_single_point_of_failure already had to be tuned out of.
properties.name: OPEN — should severability be computed as a minimum EDGE CUT, not just as articulation points?
properties.rationale: Chosen from the unused set because it maps onto an OPEN decision rather than onto a hypothetical: dec:mosa-conformance already claims most criteria are computable, and this names one that is not.

properties.decision: A design's identity is a UUID minted at genesis and stored in the graph; the friendly name is a label on top of it. A seat's identity is the harness session id it was already given. Rejected: deriving from the project name or path (two designs can share both, and the id must survive being copied), and a registry that hands out ids (that is the coordination this avoids, and there is no service to host it).
properties.name: Names are assigned with zero coordination, never derived from shared state
properties.rationale: Neither identifier is negotiated with anybody, so neither can race — unique by construction at one seat or fifteen. The fleet reached this by DELETING a whole mint-race guard: the race was an artifact of deriving the handle by reading a shared roster, so removing the derivation removed the race rather than patching it. reflow2 has the derived-identity bug twice today — every in-memory graph answered DEFAULT_GRAPH_ID until mirroring needed open_in_memory_as, and claims record a label rather than an owner.

properties.decision: BL-139's open half, and it is ANTHONY'S because it changes published behaviour rather than fixing a defect. `create_node` merges — its own description says "a partial props object edits" — and `import_graph` does not: re-importing an existing Requirement carrying only `{lineage: "derived"}` fails with `Requirement.statement: required property is missing`. The adopt workflow is import → detect → correct → re-import, so the mismatch lands precisely on the corrective step the skill prescribes. TWO OPTIONS, and the row already judged them: "(2) is honest and cheap; (1) is what the workflow actually wants." (1) MERGE AT PROPERTY LEVEL, like `create_node`. (2) SAY PLAINLY that documents must carry complete nodes — DONE 2026-08-02, in `import_graph`'s own description, so the cheap half is delivered whichever way this goes. THE COST OF (1), which is why it is not a one-word swap and why nobody should make it casually. FIRST, it crosses THREE PUBLISHED BOUNDARIES — `ifc:core-api`, `ifc:graph-export` and `ifc:mcp-tools` — measured, not guessed: `propagate_from("art:export")` reported 705 impacted nodes and `propagate_change` on this session's own edit reported 723, both crossing exactly those three. SECOND, and this is the part no boundary count shows: MERGING MAKES IMPORT NON-IDEMPOTENT FOR DELETION. Today a document is a complete statement of the nodes it names, so re-importing without a property REMOVES it and an export→import round trip reproduces the design exactly. Under (1) a property can only ever be added or changed, never dropped, and restoring a backup would silently retain whatever the live graph had accumulated since. That is a change to what an import MEANS, and it makes the migration and backup jobs this module exists for weaker in exchange for making the adopt loop smoother. THIRD, a middle path exists and should be considered rather than skipped: keep whole-node semantics as the default and let the DOCUMENT ask for merge explicitly (a per-node or per-document flag), so the adopt loop gets what it wants without redefining backup restore for everyone.
properties.name: OPEN — does import_graph merge a partial node like create_node, or keep demanding whole ones?
properties.rationale: Recorded proposed rather than decided, because AGENTS.md puts a Decision reaching `accepted` on the per-session side — that write is the user's signature. Raised now with the measurement attached because the row's framing ("make import_graph merge like create_node") reads as a small fix and the design says otherwise: this is the third time on this project that grep suggested a one-word swap and the graph reported a published-boundary change, and every previous time measuring first was what corrected it.

properties.decision: The install registers reflow2 with the agent at USER scope — the MCP server, the ten slash commands, the coherence-loop hooks and a `reflow2` command on PATH — so every project on the machine has it with no per-project setup. `reflow2_init.py` survives, but its job narrows: it writes the pointer file and project-scope config for a repo OTHER PEOPLE work on, so their agent is told reflow2 governs this code. Solo work needs none of it. Anthony's call, 2026-07-28, choosing "machine-wide, repo init optional" over "machine-wide only" and over "keep per-project, just make it one word".
properties.name: reflow2 installs once per machine; the in-repo half is optional and only for repos you share
properties.rationale:
WHY NOT "MACHINE-WIDE ONLY", which is simpler: a teammate cloning the repo would get no signal that reflow2 governs it unless they had already installed reflow2 themselves and thought to look. That is the invisibility `req:kit-reaches-the-agent` was raised for, and retiring the per-project installer would rebuild it deliberately.

WHY NOT "JUST MAKE IT ONE WORD" (`reflow2 init .` instead of a python path): it fixes the typing and none of the arithmetic. Still one step per project, still a re-run after every upgrade, and still the case that a user who forgets it experiences reflow2 as absent.

WHAT MADE MACHINE-WIDE SAFE TO CHOOSE AT ALL, and without it the answer would have been different: the server is registered with `--only-if-present`, so a directory that never opted into a design gets the LATENT surface and nothing is created in it. Without that flag, a user-scope registration would drop a RocksDB store into every folder a session is ever opened in — and litter in someone's repo is a worse first impression than the setup step it removed. The loop-nudge hook is gated the same way and for the same reason: registered globally, silent wherever `.reflow2/` does not exist.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT CHANGE: `dec:skills-served` and `req:thin-install` stand exactly as they were. The skills and working instructions are still served, still never copied, and upgrading reflow2 still produces no diff in a consumer repo. This decision is about WHERE the pointers are installed, not about what is served — and it makes the thin install thinner, since the common case now installs nothing into a project at all.

properties.decision: PROPOSED as a proof of concept, Anthony 2026-07-27, captured while fresh rather than worked: build a reflow2 design graph inside storyflow (adopt is under way, not finished) and another inside dynograph-foundation, then have an agent LINK them through their published surfaces and identify where the interfaces are incompatible. THE CASE IS WELL CHOSEN AND NOT A TOY: reflow2 and storyflow BOTH depend on dynograph-foundation, so it is a real three-way seam between three real repositories with a real answer, and both consumers were built by the same author at different times against a foundation that moved — which is precisely how interface drift happens in the wild. Each project's graph would then PUBLISH ITS OWN INTERFACE SPEC, which is what any consumer needs and what makes the seam checkable. What this would actually prove, and why it is worth doing rather than arguing: whether dec:nested-graphs (a graph per ownership boundary) and cap:mirror-surface hold up on three designs nobody built to be composed. WHAT IT DEPENDS ON: req:interface-spec-complete first — reflow2 structures roughly one and a half of the six characteristics an interface spec needs and puts the rest in one free-text string, so today two graphs can be linked and still not be comparable. Then req:seam-incompatibility, which is the finding the PoC is meant to produce.
properties.name: OPEN — prove composition on reflow2 + storyflow + dynograph-foundation
properties.rationale: Anthony's own framing, and it lands on intent reflow2 already holds: req:design-composes (accepted, blocked on dec:nested-graphs at the time), dec:nested-graphs (DECIDED — a design is its own graph when separately owned, released or shared, which is exactly three sibling repos), cap:mirror-surface and cap:publish-surface (both built). So the LINKING half exists and the COMPARING half does not. Recorded as a decision point rather than a plan because the sequencing is a real choice: structure the interface spec first and then run the PoC, or run the PoC against today's thin spec to find out what it cannot say. Also worth noting the PoC has a second payoff independent of the result — it is the first time reflow2 would be pointed at a design it did not author, twice, which is the adopt path Anthony says his real work almost always starts from.

properties.decision: RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-07-25, from work he has done: State Funerals for US Presidents (he worked President Bush's) — hundreds to thousands of people planning simultaneously, an echeloned plan (NORTHCOM OPLAN → JTF-NCR → each service → each unit), and events arriving during the run that the plan must react to in minutes. His words: "using a common github repo may no longer work". THE DECOMPOSITION THAT MAKES IT TRACTABLE IS ALREADY DECIDED: dec:nested-graphs (c) says a design is its own graph per ownership boundary, so a thousand planners are not a thousand writers on one store — they are ~100-200 graphs of 5-20 writers each, linked by mirrored published surfaces. Echelons own their plans; that is both the software answer and how the organisation actually works. FOUR ROADS for the tier itself. (a) NOTHING NEW — federation plus git, accepting minutes of latency; cheapest, and it fails only the react-in-near-real-time half. (b) ONE PROCESS PER GRAPH over streamable HTTP (rmcp has the transport, reflow2 serves stdio only), writes going to the store and the export DERIVED as the archival record; at federation scale the process-per-project cut already named in dec:central-host is also the natural sharding — one process per ownership boundary is one staff. (c) ONE SHARED MULTI-WRITER STORE, which means replacing single-writer RocksDB and owning consensus; most work, least alignment with a design that already shards by authority. (d) EVENT-SOURCED LOG plus materialised views — attractive because a plan IS a change history, expensive because every detector currently reads a materialised graph. WHAT BREAKS TODAY, in order: single-writer per graph (the six-seat outage of 2026-07-25 was this at tiny scale), the whole-document write path (769 KB for 606 nodes; a funeral federation is 10^5-10^6 nodes changing continuously), git-round-trip latency, nothing that pushes, no identity or authorization, and req:stale-seat-knows going from one bad afternoon to a systemic property.
properties.name: OPEN — does reflow2 grow a live tier for hundreds of simultaneous planners, alongside the repo file?
properties.rationale: Held as brainstorming because it is explicitly distant-future ("probably distant future") and because it challenges the PREMISE of two decisions rather than their reasoning — which is the honest thing to record, not to act on. dec:multi-writer-architecture chose repo-file-plus-merge on a rationale resting on concurrency being hypothetical; dec:central-host's rationale says outright that this tool "does not need" simultaneity "and may be harmed by it". A thousand people replanning a state funeral under events is the named counter-case both were missing, and per dec:reopen-supersedes the move is a new decision point, never flipping those back. NOTE THE PART THAT NEEDS NO DECISION: the ownership boundary federation already draws is the natural AUTHORIZATION boundary — you write your echelon's graph and read your superior's published surface — so authz needs enforcement, not a new concept, and Interface.designation internal|published is already the read primitive. Also settled by inspection: ordering without a shared git history needs no global clock, because the same federation shape gives a total order WITHIN each boundary (the store, proved by the content-hash chain) and dated coordinates ACROSS boundaries (a mirror already carries whose design, which version, when) — exactly how echelons coordinate. Full reasoning in docs/planning-at-scale.md.

properties.decision: loop_status reports what the coherence loop is owed — anchored gaps never surfaced, questions waiting or answered-but-unwritten, structural defects, capabilities claiming realized/verified with no passing check, drift awaiting disposition, claims never examined — computed entirely from current graph state. reflow2 does not track when tools were run: phase nudges are excluded (guidance, not debt), and the write tools carry static loop_hint pointers at the next loop step in their own results.
properties.name: Loop debt is computed from graph state, never from run history
properties.rationale: From the StoryFlow fleet trial (BL-74): under operational load the agent kept bookkeeping via raw tools while the loop skills silently stopped — 'a design-discipline tool that depends on being remembered will lose to operational urgency every time; fire on a trigger, not on virtue.' Run-history ('no detect_gaps since Tuesday') is not honestly computable here: the core takes no clock, and looking-is-not-writing is doctrine — recording reads so observation could be tracked would make looking mutate the record. Outstanding debt is the state-based equivalent and the actionable truth regardless of who ran what when. The hint rides the tool result the agent already reads (zero extra round-trip to see it), and loop_status is the cheap computation a client hook can fire on its own events — rung a of the BL-74 ladder builds on exactly this call. Decided 2026-07-21.

properties.decision: release_includes_all derives a release's whole manifest from the design and writes it in one call, with `apply` defaulting to false so the derivation is reported before anything is written. Entries already in the manifest are reported as already_present and their frozen as_checksum is never recomputed.
properties.name: A bulk derivation is not a bulk accept, and it writes nothing until asked
properties.rationale: BL-153 flagged the counterweight to state before building: dec:two-sided-accept and dec:ask-not-repair mean a bulk form must not become a silent one, and "a batch of 144 acknowledgements with one reason is exactly the erosion those decisions exist to prevent". Those decisions bound bulk DISPOSITIONS — a judgement taken about each item. No disposition is taken here: the graph is asked what the project contains and answers, and the one judgement a human still owns (which release ships it) is the argument the caller supplies. So the family does not apply, and a per-item disposition would be ceremony over a derivation. What DOES apply is the no-silent-write bar: hence apply defaults to false, matching reconcile_artifacts' record_events, because a call that packages a release is the one you most want to read before you run it. The frozen-checksum guard is the harder half — a derivation that recomputed every entry would rewrite the manifest of a shipped release each time the live drift baseline moved, silently and in bulk, which is the axis-Z sin the frozen copy exists to prevent.

properties.decision: The three-way merge (cap:merge-designs, dec:merge-three-way) resolves per node, per property, and per edge against the base by this case table. NODES/PROPERTIES: only one side changed a property -> take it; both changed it differently -> conflict. add/add (same id, no base) -> treated as modify/modify against an empty base: matching properties merge, each differing property is a conflict. delete/delete -> node gone, no conflict. delete/modify (one side removes the node, the other changes it) -> RETAIN-AND-ASK: the proposal keeps the modified node and raises a conflict asking the human to confirm the deletion or keep it, leaning toward keeping — deletion is the destructive side and must be re-justified, never the silent default (req:intent-preserved, retire-vs-delete). Symmetric in both directions. EDGES: first-class design content and get the identical three-way rule — one-sided add or remove -> take it; the same edge changed differently on both sides, or one side removes while the other changes it -> conflict; never silently drop an edge one side deliberately cut (req:no-silent-fallback). CONFLICT REPRESENTATION: a both-sides conflict is a Question node with source 'merge_conflict', a deterministic id (FNV over base + node/edge id + property, the existing gap-id normalization), carrying the base/ours/theirs values; it reuses the existing answer_question / open_questions machinery and writes nothing until dispositioned, and its normalized id is the key a later rerere rung (BL-80 #5) replays a recorded resolution against. No new node type — the schema stays 28.
properties.name: The merge conflict case table: retain-and-ask on delete, edges symmetric with nodes, conflicts are Questions
properties.rationale: User decided all three axes 2026-07-22, each the doctrine-aligned option, closing the sub-decisions dec:merge-three-way explicitly deferred. Retain-and-ask over a neutral conflict because losing a node is not symmetric with keeping it: req:intent-preserved and the retire-vs-delete distinction make a delete the move that must be justified, so the proposal keeps the node and asks rather than treating erasure as an equal default. Edges symmetric with nodes because they carry the golden thread — a lighter union-and-keep-wins rule would override a deliberate one-sided edge removal without asking, which is exactly the silent drop req:no-silent-fallback forbids; compare_designs already bands edge divergence, so the input is there. Reuse Question over a dedicated MergeConflict type for the recurring schema-minimalism reason (the vocabulary was already sufficient — same lesson as dec:certainty-derived and dec:component-verified-computed): the answer/open-questions machinery, the deterministic FNV gap-id normalization, and the human-decides routing all already exist, and reusing them makes the conflict rerere-ready for free (BL-80 #5) while keeping the schema at 28 node types. With this, the merge is fully specified — nothing left but the build and its verification.

properties.decision: reflow2 records how a human resolved a merge conflict and offers it back when the same conflict recurs (git's rerere), on three axes the user decided. (1) STORAGE — in the graph, as an answered Question (source=merge_resolution) whose id IS the conflict's content fingerprint: reuses the answer_question/open_questions machinery, travels with the design in the export, no schema change (stays 28 node types) — exactly what dec:merge-conflict-semantics anticipated ('reuse Question; its normalized id is the key a later rerere rung replays against'). (2) BEHAVIOR — advisory: a recorded resolution is surfaced as a suggestion on the matching conflict, and the human still confirms (dec:report-dont-judge, dec:three-party-checks). apply_merge applies only what it is given; an opt-in use_recorded lets the human bulk-accept every recorded suggestion in one move (the confirmation is passing the flag), and apply refuses if any conflict still has neither an explicit nor a recorded decision. (3) KEY — content only: the fingerprint is over (property, base value, ours value, theirs value), independent of which node, so ONE resolution replays across ALL nodes with the identical conflict — this is git's model and what delivers the motivating BL-73 win (20 near-identical conflicts, 21 near-identical hand-resolutions → resolve the shape once). apply_merge records every applied property/edge-property resolution keyed by content, so the memory grows as you work.
properties.name: rerere: record a conflict resolution content-keyed in the graph, replay it advisory-only
properties.rationale: User decided all three axes 2026-07-22, each the doctrine-aligned option. Content-only keying because it is the whole point: the BL-73 field pain was N near-identical conflicts across different nodes, and a per-node key would give near-zero reuse and miss exactly that case; content-only is git's proven model, and pairing it with advisory behavior keeps over-reach visible (the human sees each application). Advisory over auto-apply because the three-party doctrine puts the decision with the human — but the recorded suggestion plus a bulk-accept toggle kills the repetitive grind without silently resolving on the human's behalf. Reuse-Question over a new node type or a side cache is the recurring no-schema-change lesson AND keeps the memory inside the design that travels in the export (a side rr-cache would be a second source of truth that a teammate importing the design would not receive). Scoped in v1 to property and edge-property conflicts (a clear base/ours/theirs value triple, and the N-near-identical shape); node-type and delete/modify keys are deferred (no clean value triple), as is aging/pruning the memory. Extends cap:merge-designs; the conflict ids the merge already mints were built for exactly this (dec:merge-conflict-semantics).

properties.decision: When HEAL merges DUPLICATES-asserted nodes, the survivor is picked by provenance rank (authored > planned > imported > reconciled > inferred > healed); node id breaks ties. Pre-provenance graphs are unchanged.
properties.name: Merge survivor is chosen by provenance, id breaks ties
properties.rationale: User decided option 2 for BL-29 (2026-07-20): provenance is the closest thing the graph has to 'who asserted this and how deliberately'. Refinement from the 2026-07-20 self-adopt live session: a node with UNSET provenance defaults to authored, which made two genesis stubs tie against authored+verified survivors and nearly win on alphabetical id — set provenance explicitly on both sides before proposing a merge, and consider ranking unset below authored in a future revision.

properties.decision: The design merge is a three-way typed merge exposed as a core op (MCP tool + CLI flag), the write-side sibling of compare_designs. (1) Inputs are three explicit export documents — a common ancestor (base), ours, theirs; git supplies the base (git merge-base + the committed reflow2.json at that commit), so reflow2 does not build its own commit DAG for this rung. The multi-parent/ref layer that would let reflow2 find its own merge-base is deferred to BL-70/#3. (2) The algorithm is git's trivial-merge case table run per node and per property against the base over typed values, not lines: only one side changed a property -> take it; both sides changed it differently -> a structured conflict. (3) It produces a merge proposal — auto-resolved one-sided changes plus a list of both-sides conflicts rendered as Questions ('node X.prop Y: base=A, ours=B, theirs=C — which?') — and writes NOTHING to the graph. The human dispositions the conflict Questions, then an explicit apply commits the merge. Compare reports and never writes; merge does the same until the human has looked.
properties.name: The three-way merge takes explicit inputs over git's DAG, and reports a proposal it never auto-applies
properties.rationale: User decided both axes 2026-07-22, both the recommended option. Explicit-inputs-over-git because the exports are already git-committed (dec:repo-file-embedded) and git already tracks the merge-base — building a second DAG inside reflow2 would reimplement what git provides and contradicts 'export/import is the right-sized git bundle analogue' (BL-80's explicit do-NOT-import list). It keeps rung #1 shippable now and defers the ref/branch layer to where it belongs (BL-70). compare_designs already computes the typed per-property diff this consumes, so the input side is built. Report-a-proposal-never-auto-apply because a both-sides conflict IS a Question and the graph must not silently pick a side (dec:report-dont-judge, req:human-decides, req:no-silent-fallback); mirroring compare's read-only contract keeps the sibling honest, and the explicit apply is the disposition gate (dec:two-sided-accept's spirit — no silent write) without a staging area (BL-80 explicitly rejects the index). Typed per-node/per-property conflicts are strictly better than git's line markers — the key 'graph is not files' caveat. This specifies BL-12's merge problem: rung #1 (this algorithm over three documents) + #2 (the retained ancestor, here git's) = the L core of BL-12. Deferred to their own decisions: delete/modify and add/add conflict semantics (retire-vs-delete makes a delete meaningful, so delete/modify must go to the human, never auto-resolve), edge-merge banding, and the exact shape of the conflict Question.

properties.decision: UNDECIDED, RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING. Anthony, 2026-07-25, supplied the DoD MOSA Implementation Guidebook (OUSD(R&E) Systems Engineering and Architecture, February 2025, Distribution A) and was explicit about the frame: "just taking principles, concepts and ideas from this. not looking to implement mosa exactly over this document." So this records what the guidebook's concepts illuminate about reflow2, not a plan to become a MOSA tool. THE DEFINITION IT GIVES: "an acquisition and design approach consisting of a technical and business architecture that supports using system interfaces compliant with widely supported and consensus-based standards... A MOSA system structure allows for severable components to be incrementally added, removed, or replaced throughout the life cycle" (10 U.S.C. 4401, mandated for all DoD acquisition programs to the maximum extent practicable). ITS FIVE-STEP FRAMEWORK is a process, not a document: Plan, Modularize, Identify Interfaces, Define Interfaces, Standardize Interfaces — and reflow2 can already model a process rather than only a product (cap:model-process, Flow nodes), so the framework is expressible as a Flow whose steps the graph can be checked against. THE FINDING THAT MATTERS, from Table D-1 "MOSA Conformance Criteria and Verification Methods": most of what MOSA asks a program to demonstrate, reflow2 already computes for other reasons. Their MODULARITY criterion — "encapsulated, cohesive, loosely coupled, and organized into functional categories" — is the Leiden modularity score, community detection and the god-component detector that graph_report already prints. Their MOSA OBJECTIVES criterion — "demonstrate severable modular components" — is propagate_change: if the blast radius of a change inside a module stops at that module's interfaces the module is severable, and if it leaks past them the module is not modular whatever the architecture diagram says. That is severability as a COMPUTED property rather than an assertion, which is the same move dec:certainty-derived made for requirement status and cap:derived-completion made for delivery. Their MOSA MODULES criterion — "implement minimal functions, are functionally independent, encapsulated, and traceable to requirements" — is the god-component detector plus the golden thread. Their LIFE CYCLE CHARACTERISTICS criterion — severable, replaceable, interoperable, allowing competition — is the severability computation plus the alternatives layer, where interchangeable suppliers behind one interface are exactly an analysis of alternatives. WHAT IS GENUINELY MISSING, and it is one vocabulary item and one check. (1) NOTHING MARKS AN INTERFACE AS KEY. MOSA's whole discipline turns on designating major/modular system interfaces and then holding them stable and open; reflow2 has Interface nodes, provides/consumes and SPECIFIES, but no way to say "this one is the published boundary and that one is internal plumbing". BL-45 found the identical hole from the opposite direction — external dependencies between reflow2 projects — and recorded it as "nothing marks an Interface external-facing". Two independent routes to one missing property is the strongest evidence this design has for a vocabulary addition. (2) NOTHING CHECKS STANDARDS COMPLIANCE, and the vocabulary for it is present and unused: DesignRule is defined as a chosen standard or convention with an `enforced` flag, and there are zero DesignRules in any graph — the same schema-present-practice-absent shape as the temporal axis and the KPP vocabulary before them. THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT, recorded beside the idea rather than used to bury it: MOSA is domain vocabulary for defence acquisition, and req:design-anything says the vocabulary stays neutral. A MOSA conformance report is therefore a VIEW — a projection over computations that already exist, in the acquisition community's words — and not a set of new node types. Building it as a view keeps the core neutral (dec:views-are-projections) and any renderer fill-in remains a defect. If it were ever built as schema, reflow2 would have taken on one domain's language as its own, which is the thing it has refused since the beginning.
properties.name: OPEN — should reflow2 report MOSA conformance, given it already computes most of the criteria?
properties.rationale: Recorded 2026-07-25 as brainstorming from the DoD MOSA Implementation Guidebook Anthony supplied, on his framing: principles and concepts, not an implementation of MOSA. PROMOTED THE SAME DAY on his word ("let's promote both") into the two things the guidebook actually exposed as missing, both now accepted: req:key-interfaces (the design says which interfaces are the published boundaries, and computations read the distinction) and req:modularity-computed (severability and cohesion are computed from the graph, not asserted by the diagram). Both are GOVERNED_BY this decision. WHAT STAYS OPEN is the question this decision was opened on, and it is narrower now: whether reflow2 ships a MOSA-BRANDED report. The requirements are domain-neutral by construction — published boundary, severable part — so they can be built without answering it, and the acquisition community's words for the same criteria belong in a view over the computation rather than in the schema (dec:views-are-projections, req:design-anything). Deciding otherwise would adopt one domain's language as reflow2's own, which is the thing it has refused since the beginning. SEQUENCING, and it is not arbitrary: req:key-interfaces comes first because req:modularity-computed depends on it — severability is only checkable once the design knows where a boundary is. req:design-composes also links through published boundaries, so the same property serves the federation thread; that is the second independent route to it, after BL-45 found the identical hole from the system-of-systems side on 2026-07-20.

properties.alternatives: [{"option":"repo file, merge on pull","outcome":"chosen","note":"contradicts nothing; reuses the built merge machinery; needs BL-44 claims"},{"option":"hosted service","outcome":"rejected","note":"contradicts req:persistence and req:invocation (both accepted); supersedes dec:repo-file-embedded; design leaves the user's machine; permanent operational burden"},{"option":"hybrid: hosted coordination, local designs","outcome":"rejected","note":"keeps req:persistence but strains req:invocation with a second surface; the claims layer approximates the benefit without a server"}]
properties.decision: DECIDED 2026-07-25: the design STAYS a graph-in-a-repo-file, and many writers are handled by merging on pull. No hosted service, no shared writable store. Each person's design lives at ./.reflow2/graph in their own checkout, git moves it, and genuinely overlapping work is resolved by the three-way merge that already exists — typed per-node and per-property against the common ancestor, with each conflict minted as a Question carrying a deterministic id, and recorded resolutions replayable across near-identical conflicts (rerere). THIS CONFIRMS dec:repo-file-embedded RATHER THAN SUPERSEDING IT. That is the outcome worth noting: this was the first field-sourced re-opening of a settled decision, triggered because dec:repo-file-embedded's own rationale said the concurrency argument was 'hypothetical while there is one writer' and fifteen developers made it concrete. The precondition genuinely changed, the decision was genuinely re-opened, and the original answer survived contact with the new evidence. A re-opening that ends where it started is not wasted — it converts an assumption into a tested position. WHAT WAS REJECTED AND WHY. A HOSTED SERVICE: rejected on cost against confirmed intent, not on taste. It contradicts req:persistence ('the graph lives at ./.reflow2/graph inside the consumer project, so the design travels with the repo') and req:invocation ('the reflow2-mcp binary spoken to over stdio, installed into a consumer project'), both accepted, so choosing it would have required retiring or revising confirmed intent rather than merely adding machinery. It also puts the design on a machine the user does not control, carries permanent operational burden, and breaks the session-transcript identity for everyone but the local user (a local path resolves for one person and silently misses for the rest). A HYBRID — hosted claims and presence over local designs: rejected as the weaker version of the same trade. It keeps req:persistence but strains req:invocation with a second surface to run, and buys live visibility that the claims layer can approximate without a server. WHAT THIS COMMITS TO BUILDING: the scoping primitive (BL-44 cluster claims) so two people do not collide in the first place, and merge-on-pull ergonomics. The honest weakness accepted with this choice: no live view of what others hold, so overlap surfaces at merge time rather than before it — which is exactly the trade git itself makes, and the one this project's users already understand.
properties.name: Many writers keep the repo file and merge on pull — no hosted service
properties.rationale: Raised by the user and his brother, 2026-07-24, from a concrete scenario rather than speculation. This is the first field-sourced trigger to re-open a settled decision, and it is worth recording WHY it counts as one: dec:repo-file-embedded's own rationale reads "the service's strongest argument (concurrency) is hypothetical while there is one writer." Fifteen developers is that hypothesis arriving, so the decision is not being second-guessed — its stated precondition has changed. That is exactly the signal cap:revise-trigger is being built to surface automatically; here it arrived by conversation instead, which is itself evidence the trigger is worth building. Held proposed deliberately: the architecture question is upstream of every feature beneath it (req:concurrent-planning among them), and starting to build under an unmade decision is how a design acquires an architecture nobody chose. The counter-argument that belongs in the weighing, so it is not lost: reflow2's loop is built around asking a human and recording an attributable answer — deliberate, sequential, credited — and simultaneous editing may be the wrong shape for that product even where it is technically reachable. What the raised scenario actually asks for is non-colliding parallel work plus good merges, which may be reachable without a service at all.

properties.decision: DECIDED 2026-07-25 by Anthony: option (c), A GRAPH PER OWNERSHIP BOUNDARY WITH LEVELS INSIDE EACH. A design is its own graph when something at that level is separately OWNED, separately RELEASED, or separately SHARED — and a subtree of one graph otherwise. The hierarchy does not decide; authority does. That is the shape federated systems engineering actually uses, and it makes the split rule non-arbitrary: you can always answer "why is this its own design?" with a name, a release train, or a recipient. WHAT FOLLOWS, and each is an obligation rather than a detail. (1) THE COORDINATE. Edges cannot cross stores because the schema validates both endpoints, so a link between designs is not an edge: the other side's published surface is MIRRORED into your graph as local nodes, and the mirror carries the coordinate — which design it came from, at what content hash, when. Your own components then PROVIDE and CONSUME the mirrored Interface with ordinary local edges, so the golden thread works unchanged and foreignness is a property of the NODE rather than of the link. Same reasoning as dec:fork-point-address: a coordinate resolved against a document, never a live ref layer. (2) ROLL-UP. A parent's view of a composed child must derive from the child's own evidence or a requirement satisfied inside the child fires unsatisfied in the parent forever — cap:derived-completion's computation one level up. (3) FRESHNESS. A mirror is a dated claim about a VERSION, so a newer surface with a different hash makes it stale and that must be detectable, never assumed current (the cap:freshness and confirmation-ledger shape). (4) THE SEAM. Two teams changing the boundary itself still collide, in the one place the merge machinery does not reach; the published-surface document is what they are actually negotiating over. THE ROADS NOT TAKEN, kept because req:roads-not-taken says they are part of the record. (a) ONE GRAPH, ZOOM BY LEVEL was not rejected — it was BUILT FIRST and remains correct for everything inside one ownership boundary; cap:scoped-analysis delivers it, and (c) is a superset rather than a replacement. What (a) alone could not do is give two owners separate write locks, separate release trains, or a way to share one part without sharing everything. (b) A GRAPH PER SYSTEM was rejected as a RULE, not as a possibility: a system that is separately owned still gets its own graph under (c), but depth alone stops being sufficient reason, because every seam costs a coordinate, a roll-up and a freshness check, and a three-level tower of graphs inside one team buys none of what those cost. THE TENSION THIS RESOLVES, and it should be resolved out loud: docs/org-scale-vision.md records the destination as "one graph the whole company plans in". Under (c) that is no longer the destination — an enterprise is many designs federated at ownership boundaries, and the CEO's objectives are one design that others mirror rather than one graph everyone writes into. That document now describes a road not taken and should say so.
properties.name: DECIDED — a graph per ownership boundary, levels inside each
properties.rationale: Raised 2026-07-25 as brainstorming, because Anthony said plainly he was not convinced by the collaboration design and an unconvinced author is a finding rather than a disagreement to be argued down. Promoted to intent the same day, and COLLAPSED the same day on his word ("let's do (c) option"). THE SEQUENCE IS THE ARGUMENT for why this was worth holding open for a few hours rather than deciding immediately: option (a)'s scope filter was built FIRST precisely because it forecloses nothing, so by the time the decision was made there was working evidence about what per-level analysis actually feels like — and (a) turned out to be a subset of (c) rather than a rival to it. Deciding on day one would have been a guess; deciding after building the cheap half was a choice with evidence behind it. WHY (c) OVER (b), stated as the discriminator that survived from the brainstorm: every seam between designs costs a coordinate, an evidence roll-up and a freshness check, so a level earns its own graph only when it is separately owned, released or shared. A three-level tower of graphs inside one team pays all of that and buys none of it. (b) is not forbidden by this — a separately-owned system still gets its own design — it is that DEPTH stops being sufficient reason. WHAT THIS COSTS, recorded so nobody is surprised: docs/org-scale-vision.md's "one graph the whole company plans in" is now a road not taken, and req:concurrent-planning's answer changes shape — ownership boundaries become the primary isolation mechanism, with the claims layer and the merge driver serving work INSIDE one boundary rather than across all of them. The first rung built on this decision is the coordinate (cap:mirror-surface): the other side's published surface mirrored as local nodes carrying which design, which hash, and when.

properties.decision: UNDECIDED, and it is Anthony's call. The schema declares BOTH `SUPERSEDES` and `OBSOLETES` for the same relationship — one node retiring another on the record — and NEITHER is read by any computation. The choice is which one is the real vocabulary, and then making it mean something. Option A: keep `OBSOLETES` (the one the code and the retire-from-design skill already use) and delete `SUPERSEDES` from the schema and from docs/three-axes.md. Option B: keep `SUPERSEDES` (the one the schema's own doc comment describes as "target retired on the record") and migrate the code. Option C: both survive with a stated distinction — but nobody has yet said what that distinction would be, and two words for one relationship is how a vocabulary rots.
properties.name: OPEN — retirement is two edge types and neither is consulted: which one survives?
properties.rationale:
FOUND BY THE SCHEMA SWEEP, 2026-07-28, and it is the `req:supporting-is-not-conflict` shape at edge level rather than property level.

WHAT WAS MEASURED. `SUPERSEDES` has ZERO references in the entire Rust source: nothing creates it, nothing reads it. It is nonetheless documented in `nodes.rs` ("source supersedes target — target retired on the record") and named in `docs/three-axes.md` as part of what covers the time axis. `OBSOLETES` is the one actually in use — `collapse_decision` draws it when a chosen alternative retires the losers, and the retire-from-design skill instructs users to draw it for a capability or component with a successor. But `OBSOLETES` has NO READER either: grep across the whole core crate finds the constant, the one create site, and a doc comment. No rollup, detector or report consults it.

WHAT THAT MEANS TODAY, stated exactly rather than dramatised: retiring something marks it and changes nothing downstream. A retired capability still counts in every rollup, still raises its gaps, still appears in delivery arithmetic. It is currently LATENT — reflow2's own design contains zero instances of either edge, so the retire path has never been exercised on this project — but the skill is actively telling users to draw an edge that has no effect, which is worse than an edge nobody knows about.

WHY IT IS NOT JUST HOUSEKEEPING. `req:intent-preserved` ("the past is never overwritten") is the requirement retirement serves, and the retire-from-design skill exists precisely to force the question "was this ever true?" — history retired on the record versus a mistake deleted. That whole discipline currently terminates in an edge nothing reads. Whichever edge survives, the deciding question is the same: what SHOULD consult it — delivery roll-up, the gap detectors, `graph_report`'s counts — and does a retired node stop counting, or count separately?

DELIBERATELY LEFT `proposed`: this is a vocabulary choice with migration consequences for anyone who already drew either edge, and `dec:certainty-derived` forbids recording it as settled on the user's behalf.

properties.decision: single_point_of_failure candidates are Components, Interfaces, Resources, Environments.
properties.name: Only things that operate can be single points of failure
properties.rationale: The suggested fix is add_redundancy, and redundancy is only coherent for running parts; a golden thread converges on intent by design, so intent hubs are the thread working. 22 of 22 false positives cleared, 4 true survivors. Decided 2026-07-19 (https://claude.ai/code/session_013aumVdHrRHu24cLirn6Cam); BL-5.

properties.decision:
Anthony asked 2026-07-31 whether a "start here" file or node should tell a newly-cloned agent what it needs to pick up where the last person left off — offered explicitly as an idea to explore, with the observation that reflow2 often already has something. It does, and the answer is: BUILD THE VIEW, NOT THE DOCUMENT.

NO START-HERE FILE. Two recorded positions already forbid it, and neither is a stretch. `req:session-memory-in-graph`: "a summary written at the end is the one a busy session never gets to, and an end-of-session digest is a retelling rather than a record." And `dec:what-lives-where`'s whole storyflow lesson is prose-you-navigate losing to graph-you-query. A START-HERE.md is `dev_storyflow` in miniature — it would go stale, and STALENESS IN AN ORIENTATION DOCUMENT IS THE WORST PLACE FOR IT, because it is the first thing read and the reader has nothing yet to check it against.

THE NEED IS REAL AND MOSTLY ALREADY DESIGNED. Three planned capabilities cover it between them: `cap:what-next` (which of the agreed things to do now, ranked so an unmade decision outranks the work waiting on it), `cap:onboarding` (where does a new piece of work belong, for someone who did not build the system), and `cap:session-memory` (what the last session learned, queryable rather than narrated). None needs a document; all three are projections, which is what `dec:views-are-projections` already says every view is.

WHAT IS GENUINELY MISSING, and it belongs in `cap:what-next` rather than in a new thing: WHICH FEW DECISIONS SHAPE EVERYTHING ELSE. Neither what-next nor where-am-i answers it today, and it is what a newcomer actually needs — not the task list, but the handful of choices that explain why the rest looks as it does.

EVIDENCE AGAINST URGENCY, recorded because it is the kind of thing that otherwise gets built on a feeling. `where-am-i` DID orient a fresh agent on this design earlier the same day: 627 nodes, roughly six calls, using `scan_nodes` with `brief: true` and reading six Decisions in full. It scales today because reads are bounded (`cap:bounded-reads`). The concern that it stops working is a FORECAST, not yet an observation — worth watching rather than pre-solving, and worth re-measuring when the answer changes rather than assuming it has.

SO THE ORDER IS: build `cap:what-next`, whose blocker has already cleared, and add the shaping-decisions section to it. Do not add a fourth thing beside three planned ones that already answer the question.
properties.name: No START-HERE document — orientation is a projection, and writing it down would be dev_storyflow in miniature
properties.rationale:
Taken on the recommendation rather than the request, which is the point worth noting: the question was "should we write a start-here document", and the honest answer was that the artefact would work against the reason the project exists. Anthony's own framing left room for that — "maybe this isn't needed because an agent using reflow2 can already quickly know what a project is about" — and the measurement supports it.

The more useful outcome was not the answer but what looking produced: `cap:what-next` states a prerequisite that has since been met, and nothing surfaced it. A capability that records its own blocking condition in prose has written a trigger that nothing fires. That is the same shape as every other declared-but-unread property this project keeps finding, and it is the argument for the shaping-decisions section being a COMPUTATION rather than another paragraph.

The in-degree caveat is kept deliberately. The first version of the idea looked convincing because the top three results were genuinely load-bearing; the top result was not, and reporting the idea without that would have been reporting a demo rather than a measurement.

properties.decision:
OPEN — Anthony's word needed. Anthony described the role as an attribute of each NODE in an architecture (publish / subscribe / both / non_external). reflow2 already carries something very close: `Interface.designation` (internal | published), with PROVIDES and CONSUMES naming who stands on which side. So the question is whether the pairing role extends the Interface, or becomes a property every node type carries.

ALTERNATIVES WEIGHED. (1) Extend `Interface.designation` — RECOMMENDED. (2) A role property on every node, Anthony's original shape: most general, lets any node participate in a seam; costs correctness, because a Component both publishes and subscribes so the value collapses to `both` and pairs with everything, and it adds a property to 28 node types for a case nothing currently needs. (3) Neither — keep pairing manual as mirror_surface does today and let compose_and_analyse surface a bad seam as an ordinary gap once a human has wired the two sides; cheapest, but leaves exactly the hand-wiring that made this idea worth having.
properties.name: Where the publish/subscribe role lives: on the Interface, or on every node
properties.rationale:
WHY THE INTERFACE. An Interface IS a boundary — it is the one node type whose entire reason for existing is to be the place two things meet, which is exactly what pairs. The publish side already exists there, is already exported by export_surface, and already withholds internals correctly. And a role is not intrinsic to a node: the same Component publishes one contract and subscribes to another, so a single role on the Component would be wrong about half the time. Anthony's `both` value is the tell — it is needed only because the attribute is sitting on the wrong noun. On an Interface, `both` is rare and meaningful (a genuinely bidirectional contract) rather than a shrug.

WHAT MUST BE ADDED WHICHEVER WAY IT GOES, because this is the actual missing half: a way to declare what a design NEEDS from outside — a REQUIRED boundary — standing on its own, without the consumer first having modelled the provider's contract inside its own design. Concretely, a third value alongside `internal` and `published`, plus the matchable KEY Anthony named (an id and a description), which is what one design's `required` is matched against another's `published`. Without a key, pairing falls back to fuzzy name matching alone, and names are exactly what two organisations that never coordinated will have chosen differently.

NOT SETTLED HERE: how a pair is recorded — an edge between the two Interfaces, or mirroring one into the other. MIRRORS already exists for the second; there is no edge type meaning "these two boundaries are the same boundary seen from opposite sides", and adding one WOULD move the version stamp and lock out older reflow2 installs.

properties.decision: Parallel alternatives (an analysis of alternatives held open until a decision) are represented BRANCH-BY-FILE: each alternative is a separate exported design (a git branch's reflow2.json, or an export file), not a world-tag inside one live graph. This reuses everything BL-80 built — cross-branch comparison is compare_designs, collapsing the winner is merge_designs/apply_merge, retiring the loser is retire-from-design — so reflow2 owns almost no new branch machinery, consistent with the merge's 'git is the DAG' decision. Semantically, alternatives are design SPACE, not time: sibling alternatives coexist 'now' and CONTRADICT each other, held under a proposed Decision (the decision point) until it collapses — distinct from an epoch (EVOLVES_INTO, before->after). Forking is not advancing time; storage may still be a ref/epoch, but the semantic layer keeps 'the road not taken' apart from 'an earlier version' (BL-70's warning). v1 is the N-way AoA report (analyze_alternatives): measures per branch (graph_report snapshot — nodes, open gaps, allocation health, verification coverage) side by side, plus each branch's structural divergence from a named baseline (compare_designs). Rung 2 wires the decision point: a proposed Decision GOVERNS lightweight alternative pointers that CONTRADICT their siblings; collapsing accepts the Decision, merges the winner into the baseline, and retires the losers with their rationale.
properties.name: AoA alternatives are branch-by-file and live in design-space (CONTRADICTS), not time (epochs)
properties.rationale: User decided both axes 2026-07-22, each the recommended option. Branch-by-file over world-scope because BL-80 already built the comparison (compare_designs), the collapse (merge/apply_merge) and the retire machinery, so branch-by-file is the cheapest increment BL-70 itself named ('one exported graph per alternative plus a cross-export comparison report ... branch-by-file works today') and it is consistent with dec:merge-three-way's 'explicit inputs, git is the DAG'; world-scoping would bake world-awareness into every detector (possible_duplicate, allocation, SPOF, …) — a large invasive change for a simultaneous-in-one-graph benefit not yet needed, and BL-70 says branch-by-file 'teaches what the real scoping primitive must preserve' first.
