Kept separate from dec:live-tier because the mechanism choice is separable: (b) is worth building for a single team on the repo-file architecture, with no hosting at all, the moment anyone wants it.

properties.name: Reviewed: gap:034e96a2e1a7f4d0
properties.rationale: Deferred on Anthony's word, 2026-07-28, with the rest of the reflow workflow review. Accepted and not dropped, and unusually concrete for a parked item: the mechanical half is specified in the requirement and needs no LLM — does every node type and edge type NAMED in a hint exist in the merged schema, and does every relationship a hint asserts have a corresponding edge type declared between those endpoints. Both are answerable from the schema alone and both would have caught the Anchor case, where two hints assert an Anchor-to-DriftEvent DEPENDS_ON with zero instances and no code path, while passing validate_schema.py cleanly. Deferred rather than built because it is coupled to dec:anchor-retire-or-implement: writing the check before deciding whether Anchor is retired, implemented or aliased would either red-light the build on a type about to be removed, or bless prose about to be rewritten. Decide the Anchor question first, then the check has a known-good corpus to run against. Also worth carrying forward: the check must not overreach — whether a hint's ADVICE is good stays a human question, and a linter that pretended otherwise would be the flattering default this design keeps refusing.

properties.name: Reviewed: gap:07bb37be6d5cd129
properties.rationale: User (who:ajs, standing policy from 2026-07-23, re-applied 2026-07-26): validation happens through the trials programme — docs/trials/ is where "built the right thing" is exercised against operational intent; formal validation-kind Verification nodes are not this project's tracking mechanism. properties.name: Reviewed: gap:0a63dc6a6c47e039
properties.rationale: Deferred on Anthony's word, 2026-07-28. Accepted and not dropped. Deferred because the fix is a schema change and the open question underneath it is not settled: should weight_basis default at all, or be absent until a weight exists (the answer ver:interface-spec already gave for Interface.medium)? properties.name: Reviewed: gap:0a77650b58242054
properties.rationale:
Anthony's standing policy from 2026-07-23, unchanged: validation for this project is the trials programme — reflow2 used on real designs, logged in docs/trials/ and docs/trials-private/ (the brownfield ophyd-service pass, the greenfield aidrone pass) plus sustained real use of the StoryFlow fleet. Formal validation-kind Verification nodes are not this project's tracking mechanism, and recording 68 near-identical ones would turn the number green without anyone having checked anything — the dishonesty `dec:passing-is-verified` exists to prevent.

ACCEPTED AT 68 CAPABILITIES, and the count is recorded here on purpose: this gap's id is now keyed on its RULE rather than its member set (`dec:aggregate-gap-keyed-on-rule`), so this acknowledgement CARRIES as the design grows instead of expiring on every addition. That is the fix for the churn — the same disposition had been re-recorded about twenty times, at 33, 34, 35 … 65, 67 and 68 capabilities. The trade-off is deliberate: a capability added tomorrow is covered by this judgement without a fresh look, which is what a standing disposition means. The growth stays VISIBLE without the churn, by comparing the count named here against the count in the live gap's title — if that gap says 90 and this says 68, twenty-two capabilities joined under a judgement made when there were 68, and whether that still holds is a question a reader can now actually ask.

This should be the last acknowledgement this gap ever needs. If it re-fires because the id moved again, the keying regressed and `an_aggregate_gaps_id_does_not_move_when_the_population_grows` should have caught it.

properties.name: Reviewed: gap:101a69b0a4f8eed6
properties.rationale: Standing disposition for planned-but-unbuilt capabilities (user's 2026-07-23 call, applied again 2026-07-24). Naming the check now because this one is unusually easy to fake, and the obvious test would be worthless: asserting that requirements recovered from a suite come back looking correct proves nothing, since they were derived from that suite. The real check is the NEGATIVE one — recover intent from a passing suite, then assert those requirements do NOT read as verified or delivered on the strength of the same tests that produced them, and that cap:derived-completion (BL-104) refuses to count them. A companion case should recover from a FAILING test and assert it lands as an open gap rather than a satisfied requirement, since that is the one signal in this area that cannot be circular. If this capability is ever built and its verification only demonstrates successful extraction, the verification is wrong even when it passes.

properties.name: Reviewed: gap:1947285897ace4dc
properties.rationale: Deferred on Anthony's word, 2026-07-28, closing the reflow workflow review. The MCP 2026-07-28 specification removes protocol-level sessions and the Mcp-Session-Id header; reflow2's seat-per-client rests on rmcp building a service per session, which is a consequence of those sessions existing. The feature lifecycle policy guarantees a minimum twelve-month window between deprecation and removal, so there is time, but the deadline is somebody else's to set. Deferred rather than started for two reasons. The dependency is pinned at rmcp = "2" and the migration realistically lands with rmcp v3, so the work is gated on an SDK that is still in beta — starting now would be building against a moving target. And the design question underneath is not mechanical: the spec's prescribed replacement is a server-minted handle passed as an ordinary tool argument, which is arguably BETTER than inheriting identity from a transport detail (it works identically across stdio, HTTP and whatever comes next), but deciding how a client obtains and carries that handle without putting a parameter in front of every human is the actual work. Revisit when rmcp v3 stabilises; do not let it sit until the window closes.

properties.name: Reviewed: gap:c628f709c27ad035
properties.rationale:
LEFT OPEN ON PURPOSE — Anthony's call 2026-07-31. The requirement is HIS OWN idea, captured the same day; accepting this gap parks the MODELLING question, not the intent.

WHAT BLOCKS IT IS A REAL VOCABULARY PROBLEM, FOUND BY CHECKING AND RECORDED SO NOBODY RE-DERIVES IT. The first answer given was "reflow2 already has the vocabulary — model the release procedure as a Flow". THAT IS WRONG AS THE SCHEMA STANDS: PART_OF_FLOW is declared Capability -> Flow and accepts nothing else, so a Flow's steps must be Capabilities. "Bump the version in three files" is a chore, not a capability. Modelling seven release chores as seven Capabilities would put fake entries into the very set that coverage_report and the verification counts range over — 100 real capabilities plus seven chores makes every one of those reports quietly wrong, permanently. The correction is recorded here rather than edited over the earlier claim.

SO THE OPEN QUESTION IS ONE LEVEL DOWN, AND IT IS GENUINE: is a procedure step a first-class design object, or is it documentation the design POINTS AT? Making it first-class means widening PART_OF_FLOW to accept a step type — which MOVES THE STAMP and locks every older reflow2 out of the design, so it is a release-shaped decision, not a side edit. Pointing at it instead means writing the procedure as a document in the content store (which now exists) and referencing it from the Project — cheap, no schema change, but an agent reads prose rather than querying steps, which is most of what was asked for.

WHY NOT NOW: v0.20.0 was deliberately scoped to cap:changelog-view ALONE, and a schema change is not a side quest to slip in beside it. Nothing is lost by waiting — the requirement holds the reasoning and the derivability argument, and the seven recovered steps are written down outside the graph in the meantime.

THE ONE THING NOT TO DO is build it as a Flow of invented Capabilities to make this note go away. That would trade a visible open question for a silently wrong metric, which is the exact trade req:no-silent-fallback exists to forbid.

THE EVIDENCE STANDS AND IS NOT WEAKENED BY THE PARK: cutting v0.19.0 required reconstructing seven steps from `git show v0.18.0` plus a grep, and at least two of them — that an upgrade doc is owed ONLY when the schema stamp moves, and that the release manifest must be exhaustive with nothing computing it — were discoverable only from a past commit message.

properties.statement: Anthony's reframe, 2026-07-25, of what to do with the GitHub-MCP study's larger lessons: rather than hold them as a roadmap of features to build, hold them as a rule about what NOT to do now — do not take a shortcut today that would make it impossible for reflow2 to become what GitHub's MCP server is. A roadmap ages badly and gets stale in a document nobody reads; a non-foreclosure rule is checkable at the moment of the decision that would break it, which is the only moment it matters. THE SPECIFIC FORECLOSURES, from reading github-mcp-server (each one a shortcut that is tempting precisely because there is one writer today): (1) IDENTITY IN A GLOBAL. Authority must arrive with the caller and be read from the request, never stashed in a process-wide variable or resolved once at startup — GitHub constructs a fresh server per request in stateless mode for exactly this reason, and their lockdown cache carries the warning that a viewer-scoped lookup shared across requests runs under the wrong user's credentials. (2) INVENTING AUTHORITY. reflow2 must never become the thing that decides who may read what; it delegates to an authority that already exists, on GitHub's stated principle that a server must not let anyone reach more than they could reach without it. Building an account system would foreclose that by making reflow2 the authority. (3) TREATING THE SINGLE-WRITER LOCK AS A CONTRACT. One RocksDB handle is an implementation fact; the day it is a promise in a tool description or a skill, concurrency becomes a breaking change rather than a build. (4) CONFIG THAT WIDENS. Per-request configuration must only ever NARROW what the deployment allowed — GitHub's headers can restrict within static bounds and can never re-include what was excluded, and any read-only surface that a header can talk out of read-only was never read-only. (5) ONE GRAPH ASSUMED EVERYWHERE. graph_id already exists on every node and edge and is pinned to a constant; code that assumes the constant rather than reading the field is the foreclosure, not the constant itself. (6) TRUSTING TEXT BY ITS LOCATION. Once a design can arrive from someone else, text is untrusted because of where it came from, not because of which field it sits in — so the trust boundary belongs at ingress, before anything reads it. WHAT THIS RULE IS NOT: it is not a licence to build the hosted service, and not a reason to add abstraction now. Every item above is a constraint on shortcuts, satisfiable by writing the simple version carefully — the point is that the simple version stays a strict subset of the eventual one, so nothing has to be undone. ENFORCEMENT DECIDED 2026-07-25 (Anthony: "go with your recommendation"): ADVISORY, `enforced: false`, and deliberately so. VIOLATES_RULE is a vocabulary item no detector reads, so declaring this gate-blocking would promise a check that does not exist — the exact failure the KPP work was built to end ("a KPP that nothing checks is a comment"). The rule is the project's rule, confirmed by its author; the flag says only that no build has been stopped by it yet. It flips to enforced the day a detector can read a foreclosure from graph state — the honest first candidate being (4) and (5), which are mechanically checkable, unlike (2), which is a judgement about architecture.

properties.spec: Corrected 2026-07-28: this claimed `medium: REST` because REST was the schema default, and it is a Rust library API linked directly by callers — no transport, no wire, no endpoint. The false value was never chosen by anyone; it arrived by default.

properties.name: Design export document
properties.spec: Corrected 2026-07-28: claimed `medium: REST` by default. It is a JSON document written to a path and read back — a data contract, not a network one. Its shape is the export schema (nodes, edges, graph_id, stamp, content_hash, prev_content_hash).

properties.name: MCP tool surface
properties.spec: MEDIUM IS KNOWN-WRONG AND THE CORRECTION IS OWED. `REST` here was never chosen — it arrived as the schema default, which was changed to `unspecified` on 2026-07-28 (req:seam-incompatibility) precisely because a default must not assert a technology. This value could not be corrected in the same session: the live MCP server is the binary from session start and its schema predates the new enum value, so it refused the write. Fix after an /mcp reconnect. AND THE VOCABULARY HAS NO RIGHT ANSWER YET, which is the more interesting half: MCP is JSON-RPC 2.0 carried over EITHER a stdio pipe to a launched process OR streamable HTTP, and reflow2 serves both from one surface. `REST` is wrong (not resource-oriented; the HTTP transport is a single endpoint), `cli` is wrong for the HTTP case, `gRPC` is a different protocol. The enum wants `json_rpc`, or a way for one contract to name two media. Raised for Anthony rather than guessed: inventing schema vocabulary is a design decision, and asserting a wrong-but-plausible value is the exact failure that produced this whole correction.

properties.answer: Anthony, 2026-07-27: "go with your recommendation: the interface." Recorded as `dec:pairing-role-placement` (accepted) and `req:complementary-pairing` moved to accepted. The role extends `Interface.designation` rather than becoming a per-node attribute — a Component both publishes and subscribes, so a per-node role collapses to `both` and pairs with everything. AMENDED 2026-07-28 after the dynograph-foundation trial refuted the first draft of the matching key: base-compatibility is `medium` PLUS `transport_security` PLUS `auth`, because role-plus-medium alone would pair a consumer requiring REST against a public unauthenticated liveness probe. properties.question: Does the publish/subscribe role belong on the interface itself — extending the `published` flag with a third value meaning "I need one of these from outside" — or on every node, as you described it? Recommendation: the interface. A component both publishes and subscribes, so a single role on a component collapses to `both` and pairs with everything, which is the only reason `both` is needed at all. On an interface, `both` stays rare and means something real.

properties.name: v0.13.0
properties.notes: Cut 2026-07-25. A minor bump — CLAIMS gains a `seat` property (additive) — with docs/upgrading-to-v0.13.0.md written. THE RELEASE THAT MAKES CONCURRENCY HONEST, and every piece of it came from Anthony's own StoryFlow fleet. (1) A DESIGN KNOWS ITS OWN NAME: an id established on first open in <graph>.id.json, a sibling of the store because the id namespaces every stored key; minted with zero coordination; refused rather than defaulted when unreadable; and a store that already holds a design under the old shared id ADOPTS it, which is what keeps every committed export valid since graph_id is inside the content hash. Two on-disk designs can finally mirror each other. (2) CLAIMS NAME THEIR SESSION and claim_report COMPUTES liveness from the OS: a claim whose session exited is `gone`, listed in `stale` with its note, and excluded from overlaps, because a collision with nobody is not a collision; another machine is `unknown` and still counts. (3) THE LOOP'S SAFETY NET IS PROVEN AND INSTALLED: the nudge path is tested by running the REGISTERED hook command as registered, the server reports installed | absent | broken | unknown, the absence rides the handshake instructions, and reflow2_init now registers the hook it never used to — into .claude/settings.local.json, pointing at the kit so it updates with the package. Manifest: 68 artifacts with frozen cut-time checksums plus cmp:docs, cmp:skills and cmp:claims. Four of the five fleet lessons are now built; req:read-while-held remains blocked on dynograph-storage exposing open_as_secondary.

properties.name: v0.14.0
properties.notes: Cut 2026-07-26. A minor bump — no schema change, nothing breaks, nothing in a consumer repository changes — so no upgrade doc; the version moves because capabilities were added, not because anything is asked of the user. THE RELEASE THAT LETS SEVERAL SESSIONS SHARE ONE DESIGN, INCLUDING ACROSS MACHINES, and the value is in the three cases being told apart rather than blurred. (1) DIFFERENT PROJECTS ON ONE MACHINE never needed anything: each has its own graph directory, so each session runs its own server and they never meet — confirmed by measurement rather than assumed. (2) THE SAME PROJECT ON ONE MACHINE needs a SERVER (--http <addr>), because the store is single-writer PER PROCESS: six processes cannot each open the directory, but one process holding it with six sessions attached still has exactly one writer, so the constraint is satisfied rather than worked around. Underneath: the graph moved Mutex→RwLock so reads stop queueing (and the compiler audited the read/write split for free — all 32 read sites genuinely need only &DesignGraph), and seats are minted per SESSION rather than per process, without which a shared server reports every client as the same owner and claim_report tells six sessions they are each other. (3) THE SAME PROJECT FROM ANOTHER MACHINE additionally needs the host NAMED (--http-allow-host), because the transport answers only requests whose Host header is allowlisted — loopback by default. That is DNS-rebinding protection, and since reflow2 has no authentication it is the only thing between a web page the user visits and their design, so reachability off-box is a deliberate act rather than a side effect of binding a public address. The flag EXTENDS the default rather than replacing it, so naming a remote machine can never lock out the local sessions already on that server; and a reachable bind with no named host now WARNS at startup instead of refusing every remote session with a bare 403 and saying nothing. LIVE SHARING HAS A CENTRE and the docs say so: the machine running the server, which cannot sleep and cannot be offline — so it does not replace the git route for two people working independently. They compose: share live while both are at it, commit and push the export when done. Proven over real HTTP against real servers, with the Host header a remote session actually sends: 9 cases in CI. Manifest: 71 artifacts with frozen cut-time checksums plus cmp:docs, cmp:skills and cmp:claims. THE GATE EARNED ITS KEEP AGAIN — cargo fmt reordered an import after the checksum baseline had been accepted, and the drift was caught rather than shipped.

properties.name: v0.15.0
properties.notes: Cut 2026-07-26, the same day as v0.14.0. A MINOR bump because the schema moved, with docs/upgrading-to-v0.15.0.md written — and the upgrade doc's honest headline is that there is nothing to do. TWO THINGS SHIP. (1) `Verification.method` gains `demonstration` and `observation`, from Anthony's own taxonomy. Test, analysis, inspection and DEMONSTRATION are the four canonical verification methods in DoD and INCOSE practice and reflow2 carried three of them, so 'we showed it working' — which is how a great deal of acceptance actually gets closed — had to be miscoded as a test; `observation` is the as-fielded method, watching a system run without changing it, which is neither inspecting an artifact nor running a contrived example. `review` and `simulation` are KEPT, because removing a value would strand every node carrying it. Additive: an older reflow2 still READS a graph containing the new values — PROVEN by building a binary with the previous value set and pointing it at one — and only refuses to write them, since validation runs on write and the stamp counts node/edge TYPES (unchanged at 28/55). (2) THE v0.14.0 REGRESSION IS FIXED, found the same day it shipped and by hand rather than by any detector: with the graph held AND --http given, the degraded surface was served over STDIO and nothing listened on the port, so every session pointed at that URL got a refused connection — indistinguishable from reflow2 never having been configured, which is exactly the outage req:never-silently-absent exists to end. serve_http is now generic over the service it carries so both arms answer on the transport requested, and the startup line distinguishes the surfaces. The four new cases were MUTATION-CHECKED: reverted against v0.14.0 all four fail with 'nothing ever listened on the port the caller asked for'. ALSO RECORDED THIS CUT, built or not: dec:read-while-held-mechanism DECIDED (a read-only view as of open, not a catchable-up secondary) and req:verification-keeps-up ACCEPTED with cap:verification-freshness planned — the design now knows that a passing check proves only the paths it drives, which is the general form of the bug this release fixes. Manifest: 72 artifacts with frozen cut-time checksums plus cmp:docs, cmp:skills, cmp:claims.

properties.name: v0.16.0
properties.notes: Cut 2026-07-27. A MINOR bump, and the FIRST since v0.11.0 that genuinely locks an older reflow2 OUT: PERFORMED_IN takes the schema from 55 edge types to 56, and the version stamp counts edge TYPES, so a reflow2 older than this refuses a design written by it — loudly, never silently half-read. Machines sharing a graph must upgrade together; docs/upgrading-to-v0.16.0.md leads with that. The enum growth in the same window (Verification.method += demonstration/observation in v0.15.0, Environment.env_type += simulation here) does NOT do this, and the doc says why. THE RELEASE THAT MAKES A PILE OF DOCUMENTS INTO A DESIGN. (1) SP-3b/BL-7 CLOSED after months: `ingest` needed a language model, reflow2 ships no provider, and the calling agent could not be reached mid-run — so the whole extraction pipeline was unreachable from a session. `ingest_step` is the repeated-round collect-then-serve handshake agent.rs had specified since SP-2 and nothing had driven; three or four rounds, NOTHING WRITTEN until the last (prepare rounds replay against a throwaway graph, so an abandoned handshake strands nothing), and NO server-side session state, so it survives a restart and works across seats. (2) It now recovers RATIONALE and TEST EVIDENCE, not requirements alone — and both land unasserted, a recovered Decision `proposed` and a recovered Verification `planned`, because an extraction is an agent's reading of somebody's document rather than the user's signature. Making that safe required tightening unverified_capability to demand a PASSING check: it had skipped on any incoming VERIFIES, so attaching a planned one silenced the question the detect-and-ask skill has always said it should not. (3) NEAR-MATCHES ARE ASKED ABOUT: ingest reads the two thresholds the schema had declared and nothing read, and the band between them reports instead of guessing; a structural token-subset pass catches what scoring cannot, since `Gateway` vs `API Gateway` scores 74 — below any threshold, because ratios fall as length differs. Imported from storyflow, which has fought this for years. (4) BL-95: coverage_report says what the design has never been TOLD ABOUT — every other check reasons about nodes already in the graph, so a design covering a third of a system reported the same `0 open gaps` as one covering all of it. Rolled up and ranked by mass, never a score: an artifact whose location is a directory claims what is beneath it. adopt now ends by asking. (5) req:design-the-simulator ACCEPTED and its first rung built: a check records WHERE it ran, so `proven only in simulation` becomes sayable — the reason for the schema change, since simulating first only pays if you can still tell model from reality afterwards. (6) BL-107: the export lineage chain is now CHECKED by the gate, found because I broke it for six commits while nothing noticed. Manifest: 78 artifacts with frozen cut-time checksums plus cmp:docs, cmp:skills, cmp:claims.

properties.name: v0.17.0
properties.notes:
Cut 2026-07-28. A MINOR bump that locks NOBODY out: no node or edge type was added, so the stamp holds at 28/56 and an older reflow2 still opens a design written by this one — the opposite of v0.16.0, and the upgrade note leads with it. The one real cost is a slow first build, because the dynograph-foundation pin moved v0.11.0 → v0.12.0.

THE RELEASE THAT MADE TWO REPOS CHECK EACH OTHER. Almost everything here was found by running reflow2 against a second real project rather than by reviewing it: dynograph-foundation published its surface, reflow2 composed against it, and each side found defects the other could not see. Three of the fixes are in reflow2 itself, and every one was invisible to inspection and obvious the moment something real ran through it.

(1) A PUBLISHED SURFACE CAN CARRY A PROMISE (req:publishable-promise). export_surface withheld every Requirement as internal, behavioural commitments LIVE in Requirements, so the document offered as 'the published surface' carried structure and no promises. Found when a real provider could not tell a real consumer the one thing it most needed — that a missing store fails loud rather than silently falling back to memory. The promise survived only as a comment in the CONSUMER's build file, on the wrong side of the seam. Requirement.designation fixes it by reusing the mechanism whose semantics were already settled, so every existing check applies unchanged rather than through a second, unchecked channel.

(2) DECLARE WHICH VERSION OF ANOTHER DESIGN YOU DEPEND ON (req:design-dependencies-declared). The trial made it load-bearing: without a recorded pin there is nothing to take a surface AS OF, and the two real consumers sit two minors apart, so an offer from main described neither. Two facts kept apart — what you MEAN to depend on, and what the build ACTUALLY resolves — because storing only one gives either a document that drifts or a fact nothing can contradict. Proven on the real dependency and on a simulated undeclared bump.

(3) TWO DESIGNS ANALYSED TOGETHER without either being written to (compose_and_analyse), and AN INTERFACE THAT PUBLISHES ITS WHOLE CONTRACT (set_interface_spec). The composition's most useful result was a ZERO: with the seam hand-drawn, the ordinary detectors found nothing, which proved they check CONNECTIVITY and not COMPATIBILITY — no ordinary detector compares two nodes' properties across a pair. That measurement is what req:seam-incompatibility now rests on.

(4) THE INSTALL REACHES THE FILE THE AGENT READS. Installing into a repo with no instruction file wrote AGENTS.md, reported success, and stayed invisible to a harness that reads CLAUDE.md first — the same defect class the installer already documented from storyflow, in the opposite direction. The rule is now REACH WHAT READS. The eight slash commands ship with the kit as the one narrow exception to serving everything (dec:commands-are-the-exception), with the single way a command can rot — naming a skill that no longer exists — closed by a lint.

(5) CORROBORATION READS AS CORROBORATION. Recording that one decision QUALIFIES another turned the graph red, because the contradiction detector read the edge type and never alignment. Fixed with both counterweights tested: an opposing edge and an edge that says nothing are still contradictions, so no design written before this release changes meaning.

THE FOUNDATION BUMP WAS NOT HOUSEKEEPING, which AGENTS.md forbids. v0.12.0 closes a type leak reflow2 was structurally exposed to — search_fulltext returned dynograph_text::TextHit, from a crate reflow2 never names and reaches only through an optional feature — and makes the rocksdb and fulltext feature NAMES a committed contract upstream. Verified safe BEFORE the tag existed by building this consumer against the provider's unreleased tree. Migration checked rather than assumed: keys.rs and backend.rs are untouched between the tags, so a graph written by v0.11.0 reads identically.

properties.name: v0.19.0 — the planning axis runs forward: planned epochs, the satisfaction schedule, and the arrival delta
properties.notes:
Cut 2026-07-31. A MINOR bump that LOCKS OLDER REFLOW2 OUT: SCHEDULED_FOR takes the schema from 56 edge types to 57 and that moves the stamp, so a design written by this version is refused by anything earlier (BL-19/BL-94) — upgrade every machine that touches a shared graph, together. Node types hold at 28 and the dynograph-foundation pin stays at v0.12.0, so there is no slow first build. Upgrade note: docs/upgrading-to-v0.19.0.md.

THE PLANNING AXIS RUNS FORWARD. plan_epoch creates a point that has NOT happened, set_epoch_status moves it to arrived, and schedule_for hangs work off it as SCHEDULED_FOR carrying modality expected|required. arrival_delta then answers Anthony's question in his words — 'what didn't we achieve that we were supposed to in increment 10?' — with five outcomes, the fifth (outstanding) being the case the original four assumed away: nobody touched it and it did not happen. The baseline is the target's FIRST snapshot, because the last would measure only the most recent replan and the slip would vanish from the report meant to show it. Nothing about the outcome is stored; delivery stays computed from the golden thread.

THE DESIGN CAN NOW HOLD WHAT IT POINTS AT. content_put / content_get / content_exists / content_manifest — a content-addressed store, COMMITTED to the repo, for what INFORMED the design as against what it produced. Hand-rolled in the core, zero new crates compiled. The manifest is DERIVED from the graph and never stored, because a stored manifest would be a second source of truth able to drift. What bounds the store is WHAT gets stored, measured rather than assumed: 29 session transcripts came to 115.8 MB against 81 MB for the entire .git history, which inverted dec:content-manifest's assumption that images were the risk — so the control is transcripts-by-exception, not a size cap.

AND THE CUT TRIGGER STOPPED BEING VACUOUSLY TRUE. ready_to_cut now demands at least one required obligation as well as an empty miss list; an increment promising nothing used to read as ready, which is the empty-release failure dec:release-trigger was chosen to prevent arriving through its own back door.

MANIFEST: 151 INCLUDES — 98 artifacts and 53 components. THE FIRST CUT TO FREEZE as_checksum ON EVERY ARTIFACT, so this release's manifest cannot quietly rewrite itself when a baseline later moves; the nine prior cuts recorded nulls. New this release: art:content (the store), art:content-test (12 cases, registered here because every sibling core test file already was and this one was missed), art:stateless-seat-probe, and art:upgrading-v0190. Every frozen hash was verified against the file on disk after export.

epoch:v0190 at sequence 240, preceded by epoch:arrival-delta. Verified by CI on the same runners that build the release binaries.

properties.name: v0.20.0 — the changelog becomes a derived view of the graph's own delta, and three fixes found by pointing reflow2 at a real project
properties.notes:
Cut 2026-08-01. A MINOR bump that DOES NOT MOVE THE STAMP: node types hold at 28 and edge types at 57, so a design written by this version still opens in v0.19.0 and there is no upgrade doc. The dynograph-foundation pin stays at v0.12.0, so no slow first build.

THE CHANGELOG BECAME A DERIVED VIEW. changelog_view renders the delta between two moments of this design in Keep a Changelog shape, with every bucket MAPPED from vocabulary the graph already records and every entry naming the rule that placed it. It is a DRAFT by construction: no entry claims what a consumer should do, because the graph holds what moved and never what it costs downstream.

THREE FIXES, ALL FOUND BY POINTING REFLOW2 AT A REAL PROJECT — a quantum-benchmarking concept designed end to end through this tool, which logged nineteen entries of friction and produced BL-124 through BL-137. (1) A bare content hash no longer reports drift on a file nobody touched: canonical_checksum ran on the two WRITE paths and never on the comparison, so the first honest reconcile_artifacts reported 100% false drift. (2) An acknowledgement is no longer design structure: the review Decision was wired GOVERNED_BY into the island it acknowledged, enlarging it and minting a new id, which made disconnected_community permanently unclosable. Fixed at design_network() rather than the defect-id hash because that network has three consumers — and the instrument showed centrality was badly distorted (four of the eight most central nodes were review records) while surprising_connections moved the OPPOSITE way to the prediction, 16 to 32, because the bookkeeping edges were SUPPRESSING real surprises. (3) set_interface_spec accepts medium, so the library/data foundation exemption from single_point_of_failure is reachable from the tools rather than only from create_node.

AND A RELEASE THAT NAMES NO MOMENT IS NOW REPORTED. release_without_epoch found three on this project's own graph; v0.17.0 is still missing its edge to this day.

MANIFEST: 155 INCLUDES — 102 artifacts and 53 components, every artifact hash frozen as as_checksum. New this release: art:checksum-dialect-test, art:acknowledgement-not-structure-test, and art:bl124-instrument (the before/after instrument, registered because it was written during this increment and BL-95 is precisely about files the design was never told of). epoch:v0200 at sequence 243, preceded by epoch:reading-carries-options, with the three ChangeEvents of this increment pinned AT_EPOCH — the step BL-137 was filed for, because changelog_view silently drops an unpinned event.

properties.name: v0.9.0
Evidence a value was fitted to cannot also count as that value's validation
properties.statement: When a value in the design was derived from a piece of evidence, the design must record what it was derived from, and must not let a check resting on that same evidence count as independent validation of it. Agreement with the anchor a value was fitted to is a fit, not a test, and must be reported as consumed. A capability whose only passing checks are consumed in this way must read as not independently verified. This cannot be computed from the strength of the evidence, only from its structure: no check internal to a design can establish its own independence, so the design must record the relation rather than attempt to detect the circularity.

properties.name: A hint that names a skill must name it as the next CALL, not as a parenthetical — a citation is read as attribution, not instruction
properties.statement:
Where reflow2 tells an agent which skill to use, it must phrase it as the call to make next rather than as a trailing reference. MEASURED, and this is the whole evidence: `add_capability` returned `loop_hint: "loop: wire satisfies to the requirement this serves, then run detect_gaps when the capture batch lands (detect-and-ask)"`. The agent that received it DID wire `satisfies` and DID run `detect_gaps` — and did NOT load `detect-and-ask`. The imperative clauses were obeyed; the skill name in parentheses was read as an attribution for where the advice came from, not as a step to take.

So the pointer already exists and already names the right skill — `cap:read-loop-hint` and the write-side `loop_hint` are both `verified` — and it still failed. That makes this cheaper than anything else in this family: the mechanism is built, delivered and correct, and only the wording is losing the effect. `run get_skill("detect-and-ask") first` is a step; `(detect-and-ask)` is a footnote.

SCOPE: every place reflow2 names a skill to an agent — the write tools' `loop_hint`, the read-side hint, `loop_nudge.py`'s Stop message, the SessionStart orientation, and the MCP server instructions. The rule is one line: if a skill is worth naming, name the call.

NOT PROPOSED: making the hints longer or more numerous. The finding is about grammar, not volume, and a hint that grows is a hint that gets skimmed — the failure `dec:read-hint-shape` already guarded against by firing only when the debt is real.

properties.name: A design records how its project actually ships
properties.statement:
A design that has Releases shall also record the ordered procedure for producing one — the steps, their order, and the external conventions they depend on — so that cutting a release is read from the design rather than reconstructed from what was done last time.

ANTHONY'S WORDS, 2026-07-31, raised while watching the v0.19.0 cut: "should every reflow2 project have a requirement to describe its 'release instructions'? ... having a set of release instructions (what are all the steps that need to occur) would be nice. Then the agent doesn't have to look at what was done previously to release or whether it was released on pypi or whatever makes sense for the project being developed."

THE VOCABULARY ALREADY EXISTS AND SHOULD BE USED RATHER THAN EXTENDED. A release procedure is an ordered process, which is what Flow models: add_flow, part_of_flow with step_order, TRIGGERS transitions carrying a role, read back by flow_report. This wants no new node type and no new document.

WHY THIS IS NOT dec:orientation-is-computed-not-written IN REVERSE. That decision refused a START-HERE file because orientation is DERIVABLE — a projection of design state, so the answer was build the view. Release steps are NOT derivable from the graph: which registry (PyPI / crates.io / GitHub releases / a manufactured build), which workflow, which credential, what the tag format is, which files carry a version claim. These are facts about the world outside the design, and no projection can compute them. The same derivability test therefore argues FOR recording them. That distinction is the load-bearing part of this requirement: record what cannot be computed, compute what can.

EVIDENCE, from the v0.19.0 cut itself. The procedure was reconstructed from `git show v0.18.0` plus grepping AGENTS.md for "release" — seven steps that exist nowhere as a list: the version in three files plus the lockfile; the CHANGELOG heading plus a fresh empty Unreleased; an upgrade doc REQUIRED IF AND ONLY IF the schema stamp moved; version claims in docs/overview.md and AGENTS.md; the graph manifest, release epoch and prior-release retirement; export exactly once onto the committed file; tag and push. At least two of those are unguessable and were discoverable only by reading a past commit message.

WHERE IT BITES AS A DETECTOR: a Project holding Release nodes with no release Flow is a gap worth surfacing, the same shape as unrealized_capability. Scope deliberately unsettled here — whether this is a reflow2-wide obligation on every governed design or advice the genesis/adopt skills ask for is Anthony's call, not this requirement's.

PROPOSED — captured in his wording, not yet his signature.

properties.name: A gap put to the user arrives with the agent's recommendation — recommending is not deciding
properties.statement:
When reflow2 puts a gap to the user, the agent's READING of it travels with the question: what it would do and why, and what would change that answer. The user still decides; the agent stops pretending it has no view.

THE READING HAS A SHAPE, AND THE SHAPE IS PART OF THE REQUIREMENT — added 2026-07-31 on Anthony's word after the pattern was used on him for the five standing gaps: "I really like when I say something like 'go through the decisions I need to make... put them in plain and simple english and offer a recommendation' and then you give me the options to select with your recommended choice on top. I believe there is already a proposed idea... but I really like this process (I think other users will really like this process also), so I'd either like to update the proposed req or cap or backlog item to CEMENT THIS BEHAVIOR."

Three obligations, and they are separable:

(1) THE OPTIONS ARE SELECTABLE, not buried in prose. The user picks rather than composing a reply. Prose that describes three courses of action still leaves them to name one; a list they can choose from does not.

(2) THE RECOMMENDATION COMES FIRST and is marked as such. Position carries meaning: an unordered menu makes the user infer which the agent favours, which is the analysis req:no-se-knowledge exists to spare them. Marking it also makes an overrule VISIBLE — the user knows they are departing from the agent's view, which is the precondition for the finding below.

(3) EVERY OPTION STILL CARRIES ITS CONSEQUENCE, including the ones not recommended. A list of bare labels is worse than prose, because it looks complete while withholding what each choice costs. The counterweight rule below is not relaxed by the format; it is what makes the format honest.

AND THE LANGUAGE IS THE USER'S, NOT ENGLISH — Anthony, same exchange: "with agents able to understand multiple languages, the 'simple english' should be 'simple whatever_language_user_is_writing_in'." The plainness obligation is about REGISTER, not about English: no jargon, no ids, short sentences, in whatever language the user is writing in. cap:surface already says "in the user's WORDS", and this makes the wider reading explicit so nobody implements it as an English-only rule. Every English-language phrasing in these design notes is an example of the register, never a specification of the language.

WHAT IS MISSING TODAY, and it is an omission rather than a prohibition. `detect-and-ask` is explicit that the agent must "never invent an answer on their behalf", which is right and must not be weakened. But the skill says nothing about offering a reading, so the default behaviour is a bare question — `gap_to_prompt` returns "is it covered, deferred, or dropped?" and the agent relays it. `cap:surface` ("turn a gap into a question in the user's words", `verified`) delivers the translation and nothing more.

WHY THAT IS A DEFECT AND NOT NEUTRALITY. `req:no-se-knowledge` says the user never needs systems engineering. A bare gap question hands them back the analysis the agent has already done and asks them to redo it in their own head — which is precisely the SE work that requirement exists to spare them. The agent has read the graph, seen the precedents, and formed a view; withholding it is not impartiality, it is making the user pay for the agent's caution.

IT IS ALSO WHAT `dec:three-party-checks` ALREADY DESCRIBES: "The LLM speaks, the graph remembers and counts, the human decides." Offering a reading IS the LLM speaking. The decision stays with the human, untouched — and `dec:certainty-derived` still governs the write, because a recommendation changes no status until the user answers.

THE LINE THAT MUST NOT BE CROSSED, stated so this cannot be read as licence. Recommending is not deciding: no requirement moves off `proposed`, no decision reaches `accepted`, no gap is acknowledged on a reading the user has not confirmed. And a recommendation must carry WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT — the condition under which the other option wins — or it is steering rather than advising. An option presented without its counterweight is a decision taken quietly.

THE PART WORTH RECORDING, and the reason this is design rather than style: WHEN THE USER OVERRULES A RECOMMENDATION, THAT IS INFORMATION. A design where the agent advised one way and the human chose another has learned something neither party knew alone, and today it is invisible because the recommendation was never on the record. Whether the recommendation itself should be stored beside the question is left open here rather than assumed. NOTE that obligation (2) sharpens this: marking the recommendation is what makes an overrule an identifiable EVENT rather than an unremarkable choice among equals.

MEASURED, not theorised: every gap put to Anthony on 2026-07-31 needed the recommendation added by hand, and he asked for it explicitly TWICE that day — "provide your recommendation", "present them in simple english and your recommendations for how to proceed" — and a THIRD time in the same session, at which point he asked for the behaviour to be cemented rather than repeated. A shape a user has to request each time is a default in the wrong place. This requirement's own evidence therefore accumulated by the exact mechanism it describes.

SCOPE, stated because the third request widened it: this began as a rule about GAPS, and Anthony's framing — "the decisions I need to make" — is broader. The obligation is read as covering any point where the agent puts a CHOICE to the user, not only where detect_gaps produced it. Whether that widening needs its own capability rather than riding this one is left open rather than assumed.

TENSION NAMED SO IT IS NOT CONFLATED: `dec:report-dont-judge` says the confirmation ledger reports claim history and never judges a claim. That governs what a COMPUTATION may assert about evidence. It does not govern whether an agent may advise a human who asked — different actor, different act. Conflating the two would silence exactly the party `dec:three-party-checks` puts there to speak.

properties.name: A system that already exists can be brought under design control
properties.statement: Requirements, functions and structure can be recovered from a running system.

properties.name: Adopting an existing system reports how much of it was actually recovered
properties.statement: reflow2's adopt skill produces a graph of an existing system but has no measure of COMPLETENESS — nothing says what fraction of the codebase reached the design, so "we adopted it" cannot be distinguished from "we adopted the parts we happened to read." The original reflow gated on exactly this: workflow 01e-reverse_engineering.json step RE-06 (Validation and Gap Analysis) computed an extraction coverage percentage by validating the extracted architecture back against the code — identifying unmapped functions (code not in the architecture), undocumented interfaces, and inconsistencies between architecture and code behaviour — and its agent guidance made it a stop condition: "Extraction coverage < 80% requires manual review before proceeding." Its completion criteria repeat it as a required gate. DISTINCT FROM WHAT reflow2 ALREADY HAS. coverage_report measures whether INTENT has been delivered (requirements against the golden thread, per req:completion-computed); this measures whether the AS-BUILT LAYER IS COMPLETE — a different axis and the one adopt needs, because an honest brownfield model must be able to say what it did not see. reconcile_artifacts compares recorded artifacts against disk, which is nearer, but it checks the artifacts the design already names rather than finding the code the design never mentioned. The adopt skill's own doctrine already makes the case: "You only get what you see is not a limitation to paper over: the graph marks what was inferred, confesses what it cannot know" — a coverage figure is that confession made quantitative. Note the granularity caveat adopt is right about: node count tracks distinct contracts and capabilities, NOT lines of code (a 110k-LOC system landed at ~78 nodes while reflow2's own ~34k LOC lands near ~100), so this measure must be expressed in terms adopt actually models — unmapped entry points, unmodelled contracts, untouched modules — never as a nodes-per-LOC ratio, which would punish a coarse-but-honest model. Found 2026-07-28 reviewing the original reflow workflows. Anthony's word: capture it.

properties.name: What a session PRODUCES is captured too — diagrams, mockups and rendered explanations, not just the decisions distilled from them
properties.statement:
Anthony, 2026-07-31: "in many sessions, the agent will create artifacts — things like mermaid diagrams or simple html files showing how a specific feature will work or an html file showing the aesthetic layout of a webpage — having all these artifacts automatically stored in the reflow2 blob storage would be great."

THE GAP THIS NAMES. `Artifact` already exists and can point at a file with a checksum, but it models CODE the design produced — something that lives in the repo and gets built. The things a session generates to explain itself are different: a mermaid diagram of a flow, an HTML mock of a layout, a rendered comparison. They are produced to be LOOKED AT, they are usually thrown away when the session ends, and they are frequently the clearest statement of intent anyone ever made about that feature. A paragraph describing a layout is a poor substitute for the mock that was actually agreed to.

WHY IT BELONGS BESIDE THE DECISION IT SERVED: these artifacts are the visual half of `Decision.rationale`. The reasoning is recorded in text and the picture that made the reasoning obvious is not, so a later reader gets the conclusion without the thing that made it persuasive. This is the same argument `cap:session-memory` makes for the conversation — the connective tissue is what is lost — applied to output rather than dialogue.

AUTOMATICALLY is the load-bearing word, and it is the hard part. A capture that depends on the agent remembering to store its own diagram is subject to exactly the decay `req:skill-use-survives-a-long-session` measures. So this wants a trigger, not a convention — the same family, and it should be designed with it rather than beside it.

WHAT MUST NOT HAPPEN: a store full of every intermediate render nobody will ever open. What is worth keeping is what a Decision or a Capability actually points at; the rest is session litter. Where that line falls is an open question this requirement deliberately does not answer.

properties.name: An agent can drive the whole loop
properties.statement: Every capability is reachable from a coding agent over one surface.

properties.name: Any level of the design can be analysed on its own, and a narrowed answer says what it left out
properties.statement: A person or team responsible for one part of a design must be able to point the detectors at that part and be answered about it — "is my subsystem coherent, what is it owed" — without reading the whole program. Anthony, 2026-07-25, from the satellite case: an organisation building a satellite capability has a space segment, a ground/user segment and a control segment; his team owns the satellite, and more specifically inter-satellite laser communications. He must understand the system of systems, but day to day he needs his own part. Two properties are inseparable from the first. A narrowed answer must NAME WHAT IT WITHHELD — findings elsewhere in the design, and findings that belong to no part in particular — because a team shown only its own corner will conclude the program is healthy, which is the silent-drop failure req:no-silent-fallback forbids, one level up from a truncated read. And narrowing must never become the tool deciding what a team is allowed to worry about: a program-level finding that touches their work still reaches them, marked as the program's rather than theirs. Deliberately silent on WHERE the levels live: a subtree of one graph and a design of its own are both answers to this, and that is the architecture question recorded as dec:nested-graphs.

properties.name: As-designed vs as-built divergence is detectable
properties.statement: Real files on disk are registered as checksummed Artifacts realizing capabilities, so drift between the design and the build is visible rather than assumed.

properties.name: An assumption is recorded as something that can stop being true, and what rests on it is computed
properties.statement:
NOT FROM reflow. Raised 2026-07-28 from ordinary architecture and risk practice, after Anthony's instruction to bring judgement rather than treat reflow's workflows as canon. reflow had no equivalent either; this is a gap in both.

Designs rest on things believed true about the world that nobody controls, and those beliefs are what actually break architectures. reflow2 has no way to say so. Constraint BINDS (a limit the design must respect, and it is enforced). Decision records a choice with rationale (why WE chose, not what we BELIEVED). RISKS and MITIGATES describe something that might go wrong and what reduces it. None of them expresses "this design is sound ONLY WHILE X remains true, and X is not ours to decide" — which is a different object with a different lifecycle: an assumption is not enforced, not chosen, and not a risk to be reduced. It is a proposition that is checked, and that can be INVALIDATED, at which point everything resting on it needs revisiting.

THE MISSING COMPUTATION IS THE POINT, not the node type. Once an assumption is a node with things hanging off it, "assumption X no longer holds" becomes a propagate query with a real answer: these four capabilities and this interface were justified by it. Today that reasoning exists only in prose inside Decision rationale, where nothing can walk it. reflow2 already has every mechanism this needs — propagate_change computes blast radius, cap:freshness says when a claim was last confirmed, DriftEvent records a divergence against reality, and the Verification machinery already distinguishes proof against a model from proof against reality (cap:evidence-fidelity). An assumption is the node those mechanisms are missing.

WHY IT MATTERS PARTICULARLY IN THIS OPERATING CONTEXT. Several organisations, competing partially-built designs, coupled repositories each with its own graph, work delivered as increments. Almost everything load-bearing about the OTHER organisation's system is an assumption: that their interface will not change before your increment lands, that their component means what its name says, that the version they run is the version they declared. req:version-combination-is-an-object pins the versions; nothing records WHY a pinned combination was believed safe or what breaks when it stops being. Evolving a ten-year-old production stack on the fly is the same shape: most of what a change rests on is a belief about code nobody has read recently.

DISTINGUISH FROM WHAT EXISTS, because the boundary is what makes it useful: a Constraint that is violated is a defect in OUR design; an assumption that fails is a change in the WORLD, and the honest response is different — not fix the build, but revisit what was justified by it. Also distinct from a KPP (req:inviolable-intent), which is intent we refuse to weaken; an assumption is a fact we do not control.

OPEN and not decided: whether this is a new node type or Constraint gaining a kind that separates binds-us from believed-of-the-world (the second is cheaper and risks blurring the very distinction that makes it worth having); what edge carries "rests on" (DEPENDS_ON is lateral and already crowded; a dedicated relation may be clearer); and whether an assumption can carry an expiry or a confirmation cadence, which cap:freshness already models for claims and would make "nobody has checked this in six months" computable rather than remembered.

properties.name: Work that drifted can be frozen without freezing the work that did not
properties.statement: reflow2's response to unacceptable drift is all-or-nothing. tools/reflow2_check.py thresholds WHICH findings count — anchored gaps at or above --gap-threshold (default 0.8) fail the build — but the response is a single sys.exit(1) and the whole build goes red. There is no state in which some capabilities are frozen pending a decision while the rest of the work proceeds. reflow could do this. Its rigid-mode resync offered the user two options, and option B was: "Document each drift item as change request, add to context/change_requests.json, BLOCK implementation of drifted features, continue with non-drifted work." The RESYNC_to_P1 path for major drift in rigid mode likewise says "BLOCK until change request approved" — a targeted freeze, not a stopped project. WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN IT SOUNDS. On a system being evolved incrementally against functional production code — Anthony's actual case at NSLS-II, a ten-year-old bluesky stack evolving on the fly — "stop everything until this is resolved" is almost never the right answer, and "carry on regardless" is never the right answer either. Partial blocking is the only response that matches how the work actually proceeds: quarantine what is contested, keep delivering what is not. It is also what makes a gate survivable in a shared repo, where one contested capability currently reddens the build for everyone. WHAT reflow2 ALREADY HAS, so this is a smaller change than it appears: the graph can already say which capabilities are affected (propagate_change gives the blast radius; scope + claim_region give "the part I hold"), and status/proposed already expresses "not agreed yet". What is missing is that nothing READS those to scope a refusal — the gate asks one global question and gives one global answer. OPEN: whether a partial block is advisory (reported, not enforced, per dec:report-dont-judge) or actually refuses writes against the frozen region, and whether the frozen set is computed from the drift's blast radius or named by the user. Found 2026-07-28 reviewing the original reflow workflows. Anthony's word: capture it.

properties.name: Unbounded build iteration is noticed and surfaced — a HARD STOP is one option, not the requirement
properties.statement:
REASSESSED 2026-07-28, same day, on Anthony's instruction not to treat reflow's workflows as canon. First written as "the build loop is bounded, and exhausting the budget forces a return to the design", which took reflow's halt-and-resync as the requirement rather than as one candidate mechanism. The name now separates the two.

THE REAL GAP, which stands on its own: reflow2 MEASURES design erosion under repeated build rounds and never ACTS on it. The erosion trial asks the sharp question — after N rounds of test-fails/fix-code/accept, does the design still describe what it should — and is a regression gate, so the decay is known and quantified. Nothing ever interrupts. A session can iterate indefinitely and reflow2 will faithfully record the drift afterwards. That is a real hole, whatever the response turns out to be.

WHY THE HARD STOP IS DOUBTFUL AS THE ANSWER. reflow halted after three P3/P4 loops and forced a resync to architecture. Three objections. (1) It is PHASE-SHAPED: "go back to P2" presumes there is a P2 to go back to, and reflow2 has layers of a golden thread, not phases. (2) A hard stop is a poor fit for the operating context this project exists for — continual evolution against functional production code, where halting the work is rarely the right answer and is exactly the move that gets a discipline abandoned by the people it is meant to help. (3) Any fixed count is arbitrary. reflow at least ASKED for it (phases/P0_setup elicits the budget, default 3, range 1-10, alongside the mode and drift tolerance) which is better than compiling it in — but eliciting an arbitrary number does not make it meaningful, only chosen.

WHAT IS MORE LIKELY RIGHT, and it fits the discipline reflow2 already committed to. dec:report-dont-judge says report and ask rather than decide; the loop nudge and cap:read-loop-hint already surface debt when it is real without blocking anything. The natural shape here is the same: NOTICE that the build has been iterating without the design moving, and SAY SO with evidence — which is a computed observation, not a threshold. The evidence is already available: unresolved DriftEvents accumulating, a design_holds/design_updated history that confirm.rs can already read as dishonest (five holds with zero design edits), coverage moving the wrong way. Escalation, if any, belongs to req:drift-rolls-up-to-a-score, which was reassessed the same day for the same reason.

DISTINCT FROM cap:budget, which rolls a RESOURCE budget against a Constraint (mass, cost, power). Whatever is built here is about the design PROCESS, and reflow2 has no vocabulary for that.

Worth keeping from the review, because it answers the obvious objection that any of this is waterfall legacy: reflow's own P5_operations phase_definition states "P5 is typically ongoing" and routes production issues back_to_P3_P4 as "a new development cycle". Even the phase model reflow2 inherited did not assume termination. Found 2026-07-28 reviewing the original reflow workflows; reassessed the same day.

properties.name: A claim names its owner, and a claim with no live owner is reported stale
properties.statement: A claim records the session that made it (its harness session id — assigned out of band, so it cannot race), and claim_report distinguishes a claim held by a live seat from one left behind by a session that closed. Liveness is computed from the owner, not asserted by the claim: a claim nobody is working is a ghost that makes the overlap report lie.

properties.name: Design stays coherent across its lifecycle
properties.statement: When anything changes in any phase, the ripples are found and surfaced.

properties.name: Pair two designs by complementary role, so the seam is computed rather than hand-wired
properties.statement:
Anthony's idea (2026-07-27), and the analogy he reached for is load-bearing rather than decorative: RNA strands pair because the bases are COMPLEMENTARY — adenine with uracil, guanine with cytosine — never like-with-like. Applied here: each boundary declares a ROLE — it publishes, it subscribes, it does both, or it is not external at all — and each project publishes only its publish-or-both boundaries with an id and a description. Combining two designs then starts mechanically: match every publisher against every subscriber, associate them, and treat the pair as ONE graph for every ordinary reflow2 check — gaps, defects, god nodes, surprising connections. The pairing is what makes composition cheap; everything after it already exists (cap:composed-analysis).

DECIDED 2026-07-27 (dec:pairing-role-placement, accepted on Anthony's word): the role lives on the INTERFACE, extending `designation`, not on every node. A Component both publishes and subscribes, so a per-node role collapses to `both` and pairs with everything — the `both` value was the tell that the attribute was on the wrong noun.

WHAT REFLOW2 ALREADY HAS. `Interface.designation` is the publish flag (`internal | published`, defaulting to internal because publishing is a commitment). `export_surface` emits published Interfaces plus the Components either side and withholds the rest. `PROVIDES` and `CONSUMES` carry the two roles at the edge level. The publish half works end to end.

WHAT IS MISSING, and it is the whole idea: THE SUBSCRIBE SIDE IS NOT DECLARABLE. A design says what it OFFERS; it cannot say what it NEEDS from outside in a form another design can be matched against. Today a need is a CONSUMES edge pointing at an Interface the consumer modelled INSIDE ITS OWN design — so a match only happens where the consumer already guessed the provider's contract and named it compatibly. Without that half there is no complementary strand.

THREE OUTCOMES, ALL USEFUL: a publisher matched to a subscriber (the seam, computed); a publisher nobody subscribes to (dead surface); a subscriber nothing publishes (an unmet need — the loudest signal there is). Two publishers of one key is a fourth: a duplicated provider, a conflict rather than a match.

THE PAIRING KEY IS NOT NAME ALONE — AMENDED 2026-07-28 AFTER A REAL TRIAL. Complementary role plus a matching key was the first draft, and the dynograph-foundation session refuted it from the provider's side within an hour of the channel opening. Their design carries three `medium: REST` boundaries: `ifc:rest-v1` (TCP, JWT), `ifc:uds` (Unix socket, JWT, `transport_security: physical`) and `ifc:ops-probes` (PUBLIC AND UNAUTHENTICATED BY DESIGN, because an orchestrator's liveness check cannot hold a credential). Under role-plus-medium alone, a consumer declaring "I require REST" pairs against all three — including the unauthenticated probe surface. That is not a near-miss; it is the pairing rule confidently producing a wrong and security-relevant answer.

So base-compatibility is `medium` PLUS `transport_security` PLUS `auth`. Every one of those is already a property on Interface, put there by req:interface-spec-complete; the fault was leaving them out of the key, not a missing field. And the analogy survives the correction better than it started: adenine–uracil is two hydrogen bonds, guanine–cytosine three. COMPATIBILITY WAS NEVER A SINGLE POINT OF CONTACT.

A mismatch on those axes must be REPORTED AS AN INCOMPATIBILITY, never dropped as a non-match. "You publish this, I need this, and we cannot be connected the way either of us is built" is exactly the finding worth having, and silence would hide it.

NAMES ARE STILL FUZZY. `auth-api` against `AuthService` is the Bob/Bobby/Robert problem, already solved once: ingest's two-band resolution (below fuzzy_threshold = no match, between = a reported candidate, above auto_merge_threshold = act) plus the token-subset pass that catches `Gateway` vs `API Gateway`. Reuse that rather than inventing a second matcher, and ASK about the middle band (dec:ask-not-repair).

UNLABELLED MUST NOT READ AS `non_external`. A boundary nobody classified silently counting as internal means a design that never did the labelling pairs with nothing and reports a clean seam — the blindness cap:coverage exists to end. The pairing report must count and name what carries no role, as coverage_report does.

properties.name: Whether intent has been delivered is computed from the golden thread, never asserted
properties.statement: A requirement's completion must be derived from evidence already in the graph — something satisfies it, and that capability is realized and its check passes — not set by hand on the requirement itself. A hand-set "done" is a claim that outlives the truth: it survives the capability regressing, the artifact drifting, the verification starting to fail, and it degrades exactly as silently as an unreconciled checksum. Derived completion also makes the reverse question answerable without anyone maintaining it: what fraction of accepted intent is actually delivered, and which requirements are believed-done on evidence that no longer holds. The same rule applies to the rest of the lifecycle: a requirement that stopped being satisfied must be able to say so, rather than remaining green because nobody revisited it.

properties.name: Import one design into another and analyse the whole
properties.statement: reflow2 must be able to bring a dependency's design into a consuming design and run its ordinary analysis over the combined whole, so that composition problems appear as ordinary gaps rather than requiring a bespoke comparator. WHAT BLOCKS IT TODAY IS CONCRETE, not vague: import_graph writes every node under its ORIGINAL id with upsert semantics, so importing design Z into design A means Z's `cap:store` silently overwrites A's `cap:store`. It was built for layering a design onto itself — its own doc says an export can be layered onto a design it references — and using it to compose two DIFFERENT designs would corrupt the consumer without saying so. The other two composition mechanisms do not do this either, and it is worth being exact about why: mirror_surface deliberately imports only the published SURFACE and keeps it foreign, and merge_designs is a three-way merge of two versions of the SAME design. So a fourth thing is needed — a NAMESPACED import where both designs coexist and are separately identifiable. TWO THINGS THAT MUST NOT BE LOST. First, the combined graph must never be mistaken for the consumer's own design: every imported node stays attributable to where it came from, and an export of A must not start shipping Z's internals. Second, project-level detectors would now reason over both designs, so a consumer would see gaps belonging to its dependency — noise that would get the whole feature switched off. cap:scoped-analysis already narrows detection to a region and reports what it left out, so scoping the combined analysis to the seam is the likely answer rather than a new filter. NOTE THE TENSION WITH dec:nested-graphs, which chose a graph per ownership boundary precisely because edges cannot cross stores: this does not overturn that decision — the designs stay separately owned and separately released — but it does mean a THIRD, analysis-only composition alongside the two that exist.

properties.name: Several people can plan against one design without colliding
properties.statement: A team, not a single author, must be able to work on one design at the same time: each person able to see what the others hold, to work in a scope that does not collide with theirs, and to have genuinely overlapping work surfaced as decidable conflicts rather than silent last-writer-wins. Whether this extends to simultaneous editing with live presence, or stops at non-colliding parallel work with good merges, is deliberately not asserted here — it depends on an architecture question that is still open, and the weaker form may be what teams actually need.

properties.name: A pointer resolves for everyone holding the design, not only for the machine that wrote it
properties.statement:
Anthony, 2026-07-31: "as one of the features we've worked on previously was that multiple people could use reflow2, may have to think about how the blob contents can be made available to multiple users of reflow2 on multiple machines? Maybe the git repo also backs-up the blob contents?"

THE REQUIREMENT: any seat holding the design must be able to resolve a pointer to its bytes, or be told plainly that it cannot. A design where half the diagrams open for one person and not the other is worse than one with no diagrams, because the first person cannot tell that the second is missing something.

WHY IT IS THE HARDEST PART OF THE CONTENT STORE, and why it belongs as its own requirement rather than a footnote to `req:content-store-for-what-the-graph-points-at`: the graph already solved distribution by being a FILE — `dec:multi-writer-architecture` chose a repo file plus merge-on-pull precisely so that cloning gets you the design and no service is needed. Blobs do not inherit that for free. A content store that lives only where it was written recreates the exact failure `cap:session-memory` already names about machine-local paths, one layer up: it resolves for one person and silently misses for everyone else.

THIS IS ALSO WHERE THE COMMITTED-OR-GITIGNORED QUESTION IS ACTUALLY DECIDED. `dec:where-content-lives` asks it as a repo-weight trade-off; read through this requirement it is not really about weight at all, it is about whether the bytes are DISTRIBUTED BY THE SAME MECHANISM AS THE DESIGN. Anthony's own suggestion — let the git repo carry the blobs — is the option that makes distribution automatic and identical to how the design already travels, at the cost of repo size and git's poor handling of binary churn. The alternative is a second distribution channel, which means a second thing to configure, be down, or be out of step.

WHAT MUST HOLD EITHER WAY: an unresolvable pointer FAILS LOUD and is nameable (`req:no-silent-fallback`), and content is addressed BY HASH so a blob fetched from anywhere can be verified as the right one — which also makes several distribution mechanisms interchangeable rather than requiring one to be chosen forever.

NOT SETTLED HERE: the mechanism. That stays with `dec:where-content-lives`, which this requirement reframes rather than answers.

properties.name: The graph holds pointers; a content store holds the bytes — narrative, transcripts, diagrams and drawings travel WITH the design
properties.statement:
Anthony, 2026-07-31: reflow2 should capture session context — the conversation itself — as a narrative snapshot recorded in the graph, the way storyflow already does it. "storyflow has a blob storage setup to actually store all narrative context and pictures, etc, and then the dynograph-foundation just records the pointer to that storage. The benefits is that any session context and generated artifacts or user provided diagrams/drawings can be stored as part of the reflow2 and are persistent."

THE SPLIT IS THE REQUIREMENT: the graph stores a POINTER and the bytes live in a content store beside it. The graph stays small, diffable and queryable — the properties `dec:repo-file-embedded` chose it for — while the things that are large, binary or verbatim stop being second-class.

WHAT THIS UNLOCKS THAT NOTHING ELSE DOES: user-provided DIAGRAMS AND DRAWINGS. The design vocabulary is entirely textual today, and a hand-drawn architecture sketch or a whiteboard photo is exactly the kind of intent that never survives a project — it lives in someone's phone and is gone when they leave. `Artifact` can name a file on disk but nothing carries its content, so a diagram is a path that rots.

IT ALSO FIXES A FLAW THE DESIGN ALREADY NAMED. `cap:session-memory` models the session transcript as a Fragment pointing at `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/<uuid>.jsonl`, and states the problem in its own words: "a path stored as identity resolves for one person on one machine and silently misses for everyone on a shared graph." A content store IS the answer to that — content-addressed bytes travel with the design instead of referring to one person's filesystem. The requirement should be read as completing `cap:session-memory`, not competing with it.

THE CONSTRAINT THAT MUST SURVIVE, from that same capability: a pointer to a 3 MB transcript is a RECEIPT, not documentation. Storing the raw conversation must not become the excuse that stops takeaways being distilled into Decisions and findings — "it is all in the transcript" is the same failure as "it is all in the backlog file", one level down. The store makes the receipt durable; it does not discharge the obligation.

PRIOR ART, and it is a sibling rather than a stranger: storyflow already runs this and shares the dynograph-foundation substrate underneath, so the question is what to import, not what to invent. AGENTS.md rule 6 permits exactly this direction — mine the sibling repos for ideas, land the work here.

DELIBERATELY NOT SETTLED HERE: where the bytes actually live. That is a genuine architecture fork against `dec:repo-file-embedded`, and it is recorded separately as `dec:where-content-lives`.

properties.name: Context cost is MEASURED and budgeted, not estimated at design time
properties.statement:
REASSESSED 2026-07-28, same day, on Anthony's instruction not to treat reflow's workflows as canon. First written as "context consumption is modelled so a path that will not fit is knowable before it is walked", arguing from reflow's design-time estimation. The FINDING is mine and stands; reflow's MECHANISM is the weak half, and the name now says which.

THE FINDING, measured against reflow2's own design and independent of any prior art: DEPENDS_ON declares a coupling-weight facet whose schema comment states its purpose — "weight is a STRENGTH (higher = tighter); invert to a cost for shortest-path/closeness" — and over 3,250 edges, 232 carry weight_basis while ZERO carry weight, frequency or data_volume. The facet is declared and wholly unpopulated, which also explains req:edge-defaults-do-not-assert rather than merely repeating it: weight_basis asserts "estimated" over an absent weight because weights were meant to be there.

WHY DESIGN-TIME ESTIMATION IS THE WEAK PART. reflow made context_consumption a function attribute and the primary edge weight, published estimation guidelines (read_workflow_file 5000-15000 tokens, generate_architecture 5000-15000, and so on), summed along paths, and flagged CRITICAL above 160k. Three problems. (1) The estimates go stale the moment anything changes and nothing ever re-derives them, so the graph accumulates confident numbers nobody has checked — the shape this project keeps rediscovering. (2) They are model-specific: 160k was reflow's environment, tokenisers and context windows differ, and hardcoding one number as a law is the asserting default req:defaults-do-not-assert forbids. (3) Real consumption is dominated by what static structure cannot see — how much a tool actually returns, how many rounds a negotiation takes, what the user pastes in. A statically-summed path cost would be precise and wrong.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY WANTED, and reflow2 already has most of the vocabulary. MEASURE rather than estimate: real sessions produce real costs per tool call and per skill, and weight_basis already distinguishes estimated / evidence / measured — further evidence the facet was designed for observed values, not guesses. Then BUDGET at runtime against what is left, which composes with cap:bounded-reads (a read that would not fit answers with a bounded page and says what it left out) and cap:tool-search (finding a tool on a surface too large to hold) rather than replacing them. A measured cost also feeds req:friction-has-a-baseline honestly, since "this got more expensive across a release" is a regression the baseline should catch.

An estimate is defensible only as a SEED for something never measured, and must read as estimated — which is exactly what weight_basis is for. Fixing the edge default and populating the facet remain two answers to one question and should be decided together. Found 2026-07-28 reviewing 99-meta_analysis.json; reassessed the same day.

properties.name: What an agent cannot infer must travel on the tool, not only in the skill it may never load
properties.statement:
The parts of a skill that are reflow2 CONVENTION — not general good sense — must be reachable from the tool surface itself, because a capable agent reconstructs most of a skill and silently loses the rest.

THE ASYMMETRY THIS RESTS ON, observed 2026-07-31: reading `detect-and-ask` after having worked without it, roughly its first and last steps had already been done unprompted (call `detect_gaps`; re-run it to confirm). What had NOT been done was every reflow2-specific step in between — the `gap_to_prompt` handshake, `answer_question`, and the distinction between answering a gap and acknowledging one. A competent model infers the general shape and drops the local convention, and the loss is INVISIBLE: you cannot know which part of a skill you failed to load.

So the fraction worth relocating is precisely the fraction a model would never guess. A tool description that says "answering a gap and acknowledging it are different acts, and an answered-but-unacknowledged gap stays open" costs one sentence and cannot be skipped, because the schema arrives with the call.

THE TENSION, named rather than glossed: `dec:skills-served` chose to serve skills from the server so they always match the running version and nothing in a consumer's repo goes stale. That is right, and this does not reverse it. It says the IRREDUCIBLE MINIMUM also rides the tool, where it is unskippable, and the served skill keeps the depth, the worked examples and the reasoning. Two homes for two jobs, not a copy.

THE COST TO WATCH: tool descriptions are context an agent pays for on every session, and `cap:tool-search` exists because the surface is already too large to hold. So this must be a sentence per tool at most, chosen for what cannot be inferred — not a second copy of the skill wearing a different hat.
