{"decision":"UNDECIDED, and RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-07-25, explicitly not convinced by the collaboration design and thinking out loud: \"could you have small/mini reflow2 graphs inside itself... coming from a system of systems engineering approach, reflow2 may lay out the graph and how all the systems need to interact and where there are gaps, but what if we now had a mini-reflow2 graph for each system? And a mini-mini-reflow2 of the components in the system... the idea is that reflow2 has the tools to analyze the graph at each level and ensure there are no gaps and that it works with the higher level systems or system-of-systems.\" WHAT IS ALREADY TRUE, because it changes what the idea is asking for. Levels exist and are already checked: Component.level is an enum of component / subsystem / system / system_of_systems / enterprise, CONTAINS between Components is the axis-Y spine, and hierarchy_issues already reports level_mismatch, missing_intermediate_level and orphan_level — the carburetor-to-body problem, imported from chain_reflow's matryoshka insight (docs/three-axes.md). And the multi-graph primitive exists unused: every node and edge carries graph_id, pinned to the constant \"reflow2\". So the question is not whether reflow2 can express nesting. It can. The question is whether a level should be a SUBTREE of one graph or a GRAPH OF ITS OWN. THREE OPTIONS. (a) ONE GRAPH, ZOOM BY LEVEL — today's shape. What is missing is not nesting but SCOPING: no read takes a subtree as its subject, so detect_gaps and graph_report always answer for the whole design. Adding a scope argument is a filter, not an architecture, and it delivers most of what was asked — the tools analysing each level. (b) A GRAPH PER SYSTEM, COMPOSED — Anthony's idea. It buys four things one graph cannot: an independent write lock per system, which is a different and stronger answer to the collaboration problem than region claims, because separate graphs are PHYSICALLY separate where a claim is only advisory; an independent lifecycle, so a subsystem can be released, adopted or handed to a vendor on its own; selective publishing, which is exactly req:design-reachable-without-the-repo; and per-level scale, since detectors run over hundreds of nodes instead of tens of thousands. (c) A GRAPH PER OWNERSHIP BOUNDARY, LEVELS INSIDE EACH — the hybrid, and the shape federated systems engineering actually uses: you split where AUTHORITY splits, not where the hierarchy happens to have a layer. THE FOUR HARD PARTS of (b), each one real: the golden thread cannot cross a store boundary, because the schema validates both endpoints of every edge — so a parent's Component pointing at a child's design needs a typed COORDINATE (graph id + node id + the export's content hash at the moment the reference was made), which is precisely the choice dec:fork-point-address already made for fork points over a native ref layer. Gap detection goes blind at the seam: a parent requirement whose satisfying capability lives in a child graph would fire unsatisfied forever unless the child's evidence rolls up — and that roll-up is cap:derived-completion's computation applied one level higher, which is encouraging rather than novel. Freshness becomes load-bearing: a parent's view of a child is a claim about a VERSION of that child, so it is a dated examined claim and never a live truth (the cap:freshness and confirmation-ledger shape). And the seam becomes the new collision point: two people changing the interface across the boundary still collide, now in the one place with no merge machinery. THE TENSION WORTH KNOWING ABOUT: docs/org-scale-vision.md records the opposite destination — \"one graph the whole company plans in\", with the CEO's objectives at the top and everything tracing upward. Federation and one-big-graph cannot both be the end state, and nothing in the design has ever chosen between them. THE DISCRIMINATOR, offered as a finding and not a decision: depth alone does not justify a separate graph. Nesting three levels of graphs costs a coordinate, a roll-up and a freshness check at every seam, and buys nothing that a scope filter would not have delivered — unless something at that level is separately OWNED, separately RELEASED, or separately SHARED. Where those hold, a graph of its own is right. Where they do not, it is ceremony.","name":"OPEN — one graph with levels, or a graph per system composed into a bigger one?","rationale":"Recorded 2026-07-25 because Anthony said plainly he was not convinced by the collaboration design, and an unconvinced author is a finding rather than a disagreement to be argued down. PROMOTED THE SAME DAY on his word (\"let's promote both\"): the brainstorm produced two accepted requirements and stays open on the mechanism, which is the split that keeps both halves honest. req:analyse-at-any-level is the part he needed day to day and is ALREADY DELIVERED by cap:scoped-analysis (option (a), built first because it forecloses nothing). req:design-composes is the federation intent — a system's design as a unit that composes through interfaces — GOVERNED_BY this decision, so nothing gets built toward it until the mechanism is chosen. THIS DECISION THEREFORE STAYS PROPOSED, and that is not hedging: promoting an idea to intent is not the same act as choosing between three architectures, and collapsing this one would assert a shape Anthony has never chosen. Its options and the four hard parts of federation are unchanged above. The discriminator recorded then still stands as the thing to test when it is decided: depth alone does not earn a separate graph — ownership, separate release, or separate sharing does. NOTE FOR WHOEVER COLLAPSES IT: docs/org-scale-vision.md still records the opposite destination (one graph the whole company plans in), and req:design-composes now sits in the graph as accepted intent pointing the other way. That tension is real, on the record, and undecided; it is the strongest reason this decision should be made deliberately rather than discovered.","status":"proposed"}

{"decision":"RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony asked to think through the mechanics of using git to capture epoch and increment snapshots; these are the options and their costs, not a settlement.

THE TENSION THAT ORGANISES EVERYTHING: git can only store the past. A commit is something that happened. A planned epoch is a claim about a future that has not happened, so there is nothing for git to hold unless someone AUTHORS a speculative design and commits it.

(a) EPOCH BRANCHES — Anthony's original idea, 2026-07-28: "epoch branches: project_x:epoch_1 captures what we expect the graph to look like at epoch_1." A branch is a real place to work: you can draft a future design there, run the detectors on it, and diff it against main with machinery that already exists.
    Costs, recorded beside it rather than against it: a branch is a MOVING POINTER and a plan is a DATED CLAIM — when the plan changes the branch moves, and nothing records that it moved, which is exactly what `req:plans-move-honestly` needs. A speculative full export also restates the entire design to express a delta about a handful of requirements, so it is expensive to author and stale on the next merge to main. And N repos times M epochs is N times M branches, each drifting independently.

(b) PLANS LIVE ONLY IN THE GRAPH. A planned epoch is a node plus scheduled edges — no git object at all, because there is no past to point at. "What does the design look like at epoch 3" becomes a COMPUTED view (today's design plus what is scheduled to be satisfied by then) rather than a stored artifact.
    Cost: you cannot open a future design in an editor or run a detector over it as a whole; you get a projection, not a document.

(c) BOTH, SCOPED DIFFERENTLY — the shape the costs seem to point at. Branches are a fine WORKSPACE for exploring a future architecture and a poor RECORD of a plan. The record lives in the graph as a dated, versioned claim; a branch is somewhere to prototype one when a person wants to see it whole.

WORTH KNOWING BEFORE DECIDING: the forward half of the CAPABILITY view already exists in the vocabulary. `Release.status` is `planned | built | deployed | retired`, so a planned increment is expressible today. The forward half of the TIME view does not: `DesignEpoch.epoch_type` is `baseline | revision | milestone | incident_response | release_cut` with no value meaning "this has not happened yet". That asymmetry is real and is the smallest concrete gap found while thinking this through.","name":"OPEN — does a planned epoch live in git, or only in the graph?","rationale":"Anthony's idea and Anthony's question; recorded so the reasoning survives whichever way it goes. The framing "two paired views of the same architecture" and the epoch-branch mechanism are both his (2026-07-28), as is the request to work out the git mechanics (2026-07-30).

Not argued down: option (a) is recorded with its virtue stated first, because a branch genuinely is the only place you can look at a future design as a whole, and that is not nothing.","status":"proposed"}

{"decision":"RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL.

ANTHONY'S CLARIFICATION, 2026-07-30, and it corrects the framing this node was first written with: what he wants committed is NOT the realized product or a future codebase. It is a SLICE OF THE REFLOW2 GRAPH ITSELF — "this is the planned capabilities of epoch_1, epoch_2 … epoch_n" — so that he can open the repo and see "that is when I get capability X", or "capability Y is not expected until increment_13". His words: "it isn't the realized product/artifact of the project, but snapshot of the project at epoch or increment that I'm looking to capture in git." He is explicitly open to something other than git.

THE FIRST FRAMING HERE WAS WRONG AND IS CORRECTED. This node originally organised everything around "git can only store the past, and a plan is not a past". That is too glib. A plan document is a PRESENT artifact describing a future, and committing one is ordinary — git stores plans perfectly well. The real objection was never to committing plans; it was only ever to using BRANCHES as the record, and that narrower objection stands.

(a) BRANCH PER EPOCH — `epoch_1`, `epoch_2`, each holding a projected design. Matches the mental model directly: check out `epoch_n`, look.
    Costs: checking out a branch normally makes the whole REPO reflect that state, and here there is no future code to reflect, so the branch buys nothing the file would not. A full export is 1.6 MB today, so N epochs is N × 1.6 MB of near-identical JSON, rewritten on every replan. Branches also invite merge semantics that do not apply — nobody merges epoch_2 into main. And the plan's MOVEMENT stays invisible: a branch pointer moves silently, which is exactly what `req:plans-move-honestly` needs to see.

(b) A FILE PER EPOCH ON MAIN — `docs/design/epochs/epoch_3.{md,json}`. Browsing is easier than a checkout, there is one history rather than N, and every replan is an ordinary commit to that file.
    THE PROPERTY THIS BUYS FOR FREE: `git log -p docs/design/epochs/epoch_3.md` IS the plan's revision history. A large part of `req:plans-move-honestly` — "when a planned epoch's content moves, the plan's own change is a dated event on the record" — would be satisfied by git doing what git is good at, rather than by new machinery in reflow2.

(c) RENDER IT, DO NOT AUTHOR IT — and this is what (b) should probably be generated BY. An epoch slice is a VIEWPOINT. `tools/render_views.py` already renders viewpoints as pure projections of the graph, already confesses anything a view needs that the graph cannot supply, and ALREADY RENDERS THE EPOCH CHAIN BACKWARD ("Axis Z as a viewpoint: the epoch chain, and what happened at each"). The forward direction is the same renderer reading scheduled edges instead of recorded ones. Under this option the graph holds the schedule as single source of truth, the renderer emits one small file per epoch, and git holds their history.
    Cost: a generated file can go stale against the graph — which is a drift check reflow2 already knows how to do, and the same one `dataflow.html` staleness already gets in another repo.

WHAT A SLICE ACTUALLY CONTAINS, since "slice" is the word he used and it is much smaller than an export: the epoch and its date, capabilities expected by then, requirements expected satisfied, KPPs required by then, the version combination pinned once it arrives, and the delta against the previous epoch. Kilobytes, not megabytes.

THE OPEN QUESTION IS NARROWER THAN IT WAS: not "git or not git", but WHICH JOB GIT DOES. Git looks right for the HISTORY of the plan document and for pinning arrived epochs; the graph looks right for the schedule itself. The failure mode to avoid is making git the source of truth for the schedule, because then two places disagree about when capability X arrives and neither is wrong.","name":"OPEN — how per-epoch slices of the design become browsable: branches, files, or a rendered viewpoint","rationale":"Anthony's idea, his clarification, and his invitation to suggest something better; recorded so the reasoning survives whichever way it goes.

The snapshot at `epoch:wire-planning-cluster` holds the earlier wording.

Not argued down: option (a) is his own original mechanism and is recorded with the mental model it serves stated first. Its costs are listed beside it, not in place of it.","status":"proposed"}

A digest is a digest whichever dialect it arrives in (crates/reflow2-core/tests/checksum_dialect.rs) — 14 cases, 9 new for BL-160. PREFIX (BL-125): a bare hex digest matches its own `sha256:`-prefixed baseline and vice versa, the drift event id is identical whichever dialect was observed, and both counterweights hold — a genuinely different digest still reports `checksum_change` with its `realizes` edges intact, and a non-hex fingerprint is left verbatim. LENGTH (BL-160): a full 64-char digest matches a 16-char baseline and a truncated observation matches a full baseline, on the drift comparison AND on `set_artifact_checksum`'s would-move-the-baseline guard — the half that is not a gate problem at all but a BL-157 bulk sweep failing on every short-registered artifact for a change that never happened. When the two dialects agree the LONGER digest stays on the record, which also makes the accept idempotent ACROSS dialects: re-stating it coarsely mints one claim, not two. FIVE COUNTERWEIGHTS, and they are what keep the length rule from being a way to stop noticing: two FULL digests sharing their first sixteen characters are still drift (the case a truncate-both-to-N would pass); a truncated observation that disagrees WITHIN its own length is still drift; a genuinely different digest is still refused as a first baseline, still naming the disposition that would be honest; prefix tolerance does not escape the `sha256:` dialect, so `blake3:zz` and `blake3:zzzz` stay different; and an EMPTY digest agrees with nothing, because every string starts with the empty string. No minimum prefix length is imposed, deliberately — a short baseline is a weak baseline, but its strength is decided when it is REGISTERED, and a read side refusing to honour what the write side accepted is the same write/read disagreement this suite exists to close. WRITTEN BEFORE THE FIX: the four bug cases failed and all five counterweights passed. MUTATION-CHECKED SEVEN WAYS, each failing exactly the tests that name it: make agreement always-true and all seven counterweights fail while every bug case passes (which is what proves the counterweights carry the weight); revert to `==` and exactly the four bug cases fail; drop the sha256-dialect restriction and only the two dialect-boundary cases fail; truncate both sides to 16 and only the two sharing-a-prefix cases fail; drop the both-non-empty guard and only the empty-digest case fails; fix drift.rs alone and only the two accept-path cases fail; drop the longer-digest-wins rule and only the idempotence case fails. THE TEST WAS CORRECTED BY MEASUREMENT: the first version of the still-refused counterweight used a SHORT baseline, and against a 16-char baseline `NEAR` is a legitimate extension rather than a different digest — a 16-char baseline only ever pinned 16 characters, which was established by writing it wrong rather than assumed. PROVEN ON THE REAL DESIGN, and it is the row's own scenario replayed: the built binary driven over stdio JSON-RPC against a throwaway copy of reflow2's own 1221-node design, sweeping all 109 registered artifacts off the actual working tree with the FULL 64-char digest — 51 truncated baselines, all 51 unchanged, and the only 4 `checksum_change` findings are the four files this change edited. `tools/reflow2_check.py`'s Python workaround is DELETED, and tools/test_reflow2_check.py pins the pair end to end: an untouched file registered short gates GREEN, and the same short baseline on a genuinely edited file still gates RED.

Proven end to end over stdio with a genuinely exited server process: gone vs live, zero false overlaps, the ghost named in `stale`.

Manifest completeness, both directions: every content hash the graph references appears in the manifest with its original filename and what points at it; a referenced hash whose bytes are ABSENT is reported by name (the case someone holding only the export hits); a blob present but referenced by nothing is ALSO reported, because orphaned bytes are how a store silently grows; and `.gitattributes` marks the blob directory `binary`, pinned by a case that would otherwise let line-ending conversion corrupt a PNG. Content store round-trip and failure modes: the same bytes yield the same hash and are stored once; get(hash) returns exactly what put() took; a blob whose bytes no longer match its hash is REFUSED on read rather than returned (content addressing is only worth having if it is checked); a missing blob fails loud naming the hash and what referenced it; an interrupted write leaves no partial file, proven by writing to a temp path and renaming. PLANNED — written before the build so the shape of the proof is settled first.

The CONTRACT is checked, not the judgement. skill_lint asserts detect-and-ask states all of it: offer a reading; carry what would change it; present the options as a SELECTABLE list; put the RECOMMENDATION FIRST and mark it; give every option its consequence including the ones not recommended; and answer in the USER'S language, stated language-independently. Plus two negative checks that are the load-bearing half: NO served text hardcodes English as the answer language (so the rule cannot be implemented as English-only — the trap Anthony named), and NO requirement status, decision status or gap acknowledgement is written in the same act as a recommendation. Whether a recommendation is GOOD, and whether the language was correctly matched, are semantic and stay evidenced by trials — deliberately no LLM evals in CI. PLANNED.

PLUS the degree-zero Decision rule (2026-08-01, crates/reflow2-core/tests/unreachable_decision.rs, 6 cases): a Decision with NO edges in either direction is reported by `orphan_node`, Warning when its status is `accepted` and Info otherwise. FOUND BY RUNNING THE HEALTH SKILLS ON OUR OWN DESIGN AND DISBELIEVING THEM: check-health and detect-and-ask both returned clean — detect_defects 0, hierarchy_issues 0, dimension_drifts 0, propose_heal 0 operations — and a hand count of zero-degree nodes then found `dec:sanitize-spof-accepted`, an ACCEPTED single-point-of-failure disposition with no edges at all, the only one of five such dispositions not linked to what it disposes. `disconnected_community` cannot see it: it reports clusters of ≥2, and a node joined to nothing is never a cluster. THE STAKE IS NOT TIDINESS — a zero-degree Decision is unreachable by propagation so it never enters an impact analysis, and a disposition specifically can never EXPIRE, because expiry is computed from the affected set (`ver:reviewed-defects`), so a conditional judgement silently becomes permanent. THE RULE IS DEGREE-ZERO, AND MEASUREMENT CHOSE IT AGAINST THE STATED RECOMMENDATION: the narrow-looking form, an accepted Decision with no incoming GOVERNED_BY, fires on SIX of reflow2's own, five with degree 1–3 — connected, merely not through that edge. The nudge's counting AND its own promise are both trustworthy (tools/test_loop_nudge.py) — 47 cases, 11 new in BL-163 on top of the 8 across BL-161 and BL-111. BL-163 · PRECEDENCE, NOT PRESENCE: a session that edits code, records a ChangeEvent and never calls propagate_change is nudged — the defect was that the impact-check shape keyed on `changes == 0`, firing only when a session recorded NOTHING, so writing the ChangeEvents up AFTER the edits satisfied the very trigger meant to catch writing them up after the edits. ROOT CAUSE IN ONE LINE: `CHANGE_OPS` held `record_change` and `add_change_event`, both RECORDING ops, and no set counted `propagate_change` or `propagate_from` at all — the hook could not separate recording from looking because it never counted looking. THE COUNTERWEIGHT THE ROW DEMANDED AND THE CASE PINNED FIRST: a session that propagated gets NOTHING, and `propagate_from` counts as looking too, because the impact-check skill sends a speculative "what would this touch?" straight to it. THE CONJUNCTION IS THE GUARD, all three clauses load-bearing and each with its own test: `edits > 0` (a pure design session has no blast radius to compute), `changes > 0` (what keeps this from becoming a second, thresholdless bypass nudge), `propagates == 0`. BL-161'S PRECEDENT HELD: "you never propagated" is a NEGATIVE claim, so a tally rebuilt after an unreadable one drops it, exactly as "the graph was never consulted" does. THE WRITE NUDGE STILL TAKES PRECEDENCE and that test is not vacuous — disabling the write branch fails it. MUTATION-CHECKED SEVEN WAYS, each failing exactly the tests that name it: never count propagation (6 failures, both counterweights); drop `changes > 0` (7 failures, including BL-90's ENTIRE bypass family — the measurement that proves that clause is what stops this swallowing the older branch); drop `edits > 0` (1); drop `propagate_from` (1); drop the once-only claim (1); remove the branch entirely, i.e. ship the defect (5); and disable the write branch (14, including the precedence case). A FOURTH DEFECT WAS FOUND BY THE TESTS FAILING, not by reading: `update_state` re-serialises from an explicit key whitelist — a THIRD hand-kept copy of the state's key set beside `blank_state` and `parse_state` — so the new counter incremented in memory and was silently dropped on every write. That is BL-159's shape a third time, inside one file. BL-161 · STATE INTEGRITY: a 60-hook CONCURRENT burst against a seeded tally lands every increment and wipes no sticky field; against the pre-fix script the same burst returned touched=false, artifacts=0 and 6 of 60 edits, because a non-atomic write plus an error-swallowing read let one hook store zeros over the session's record. COUNTERWEIGHT: a tally rebuilt after an unreadable one keeps counting — an existing case required that and was right — but can no longer support the hook's negative claims, because the calls that would refute them are exactly what was lost; and the POSITIVE claim, "N writes went unchecked", still fires after a restart, so the flag is not an off switch. BL-111 · FIRES ONCE: a second stop CYCLE does not nudge again (the promise is per SESSION, and it rested on the harness's stop_hook_active, which is per cycle and never persisted), all THREE blocking branches keep it, and TWO CONCURRENT HOOK PROCESSES on the same Stop produce exactly ONE message — which is the case it was filed from and is not exotic, since reflow2 installs machine-wide AND a project may carry its own registration and the two command spellings do not dedupe. THE WORKED EXAMPLE IS THE ROW'S OWN: laser satellite refuelling, where the demonstrator and the fielded increment demand TRL 3 and TRL 7 of the SAME converter and get two different answers — which is the whole reason the threshold rides the edge rather than either endpoint. THE TWO REFUSALS ARE WHAT IS ACTUALLY PINNED: an increment with no stated threshold reports `ungated` and NEVER ready (mutating that verdict to achievable_now fails exactly the one test the item rests on), and a gate whose technology has no level and no clearing forecast makes the whole answer `indeterminate` — skipping it instead, and computing a date from the gates that happen to carry evidence, fails FIVE. REGRESSION PROOF, the step that makes this more than a decoration: the pins were temporarily reverted to dynograph-foundation v0.10.0 and the suite re-run. Cases (1) and (2) FAILED against the pre-fix build with exactly the reported symptom (SearchResult { hits: [] }) and PASS against v0.11.0; case (3) passes against both, correctly, since AND semantics also refused an unrelated question. A test that passes on the broken build proves nothing, so this was verified rather than assumed. Root cause fixed upstream in dynograph-foundation v0.11.0 (PRs #76, #77): TextIndex::search now matches tokens as a ranked disjunction — at least one token required, BM25 ordering — instead of requiring every token.

skill_lint.py — the contracts the build refuses to let drift, enforced in CI on every push. (1) THE SKILLS' contract with the served surface: every tool a skill names is served, the three mirrors are byte-identical, frontmatter, the standing rule, the tool-convention register and its description budget, the detect-and-ask obligations. (2) THE BUILD'S OWN GATE LIST (BL-159, 2026-08-01), four checks over AGENTS.md's "A change is done when all of these are clean" block and `.github/workflows/ci.yml` — two hand-kept records of one contract, where following the documented one exactly still produced a red build (PR #27). COVERAGE: every cargo/python3 gate ci.yml runs is either in the block or named in the blockquote as deliberately omitted, because a gate in neither is one a developer cannot know to run. FIDELITY: a listed gate is spelled exactly as CI runs it, FLAGS INCLUDED — and this is the load-bearing one the row did not ask for, because the defect that filed BL-159 was a flags difference on a gate that WAS listed (`-p reflow2-core` clippy lacking `-D warnings`), which coverage alone cannot see. Both rot directions are closed too: a documented gate ci.yml does not run, and an omitted name ci.yml has stopped running. THE SPLIT THAT KEEPS IT HONEST: the lint OBSERVES (is this line a gate at all — mechanical) and the document JUDGES (does it belong in the everyday subset — in AGENTS.md, where a human reads it). FOUND ON DAY ONE: `cargo test -p reflow2-core --no-default-features` and `test_check_doc_versions` sat in ci.yml and in neither list — the second being the exact trap the design anticipated, since `check_doc_versions` is a SUBSTRING of it and a substring match would have called it covered. MUTATION-CHECKED SEVEN WAYS, each failing exactly the check that names it: an undeclared gate in ci.yml → coverage; stripping `-D warnings` from the block → fidelity, which is BL-159's own defect reproduced; ci.yml dropping a listed gate → the phantom check; ci.yml dropping an omitted one → the stale-omission check; dropping the comment stripper → fidelity plus its own hermetic case; dropping the paragraph scoping → its two hermetic cases; dropping scoping AND the runner-word exclusion → the stale-omission check. THE CHECK CAUGHT A DEFECT IN ITSELF ON ITS OWN COMMIT: scanning the whole blockquote read the backticked words `cargo` and `python3` out of the new paragraph describing the lint and reported them as gates CI had stopped running. AND ONE REDUNDANCY IS REPORTED RATHER THAN HIDDEN — reverting the paragraph scoping ALONE leaves every real-file check green, because the runner-word exclusion covers the only two words today's prose backticks; the two are not redundant in general, so the scoping is pinned on synthetic text in tools/test_skill_lint.py where the redundancy cannot hide it. 14 hermetic cases there covering the parsing the real files cannot exercise.
